Recent research has thus focused on  reranking  approaches, where an initial set of candidate parse trees generated by a probabilistic parser are subsequently re-scored by a discriminative model aiming to distinguish high-quality parses from lower-quality ones (Farkas et al., 2008;Flor et al., 2014). These discriminative models can learn more complex and expressive features than probabilistic models, potentially leading to improved parsing accuracy. In this work, we explore a discriminative reranking approach based on tree kernels (TKs). Tree kernels provide a powerful framework for capturing structural similarities between trees, and have been successfully applied to various NLP tasks, including syntactic parsing and semantic role labeling (Collins & Duffy, 2002;Moschcowitz, 2004). However, applying TKs directly to discourse trees often falls short of its potential. Existing discourse tree kernels typically rely on simple node or subtree matching, failing to adequately capture the rich relational structure inherent in discourse representations. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach to discourse reranking using enhanced tree kernels. Specifically, we design new computational structures that represent key relationships within the discourse tree – capturing characteristics of rhetorical relations, span lengths, and hierarchical relationships between discourse units. These new structures, when combined with standard TKs, give rise to a family of novel discourse-specific tree kernels. The resulting reranker is trained to discriminate between correct and incorrect discourse trees, leveraging the expressive power of the enhanced tree kernels to learn complex structural patterns. Empirical evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant improvements in both sentence-level and document-level discourse parsing accuracy compared to state-of-the-art systems.

Temporal relation extraction (TRE) is a crucial subtask of information extraction, aiming to identify the temporal ordering between events described in text. Accurate temporal reasoning is fundamental for various downstream applications, including event timeline construction, question answering, and summarization (Chambers et al., 2016; Bethard et al., 2007; Grishman et al., 2013). Significant progress has been made in TRE, particularly using supervised machine learning techniques (Freitag et al., 2001; Sauri and Sporleder, 2008; Ning et al., 2018). However, most existing approaches focus on identifying temporal relations within a limited scope, such as individual sentences or closely adjacent sentences. These approaches often struggle to capture long-range temporal dependencies expressed across a broader discourse context. Consider the following example: “On Monday, the company announced its new CEO. The board meeting was held on Wednesday to officially approve the appointment. Following the meeting, the new CEO outlined her vision for the future.” While the temporal relations between "announced" and "held" and between "held" and "outlined" can be locally inferred from their sentence context, establishing the overall temporal ordering between “announced” and “outlined” requires a wider understanding of the document’s narrative flow. This illustrates the challenge of identifying discourse-level temporal relations, those spanning non-adjacent sentences, which are frequently encountered in real-world texts. Prior work has explored incorporating discourse information into TRE, primarily through enforcing coherence constraints on temporal relation types (Laju et al., 2006; Oepen et al., 2007). These methods typically focus on ensuring consistency among the relations identified within a local window, but rarely address the global optimization of temporal ordering across the entire document. Furthermore, existing methods often rely on hand-engineered features representing syntactic or semantic properties of events and discourse markers. In this paper, we address the challenge of discourse-level TRE by proposing a novel global inference model. Our approach moves beyond local sentence-level analysis and considers the entire document as a unified structure for inferring temporal relations between event mentions. This global perspective enables us to capture long-range dependencies and effectively resolve conflicts that arise from potentially ambiguous local cues. Moreover, we integrate discourse-level constraints derived from event semantics – recognizing inherent temporal properties and causality relationships between events – to further refine our inference process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a Chinese corpus specifically annotated for temporal relations, showing significant performance gains over strong baseline models that focus on local information.

Relation extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities in text – is a core component of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, including knowledge graph completion (Toutanova & Chen, 2015), question answering (Bordes et al., 2015), and information retrieval (Guo et al., 2016). Traditionally, RE systems have relied on manually annotated datasets, a time-consuming and expensive undertaking, particularly for complex or domain-specific relations. Distant supervision (DS) (Craven & Niebler, 2002) offers a compelling alternative, leveraging existing knowledge graphs (KGs) – such as Freebase, Wikidata, and DBpedia – to automatically generate training data by aligning entity pairs in text with known relations in the KG. However, a significant challenge in DS-RE is the  wrong labeling problem  (Mintz et al., 2009). Due to the many-to-one mapping from text to KG relations, the assumption that any sentence mentioning two related entities expresses that specific relation is often incorrect. This introduces substantial noise into the training data, hindering model performance. Numerous approaches have been proposed to mitigate this issue, broadly categorized into instance selection (Min et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2017) and relation-specific adaptation (Liu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017). Instance selection aims to identify and filter out noisy instances, while relation-specific adaptation focuses on learning more robust relation classifiers. Critically, most existing DS-RE methods treat relations in isolation, neglecting the inherent semantic structure and dependencies present in relation hierarchies. Real-world KGs are often organized hierarchically, reflecting is-a or subclass-of relationships between relations (e.g., “employed_by” is a subclass of “organization_affiliation”). This hierarchical structure embodies valuable semantic correlations; for instance, evidence supporting a higher-level relation like “organization_affiliation” often transfers to its subclasses, including “employed_by”, particularly when data for the subclasses is scarce. This is especially poignant for  long-tail relations  – those with limited instances in the KG and, consequently, fewer training examples generated via distant supervision. In this paper, we propose a novel Hierarchical Relation Extraction (HRE) framework that explicitly incorporates hierarchical information into the DS-RE process. We introduce a coarse-to-fine grained attention scheme to effectively model these hierarchical dependencies. Our model utilizes multiple layers of attention, progressively refining the focus from broader, more general relations to specific, fine-grained ones. This allows the model to leverage evidence from higher-level relations to bolster the representation of long-tail relations, thus improving their extraction accuracy. We demonstrate through comprehensive experiments on a large-scale benchmark dataset that our approach significantly outperforms existing baseline methods, showcasing the benefit of incorporating relational hierarchies into distantly supervised relation extraction.

Multi-label text classification – the task of assigning multiple, potentially overlapping categories to a given text – is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from news categorization and topic detection to biomedical information extraction. While significant progress has been made in this area, particularly with the advent of deep learning techniques, a persistent challenge remains: the inherent class imbalance present in many real-world datasets. This imbalance isn’t simply a matter of some labels being more prevalent than others; it manifests in a long-tailed distribution where a small number of “frequent” labels dominate, while a significant portion of labels fall into “few-shot” (very few examples) and “zero-shot” (no examples in the training data) categories. Traditional multi-label learning algorithms often struggle with these rare and unseen labels. Models trained on imbalanced datasets tend to favor the frequent classes, leading to poor performance on the less represented ones. This is particularly problematic in domains like medical text classification, where many disease codes or clinical findings are relatively uncommon. Ignoring these infrequent labels leads to incomplete, and potentially misleading, predictions. Moreover, the ability to accurately predict zero-shot labels – a critical capability for adapting to evolving knowledge bases and novel situations – remains largely unexplored in the context of large, structured label spaces. Existing approaches to address this challenge broadly fall into two categories: data augmentation techniques and meta-learning methods. Data augmentation aims to synthetically increase the number of examples for rare labels, but can introduce noise or fail to capture the underlying complexities of the data. Meta-learning approaches seek to train models that can quickly adapt to new tasks with limited data, but often require careful task design and can be computationally expensive. Furthermore, these methods often treat the label space as a flat, unstructured set, ignoring the valuable information encoded in hierarchical or relational structures between labels. In many domains, such as medicine (where ICD codes represent a hierarchical taxonomy of diseases), labels are not independent but are organized according to a meaningful structure. Exploiting this structure can considerably improve the generalization ability of models, especially for rare labels. For example, knowing that a patient is diagnosed with a specific type of pneumonia (a rare label) can be informed by the broader knowledge that they have a respiratory infection (a more frequent label). In this paper, we undertake a thorough investigation of multi-label few-shot and zero-shot learning with structured label spaces.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), the task of identifying the correct meaning (sense) of a word in context, remains a core challenge in Natural Language Processing despite decades of research. While significant progress has been made, particularly leveraging large knowledge resources like WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998) and employing sophisticated machine learning techniques, current systems persistently struggle with low-frequency senses (Verhagen, 2007; Mihalcea & Trusca, 2010). This disparity in performance across sense frequencies is a well-documented phenomenon, and stems fundamentally from a mismatch between the distribution of senses in training data and the distribution encountered in real-world text, effectively representing a data imbalance problem. The dominant approaches to address this issue have largely focused on increasing the quantity of labeled training data (e.g., through distant supervision or crowd-sourcing) or employing techniques that actively down-weight less frequent senses during training or inference. For example, work by Chen et al. (2014) proposes a knowledge-enhanced WSD system that incorporates external knowledge to improve the disambiguation of rare senses, while others have focused on utilizing contextual information to better estimate sense probabilities (e.g., using neural network models). A common, though often implicit, assumption is that  more data  is always better, or that selecting a single predominant sense is sufficient to drive performance. However, this assumption overlooks the crucial properties of the training data itself. Beyond simply the volume of data, factors such as the  provenance  of the data (i.e., where it comes from, and therefore what inherent biases it might contain) and, critically, the  balancing  of sense distributions within the training set, likely play a significant role in the effectiveness of WSD systems. A large corpus dominated by a few frequent senses may be less effective than a smaller, more carefully curated corpus with a more even distribution of senses, especially when evaluating all-words WSD, where encountering all possible senses is essential. In this paper, we systematically investigate the impact of these meta-properties – volume, provenance, and balancing – on WSD performance. We conduct a series of experiments using a state-of-the-art WSD system evaluated on the challenging SemEval-2013 English all-words task (Senseval/SemEval 2013). Our results demonstrate that while both volume and provenance are important considerations, achieving a better approximation of the ideal sense distribution within the training data leads to a substantial performance improvement – a 21-point gain in F1 score. Notably, this improvement is achieved using relatively simple features, and exceeds current state-of-the-art results by 14 points.

Understanding consumer opinions is paramount for businesses in the modern digital age. Social media platforms, such as Twitter and Facebook, have emerged as invaluable resources for gauging public sentiment and tracking the formation of opinions toward products, brands, and services. This wealth of data presents a unique opportunity to move beyond traditional market research methods and gain insights into  how  individuals’ opinions are shaped, particularly by their social networks. The study of opinion dynamics, also known as social influence modeling, seeks to unravel the mechanisms driving this process. While a substantial body of research exists in this area, much of it treats opinions as solely quantifiable values – represented either discretely (e.g., positive/negative) or continuously (e.g., a sentiment score between -1 and 1). This simplification often overlooks a crucial aspect: the semantic content underlying those opinions. People are not simply expressing a positive or negative feeling; they are articulating  reasons  for their opinions, based on features, attributes, and experiences. Existing work on opinion formation frequently focuses on modeling social network structure and its impact on opinion propagation (e.g., the Independent Cascade Model, Linear Threshold Model). These models demonstrate that network topology plays a significant role, but they often lack the capacity to incorporate the rich semantic information contained within the content of user expressions. Some approaches attempt to address this by considering sentiment as a function of weighted network connections, but still treat the sentiment itself as an abstract value detached from its textual origin. More recent efforts have explored the incorporation of topic models to represent the content, but frequently do so as a separate feature, without fully integrating it into the influence modeling process. In this paper, we propose a novel approach, the Content-based Social Influence Model (CSIM), designed to address these limitations. CSIM explicitly aims to capture the implicit mechanisms driving opinion change by simultaneously considering both the semantic content of expressed opinions and the influence of social relationships. Our model decomposes influence into two key components: (1)   opinion influence derived from content information  , capturing how the features and arguments presented in a message affect a user's opinion; and (2)   social relation factors  , representing the influence exerted by a user's connections within the social network. CSIM learns these components concurrently, effectively bridging the gap between structural and semantic aspects of opinion formation. The core innovation of CSIM lies in its ability to represent and leverage the semantic similarity between opinions expressed by different users.

Documenting the world’s linguistic diversity is a critical endeavor, yet it is frequently hampered by the resource constraints faced by field linguists. These linguists, working directly with native speakers, are tasked with eliciting and analyzing language data to create grammars, dictionaries, and other essential resources. A significant bottleneck in this process is the time-consuming nature of syntactic annotation – the process of identifying the grammatical relationships between words in a sentence. Traditional annotation relies heavily on manual effort, requiring linguists to painstakingly label each word with its part-of-speech and its dependencies to other words in the sentence. This is particularly challenging when dealing with previously unstudied languages where existing linguistic tools and resources are unavailable. To address this challenge, we investigate the application of dependency parsing – a core task in modern natural language processing – to language documentation in field linguistics. Dependency parsing aims to uncover the grammatical structure of a sentence by identifying head-dependent relationships between words. A dependency parser takes a sentence as input and outputs a tree-like structure representing these relationships. By automating this process, we aim to significantly accelerate syntactic annotation and empower field linguists to focus on higher-level linguistic analysis. However, a crucial challenge in applying dependency parsing to language documentation is the scarcity of labeled training data. Field linguists often begin their work with extremely limited resources, making it impractical to train high-performing parsers on large corpora. Therefore, this work focuses on  incrementally  learning a dependency parser, meaning adapting and improving the parser's performance as small amounts of annotated data become available. Our goal is to determine whether even limited training data can yield a parser useful for assisting with annotation, and to identify which parsing algorithms are best suited for this low-resource setting. To facilitate this research, we have created a novel parallel corpus specifically designed for the task of modeling spatial descriptions and motion events. These types of descriptions are commonly elicited by field linguists using pictures and video clips to encourage informant conversation and capture nuanced grammatical constructions. The corpus comprises descriptions of the same set of visual stimuli – pictures and short video clips – collected from native speakers of English, Spanish, German, and Egyptian Arabic. The parallel nature of the corpus allows us to compare parser performance across languages and to explore cross-lingual transfer learning techniques in future work. In this paper, we compare the performance of two widely used dependency parsers – MSTParser (McDonald et al., 2006) and MaltParser (Nivre et al., 2006) – when trained on incrementally increasing amounts of our newly created corpus.

Machine Translation (MT) has made significant strides in recent years, fueled by the rise of statistical and neural approaches. However, a persistent challenge remains: accurately translating named entities (names of people, organizations, locations, etc.). Traditional MT systems often struggle with names due to their low frequency, morphological complexity, and the fact they frequently defy typical translation patterns. A direct, literal translation can yield nonsensical or misleading results, while transliteration – converting the name using the target language's script – may obscure the entity's identity or significance. Existing approaches to address name translation often treat it as a post-editing task, or rely on separate, hand-crafted transliteration dictionaries. These methods lack the ability to integrate name processing seamlessly within the core MT framework. In this paper, we introduce a novel Name-aware Machine Translation (NMT) approach, designed to address these limitations. Our approach centers around the core principle that names should not be treated as ordinary words during the translation process. Instead, we advocate for a tightly integrated strategy where name processing is woven directly into the MT model. This is achieved through a multi-faceted process. First, we propose a method for jointly annotating parallel corpora with named entity tags and their corresponding translations. This provides the model with explicit supervision regarding correct name translations. Second, we leverage these annotations to extract name-aware translation grammar and rules, enriching the model's understanding of name translation patterns. Third, we augment the standard phrase table with dedicated name phrase entries, capturing frequently occurring name translations. Finally, we implement a name translation driven decoding mechanism, biasing the decoder to favor accurate name translations. Beyond improving name translation quality, we recognize that evaluating MT systems requires a nuanced understanding of linguistic importance. Traditional metrics, such as BLEU, treat all words equally, potentially overlooking the significance of informative words – including, crucially, named entities. Therefore, we also propose a new MT evaluation metric. This metric assigns differential weights to words based on their estimated importance within a document, allowing for a more accurate assessment of translation quality, particularly for content-bearing terms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our NMT approach through comprehensive experiments on Chinese-English translation. Our results consistently show significant improvements over a strong, high-quality MT baseline in terms of overall translation quality, the accuracy of name translations, and the quality of word alignments. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly incorporating name awareness into the MT process and provide a promising direction for future research in this area.

Human communication is a remarkably efficient process. Despite the inherent ambiguity of natural language, and the potential for misinterpretation, people routinely convey complex ideas to one another with surprising ease. This efficiency is often explained by appealing to principles of rationality and shared understanding. Perhaps the most influential account comes from Paul Grice (1975), who proposed that successful communication hinges on a “cooperative principle”: a tacit agreement among conversational participants to make contributions that are truthful, relevant, and appropriately informative. Grice formalized this principle with a set of “maxims” – guidelines governing the manner in which information is exchanged. While Grice’s framework provides a compelling description of communicative behavior, it leaves open the question of  why  these maxims are so consistently followed. Are they innate constraints on human cognition? Are they learned social norms? Or, are they a natural consequence of rational action in a multi-agent environment? This paper addresses the latter question, offering a novel perspective on the origins of Gricean communication. We argue that the cooperative principle and its associated maxims are not externally imposed rules, but rather  emergent  properties of rational decision-making in situations where agents must coordinate their actions through communication. Specifically, we demonstrate that Gricean behavior arises naturally within the framework of multi-agent decision theory, even when agents are equipped with only minimal cognitive capacities. Our core theoretical framework is the Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP). Dec-POMDPs provide a mathematically rigorous model of sequential decision-making in environments where agents have incomplete information and must reason about the beliefs and intentions of others (Shoham and Leyton-Brown, 2009). Crucially, our model does not assume any pre-programmed adherence to Gricean principles. Instead, rationality, defined as maximizing expected joint utility, is the sole driving force. To make the complex task of joint reasoning tractable, we incorporate cognitively-inspired heuristics that allow agents to approximate the beliefs of their collaborators. We investigate this emergent communication in a cooperative language game environment. In this setting, agents must effectively communicate to achieve a shared goal – in our case, identifying a target object. Our results demonstrate a striking correlation between rational decision-making within the Dec-POMDP framework and the adoption of Gricean communicative strategies. Agents that explicitly reason about the belief states of others, and tailor their utterances accordingly, exhibit behavior strikingly similar to human communication. Furthermore, this emergent Gricean behavior leads to a significant improvement in task performance, lending further support to the notion that these principles are fundamentally linked to successful collaboration.

The task of semantic parsing – mapping natural language sentences to formal meaning representations – has witnessed significant progress in recent years, driven by applications in question answering, dialogue systems, and information extraction. A central challenge in building semantic parsers is the acquisition of a grammar that effectively mediates between the surface form of language and its underlying meaning. Traditionally, these grammars have been handcrafted, a time-consuming and expertise-dependent process, and often brittle when applied to new domains or languages. Consequently, methods for automatically learning semantic parsers from data have become increasingly important. Early approaches to learning semantic parsers often relied on feature engineering and supervised learning techniques applied directly to parse trees or logical forms (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005; Liang et al., 2011). More recently, the focus has shifted towards learning the underlying grammar itself, often employing techniques like grammar induction or probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG) learning. However, many of these methods are tailored to specific meaning representations (e.g., lambda calculus) or languages, lacking the generality needed for broad applicability. For instance, work by Kwiatkowski et al. (2010) focused on learning CCG grammars for a specific question answering task, while others have targeted particular fragment of natural language. Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) provides an appealing framework for semantic parsing due to its compositional nature and ability to capture long-distance dependencies. Furthermore, the inherent flexibility of CCG allows for a more natural representation of different meaning representations. Existing approaches to learning CCG grammars for semantic parsing have typically focused on inducing grammars for specific meaning representations, often relying on simplified learning algorithms that restrict the hypothesis space (Stauffer, 2011; Dugas et al., 2014). These restrictions can limit the expressiveness of the learned grammar and hinder performance on complex sentences. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to inducing probabilistic CCG grammars directly from paired sentences and logical forms. Our method distinguishes itself through its generality – it is not tied to a specific language or meaning representation – and its expressive power, enabled by the use of higher-order unification. We define a rich hypothesis space containing all CCG grammars consistent with the observed data, using higher-order unification to represent variable binding in the logical forms. We then develop an efficient online learning algorithm that searches this hypothesis space while simultaneously estimating the parameters of a log-linear parsing model, allowing us to effectively balance grammar learning and parsing accuracy.

Coreference resolution, the task of identifying mentions in text that refer to the same real-world entity, is a fundamental problem in natural language processing (NLP). Accurate coreference resolution is crucial for a wide range of downstream applications, including machine translation, question answering, text summarization, and information extraction (Barrón-Cedillo, 2009;Diósy et al., 2013). Traditionally, coreference resolution has relied heavily on supervised learning techniques, which require large amounts of manually annotated data. While supervised methods have achieved high accuracy, the cost and effort associated with annotation limit their applicability to new domains or languages. Consequently, there is significant interest in developing unsupervised coreference resolution methods that can perform well without labeled training data. Existing unsupervised approaches typically rely on various heuristics, such as string matching, pronoun resolution rules, and distributional similarity (Soon et al., 2001;Ng and Cardie, 2002;Daumé III, 2007). More recently, approaches leveraging clustering algorithms and graph-based methods have gained prominence (Florian et al., 2004;Benzmann and Niekler, 2009). However, many unsupervised methods struggle to balance precision and recall, often plagued by a large number of false positives. A key challenge lies in effectively identifying the most relevant relationships between mention pairs without the guidance of labeled examples. Many approaches consider all possible relations between mention pairs equally, leading to noisy inferences and reduced performance. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised coreference resolution method that explicitly focuses on identifying and utilizing the  most informative  relations between mention pairs. Our approach is built on a precision-oriented inference framework where a candidate entity for a given mention is scored based on the strength of its relation to the original mention. Crucially, we introduce an ‘informativeness score’ that dynamically assesses the precision of these relations with respect to coreference decisions. This informativeness score is not predefined but rather learned robustly through an iterative expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. By prioritizing the most informative relations, our system aims to minimize spurious links and improve overall coreference accuracy. We hypothesize that not all mention pair relationships contribute equally to determining coreference. For example, a shared noun phrase and a preceding pronoun are likely more indicative of coreference than two distant noun phrases with dissimilar semantic characteristics. Our informativeness score attempts to capture this intuition, highlighting the relations most likely to signal true coreference links. Through experiments on standard benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing unsupervised coreference resolution systems, achieving significant gains in both precision and F1-score.

The field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has witnessed a paradigm shift with the rise of deep learning techniques. While these methods have achieved remarkable success across a range of tasks, they often rely on representing linguistic units – such as characters or words – as discrete, one-hot encoded vectors. This approach, while simple, can discard valuable linguistic information and limit the model’s ability to generalize (Bengio et al., 2003; Mikolov et al., 2013). Increasingly, researchers are exploring the benefits of incorporating linguistically motivated, information-rich representations into neural network architectures (Coté, 2017; Kann et al., 2018). This paper contributes to this trend by introducing PanPhon, a novel resource designed to bridge the gap between phonetic symbols and their underlying articulatory properties. PanPhon is a database meticulously constructed to map over 5,000 International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) segments to 21 subsegmental articulatory features. These features – encompassing characteristics such as tongue body height, tongue backness, lip rounding, and glottal constriction – provide a detailed description of  how  each sound is produced. This contrasts sharply with the purely symbolic representation offered by the IPA itself. The core premise behind PanPhon is that providing models with articulatory information will allow them to capture phonetic similarities and distinctions that are lost in simple IPA representations. This is based on established phonetic theory, and recent work applying articulatory phonology to speech recognition (Ladefoged & Johnson, 2015). We hypothesize that leveraging PanPhon’s rich feature set can enhance performance on various NLP tasks, particularly those sensitive to morphological and phonetic patterns. To test this hypothesis, we evaluated PanPhon’s effectiveness in Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Orthography-to-IPA conversion. We integrated PanPhon features into neural Conditional Random Field (CRF) models – a common choice for sequence labeling tasks like NER – and compared their performance against strong baseline models relying solely on character-based representations. Our experiments, conducted on monolingual NER tasks for Spanish and Turkish, demonstrate that phonologically aware models built on PanPhon features achieve performance comparable to character-based models. Significantly, and perhaps more importantly, when applied to cross-lingual transfer scenarios (specifically, transferring knowledge from Uzbek to Turkish), PanPhon-enhanced models outperform their character-based counterparts. This suggests that the articulatory features provide a stable and generalizable representation that facilitates knowledge transfer between languages. Furthermore, we demonstrate a measurable contribution of PanPhon features to the task of converting orthographic representations to their corresponding IPA transcriptions. This work demonstrates the value of incorporating articulatory features to language models, delivering an accessible resource and demonstrating its impacts across multiple NLP tasks.

Modern dialog systems are increasingly expected to handle complex, multi-turn interactions with users. A core component enabling such interactions is the dialog manager, responsible for interpreting user input and determining the system’s appropriate response. Crucially, this relies on accurately identifying the  user intent  behind each utterance. Traditionally, dialog systems have relied on manually crafted rules or carefully annotated training data to map user inputs to predefined intents. However, this approach is brittle, expensive to maintain, and struggles to generalize to unseen variations in user language. As dialog systems move towards open-domain interactions and support a wider range of user needs, the need for more robust and scalable intent recognition methods becomes paramount. One promising avenue is to leverage unsupervised or semi-supervised learning techniques to automatically group user questions into intents. This is particularly valuable in the early stages of dialog system development, where identifying the key user intents is a non-trivial task. However, directly applying standard clustering algorithms to textual data, such as user questions, often yields suboptimal results due to the inherent semantic ambiguity and shortness of the input. Questions often rely on implicit context and require a strong understanding of natural language to accurately determine their underlying intent. Recent advancements in question duplicate detection and semantic textual similarity (STS) offer a potential solution. Models trained to identify paraphrases or semantically equivalent questions have demonstrated remarkable performance in capturing nuanced meaning. We hypothesize that these models can be effectively adapted to the intent clustering problem, providing a strong semantic foundation for grouping questions. However, simply applying these models as a similarity metric within a traditional clustering framework overlooks the structured nature of the output – namely, the desired grouping of questions into distinct intent categories. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to supervised clustering that combines the power of semantic classifiers learned from question duplicate research with a structured output learning framework. Our method leverages pre-trained semantic models to generate similarity scores between questions and then employs a supervised learning algorithm to explicitly optimize for clustering performance as measured by established intent clustering evaluation metrics. This allows the model to learn the relationships between questions and intents directly, resulting in more accurate and coherent clusters. We evaluate our approach on two publicly available intent clustering corpora, for both English and a second language, demonstrating substantial improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

Sentiment analysis has become a cornerstone of natural language processing, enabling applications ranging from market research to social media monitoring. While significant progress has been made in identifying the overall sentiment of a document, a crucial yet often overlooked challenge lies in accurately determining the sentiment expressed towards specific entities or concepts within that document – a task known as aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA). However, even within ABSA, a subtle complexity arises when dealing with  collocations , particularly those exhibiting polarity inversion. A collocation, in this context, refers to a pairing of a polarity word (e.g., “long,” “strong,” “hard”) with a target word or phrase (e.g., “battery life,” “coffee,” “labor”). Crucially, the sentiment orientation conveyed by the polarity word is not fixed but is dependent on the specific target it modifies. For example, “long battery life” carries a positive sentiment, while “long startup” carries a negative sentiment. This phenomenon is often referred to as polarity inversion or contextual polarity shifting. Traditional approaches to sentiment analysis and even many ABSA systems predominantly rely on analyzing the local context surrounding a target to infer its sentiment. For instance, a system might look at the words immediately preceding and following a collocation to determine its overall polarity. However, this approach is fundamentally limited by the sparsity and often insufficient expressiveness of such local contexts. The information required to disambiguate a collocation’s polarity may not be readily available within the immediate vicinity of the collocation itself. Consider the example “strong coffee.” While nearby words may offer clues, a truly robust system needs access to a broader understanding of the typical sentiment associations between "strong" and different types of beverages. To address this limitation, we propose a novel, unsupervised framework for collocation polarity disambiguation that leverages the vast resource of information available on the web. Recognizing that a collocation’s sentiment is often implicitly encoded in the way it is used in various contexts, we aim to augment limited local contexts with  pseudo contexts  derived from web search results. The core idea is to identify sentences containing the target word alongside the polarity word, treating these web-harvested sentences as representative instances of the collocation’s usage. These pseudo contexts, significantly expanding the scope beyond merely local windows, offer a richer and more informative basis for determining the collocation’s polarity. Our approach unfolds in three key components: (1) web query generation, employing strategic search terms to retrieve relevant pseudo contexts; (2) polarity extraction from the downloaded web snippets using existing sentiment analysis tools; and (3) polarity aggregation, combining the extracted polarities to arrive at a final disambiguated polarity score for the collocation.

Dialogue systems are rapidly evolving, transitioning from simple task-oriented bots to more sophisticated conversational agents capable of engaging in extended, multi-turn interactions. A crucial component enabling these more advanced systems is the ability to understand and maintain  context  – specifically, the ongoing  topic  of conversation. Accurate dialogue topic tracking is therefore essential for effective dialogue management, personalized responses, and ultimately, a more natural and engaging user experience. This task, formally defined as recognizing the topic state at each turn in a dialogue, presents significant challenges. Unlike single-sentence topic classification, dialogue topic tracking necessitates modelling not only the semantic content of each utterance but also the conversational flow and dependencies between utterances across multiple turns. Early approaches to dialogue topic tracking relied heavily on hand-crafted features, such as bag-of-words representations, n-grams, and lexical chains (Galley et al., 2003; Stolcke et al., 2000). While these methods demonstrated some success, they often struggled to capture the nuanced semantic relationships and long-range dependencies inherent in natural language dialogue. More recently, machine learning techniques, including Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), have been employed to improve performance (Wong et al., 2004; Papineni et al., 2007). These models allowed for more sophisticated sequential modelling, but still typically relied on carefully engineered features. The recent resurgence of deep learning has opened up new opportunities for dialogue topic tracking. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) offer the potential to automatically learn complex representations directly from raw textual data, bypassing the need for manual feature engineering. Specifically, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have proven effective in capturing local semantic patterns within individual sentences (Kim, 2014), while Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), particularly LSTMs and GRUs, excel at modelling sequential data and capturing long-range dependencies (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Cho et al., 2014). In this paper, we explore the application of both CNNs and RNNs to the task of dialogue topic tracking. We propose several neural network architectures, leveraging the strengths of each approach. Our models incorporate CNNs to encode the semantic content of individual utterances and RNNs to model the conversational context across multiple turns. Through extensive experimentation on human-human conversation data, we demonstrate that our proposed models significantly improve upon existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance in topic tracking accuracy. This work contributes to the growing body of research examining deep learning techniques for dialogue understanding and lays the foundation for more robust and adaptive dialogue systems.

Aspect extraction, the task of identifying the specific attributes or features of entities that are discussed in text, is a crucial step in fine-grained sentiment analysis and opinion mining. Unlike simply determining the overall sentiment expressed towards an entity, aspect extraction allows for a more nuanced understanding of  what  specifically people like or dislike. For example, understanding that a customer review expresses positive sentiment towards the “battery life” but negative sentiment towards the “camera” of a smartphone is far more informative than merely knowing the overall sentiment is mixed. A prevalent approach to aspect extraction relies on unsupervised topic modeling (Titov & McDonald, 2008; Mei et al., 2007). Techniques like Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) are often employed to discover latent topics within a corpus of reviews, with each topic ideally representing a distinct aspect. However, despite their popularity, unsupervised topic models often struggle to generate coherent and interpretable aspects. This is because they lack the ability to leverage domain-specific knowledge or prior information about the potential aspects that might be discussed. The resulting topics can be noisy, overlapping, and difficult to map to meaningful attributes. To address these limitations, researchers have explored knowledge-based approaches. These methods incorporate prior knowledge, often provided manually by human experts, to guide the topic modeling process (Lin & Jiang, 2016; Bian et al., 2017). For instance, a predefined lexicon of aspect-related terms can be used to bias the model towards discovering topics that align with those terms. While effective, these knowledge-based approaches suffer from a significant drawback: the reliance on manual curation of prior knowledge. Creating and maintaining such knowledge bases is a costly and time-consuming endeavor, particularly for applications dealing with a large number of diverse domains. Moreover, the quality of the extracted aspects is highly dependent on the accuracy and completeness of the provided knowledge. In this paper, we argue that the widespread availability of large-scale review data on the Web presents a unique opportunity to overcome these limitations. We propose a novel framework for aspect extraction that automates the process of prior knowledge learning, eliminating the need for manual input. This is a significant step forward, particularly in the “big data” era where vast amounts of unlabeled text are readily available. Our approach leverages the collective wisdom embedded within these large corpora to discover implicit relationships between terms and entities, forming a rich source of prior knowledge.

Dependency parsing, the task of analyzing the grammatical structure of a sentence by establishing relationships between words, has seen significant progress in recent years. A widely adopted paradigm involves scoring candidate parse trees using a linear model trained on a set of features (McDonald et al., 2005; Nivre et al., 2007). These features are typically defined using templates – predefined patterns that examine specific aspects of the dependency tree, such as the words themselves, their part-of-speech tags, or their morphological properties. The combination of these properties, as defined by the templates, constitutes the final feature value. While effective, this template-based approach suffers from a critical limitation: the feature space is effectively hand-engineered and, as a result, is restricted to a carefully curated subset of all possible combinations. The reason for this restriction stems from both statistical and computational constraints. A naive expansion of the template set leads to a combinatorial explosion in the number of features, increasing the risk of overfitting and demanding substantial computational resources for training and parsing. Consequently, developers are often forced to prioritize templates based on linguistic intuition or empirical experimentation, potentially overlooking valuable combinations that could improve parsing accuracy. In this paper, we present a novel approach to dependency parsing that mitigates these limitations by leveraging the power of kernel methods. Specifically, we introduce a  template kernel  – a kernel function designed to implicitly represent a vastly larger feature space than is practical with traditional explicit feature representations. Our kernel allows us to score parse trees based on combinations of template properties without explicitly enumerating and storing all possible features. This substantially expands the representational capacity of the model while maintaining computational efficiency. The core idea behind our approach is that the kernel function computes a similarity measure between parse trees based on their shared template-based properties. It implicitly defines a feature space where each dimension corresponds to a potential template combination, and the kernel value represents the degree to which two parses activate that combination. By operating directly on the kernel values, we avoid the need for explicit feature extraction and storage, considerably reducing memory requirements and enabling the exploration of a far richer feature space. We integrate this template kernel into a parse reranking system, utilizing the output of a baseline parser as input. This allows us to refine existing parses by leveraging the expressive power of the kernel. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on four languages – Arabic, Chinese, German, and Japanese – from the CoNLL-X shared task, achieving significant improvements over strong baseline systems.

Knowledge Base Population (KBP) is a central task in Natural Language Processing, aiming to automatically expand and refine existing knowledge bases (KBs) like Freebase and Wikidata. The goal is to extract relational facts from unstructured text, enriching the KB with new entities, relations, and attributes. Recent years have witnessed significant progress in KBP, spurred by shared tasks like the Automatic Knowledge Base Construction (AKBC) workshop series, which feature challenging tasks such as Cold Start Slot Filling (CSSF) and Tri-lingual Entity Discovery and Linking (TEDL). These tasks necessitate robust and adaptable systems capable of handling incomplete information and diverse linguistic phenomena. Traditionally, KBP systems have relied on supervised learning methods, leveraging labeled data to train models for relation extraction, entity linking, and slot filling. These approaches often achieve high performance when sufficient labeled data is available. However, KBP inherently suffers from data sparsity—new entities and relations constantly emerge, and obtaining labeled data for every possible combination is impractical. This limitation motivates the development of unsupervised and distant supervision techniques, which leverage existing KB structures and large, unlabeled corpora to automatically generate training data or directly infer facts. While unsupervised methods offer scalability and adaptability, they often struggle to match the accuracy of supervised approaches, especially in complex scenarios. Consequently, a natural strategy is to combine the strengths of both paradigms—leveraging the precision of supervised models with the coverage of unsupervised methods. Ensembling techniques, which aggregate the predictions of multiple systems, provide a powerful means of achieving this synergy. Existing ensembling methods range from simple averaging to more sophisticated techniques like stacking, where a meta-learner is trained to combine the outputs of base learners. In this paper, we present a novel algorithm that combines supervised and unsupervised ensembles for KBP. Our approach goes beyond simply averaging predictions; it dynamically weights the contributions of different systems based on their performance on a development set and their agreement with the KB itself. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique on the CSSF and TEDL tasks from the 2015 KBP competition. Remarkably, our system outperforms the top-performing system in both competitions, as well as several standard ensembling baselines and a state-of-the-art stacking approach. The success of our method across two distinct and challenging KBP tasks highlights its generality and potential for broader application. This paper details our algorithm, experimental setup, and a thorough analysis of the results, demonstrating the power of a carefully constructed combined supervised-unsupervised ensemble for knowledge base population.

Distributed representations of words, also known as word embeddings, have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP). Introduced initially by Bengio et al. (2003) and popularized by Mikolov et al. (2013), these representations map words from a high-dimensional, sparse, one-hot encoded space into a lower-dimensional, dense, continuous vector space. This transformation captures semantic and syntactic relationships between words, enabling substantial improvements in performance across a wide range of NLP tasks, including language modeling (Bengio et al., 2003), machine translation (Cho et al., 2014), and sentiment analysis (Socher et al., 2013). A key advantage of these representations is their ability to mitigate data sparsity issues inherent in many supervised learning approaches. By representing words as dense vectors, the model can generalize better to unseen words or phrases, especially when trained on large amounts of unlabeled text. The success of word embeddings has spurred a great deal of research into methods for inducing these representations, primarily relying on unlabeled text data. Techniques such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in learning meaningful word representations from monolingual corpora. However, these methods typically operate on a language-by-language basis, resulting in separate embedding spaces for different languages. This poses a challenge for crosslingual NLP tasks, where the goal is to leverage knowledge learned from one language to improve performance in another. In this work, we address the challenge of learning crosslingual word representations by jointly inducing embeddings for a pair of languages. Our approach frames the problem as a multitask learning task, where each “task” corresponds to predicting the context surrounding a given word. The relatedness between tasks is determined by co-occurrence statistics gleaned from bilingual parallel data – that is, text available in both languages. By learning shared representations informed by parallel data, our method seeks to align the embedding spaces of the two languages, enabling effective transfer of knowledge and improved performance on crosslingual tasks. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on crosslingual document classification, a representative crosslingual learning task. Our results demonstrate that classifiers trained using our crosslingual representations outperform strong baselines, including traditional machine translation-based approaches, when applied to test data in a new language. This demonstrates the utility of our induced representations in bridging the gap between languages and enabling efficient crosslingual transfer learning. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work in crosslingual representation learning.

Style transfer, the task of automatically altering the stylistic characteristics of text while preserving its semantic content, has emerged as a vibrant area of research within natural language processing (NLP). The potential applications are broad, ranging from enhancing the readability of technical documents to adapting communication to different social contexts or audiences (Rude et al., 2019;Lample et al., 2019). A compelling example is the transformation of text along a formality spectrum – converting informal language (e.g., social media posts, casual conversations) into a more formal tone (e.g., professional emails, academic writing), and vice versa. However, despite increasing interest and some promising initial results, progress in formality style transfer has been hampered by a critical bottleneck: a dearth of high-quality, large-scale datasets specifically designed for this task, coupled with a lack of standardized benchmarks and reliable evaluation metrics. Existing datasets for style transfer are often small, limited in scope, or focus on stylistic attributes other than formality (Fu et al., 2018;Shen et al., 2017). This scarcity restricts the training of robust models and makes it difficult to fairly compare different approaches. Furthermore, evaluating the success of style transfer is non-trivial. While preserving semantic meaning is paramount, assessing stylistic changes accurately requires careful consideration. Traditional metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) – commonly used in machine translation – often fail to capture subtle stylistic nuances and may even penalize desirable transformations. Human evaluation is considered the gold standard, but is expensive, time-consuming, and susceptible to subjective biases. To address these challenges, we introduce the GYAFC dataset (Get Your Act Formal, Corpus), a substantial resource specifically curated for formality style transfer. Constructed from a diverse range of online sources, GYAFC comprises [mention dataset size - e.g., over 150,000] sentence pairs, each consisting of an informal and a formal version of the same content. To facilitate reproducibility and encourage further research, we establish clear benchmark tasks based on GYAFC and provide a detailed analysis of commonly used automatic metrics, highlighting their strengths and limitations in the context of formality style transfer. Recognizing the success of sequence-to-sequence models in machine translation and their ability to capture long-range dependencies, we also explore the application of established machine translation techniques as strong baselines for formality style transfer. Our experiments demonstrate that these methods achieve surprisingly competitive performance, establishing a solid foundation for future advancements and prompting further investigation into the applicability of transfer learning from related NLP tasks.

The meaning of a word is not static; it’s remarkably fluid, shaped by the context in which it’s used and the community employing it. This dynamic nature of word semantics presents a significant challenge in natural language processing (NLP). While traditional lexical resources like WordNet offer a valuable foundation, they often fall short of capturing the subtle, nuanced meaning shifts that occur within specific domains, communities, or even time periods (Resnik & Baroni, 2006). Consider the word “sick,” for instance. In a general context, it denotes illness; however, within certain online communities, particularly those centered around extreme sports or artistic expression, “sick” functions as a positive descriptor, signifying something impressive or excellent. This variation underscores the need for methods that can identify and characterize domain-specific word semantics – moving beyond a one-size-fits-all approach to word meaning. Recent advancements in distributional semantics, particularly the use of word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), have provided powerful tools for representing word meaning as dense vectors in a high-dimensional space. These embeddings capture semantic relationships based on word co-occurrence patterns. A common extension of this approach is to leverage the first principal component of word embeddings to approximate the sentiment axis (Kiritchenko et al., 2014). While effective in many cases, this method inherently limits our understanding of semantics to a single dimension – sentiment – neglecting the rich tapestry of other domain-specific meanings that may be embedded within the vector space. This paper introduces SEMAXIS, a lightweight framework designed to address this limitation. SEMAXIS expands upon existing methods by identifying and characterizing  multiple  semantic axes within word vector spaces. Instead of solely focusing on sentiment, SEMAXIS utilizes a variety of techniques to uncover axes representing diverse semantic dimensions relevant to specific domains. We hypothesize that these axes, when considered collectively, provide a more comprehensive and accurate representation of domain-specific word semantics. To validate this hypothesis, we conduct experiments across a range of online communities, demonstrating SEMAXIS’s ability to detect nuanced semantic variations. Furthermore, we show that even when applied to the sentiment axis specifically, SEMAXIS outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in the creation of domain-specific sentiment lexicons. Our framework's simplicity and effectiveness make it a valuable addition to the toolkit of researchers aiming to understand and harness the dynamic nature of word meaning in diverse contexts. Resnik, P., & Baroni, M. (2006).

Paraphrase generation, the task of expressing the same meaning using different words, is a core problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from text simplification and machine translation to dialogue systems and information retrieval. Traditionally, this task has been approached using rule-based methods (Barzilay & McKeown, 2001;Johnson et al., 2007), statistical machine translation (SMT) (Callison-Burch et al., 2008;Madnani et al., 2011), and more recently, neural network models (Chung et al., 2014;Cho et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015). Among these, sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models with attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2015;Luong et al., 2015) have become dominant due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies and generate grammatically fluent paraphrases. However, despite their success, seq2seq models often struggle with semantic adequacy. They tend to memorize frequent phrases and patterns from the training data, leading to paraphrases that are syntactically correct but lack genuine semantic variation or introduce unintended meaning changes (Li et al., 2018;Zhao et al., 2018). This memorization issue is particularly problematic when dealing with limited training data or when the target paraphrase requires a significant shift in wording and conceptualization. The core issue we identify is that these models often operate at the surface level of text—predicting words based on their sequential context—rather than reasoning about the underlying semantic representations. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that explicitly leverages distributed word representations (i.e., word embeddings) during paraphrase generation. Our model, termed the Word Embedding Attention Network (WEAN), operates within the encoder-decoder framework, but differs fundamentally in how it generates output words. Instead of directly predicting words from the vocabulary, WEAN  queries  the embedding space to identify words whose embeddings best match the desired semantic context. This process encourages the model to focus on meaning rather than relying on superficial similarities between input and output sequences. Specifically, WEAN utilizes a novel attention mechanism that not only attends to the encoder's hidden states, but also attends to the word embeddings themselves. By incorporating information from the embedding space, the decoder can better capture the semantic relationships between words and generate more appropriate paraphrases. The model essentially learns to represent the desired meaning as a point in the embedding space and then searches for the words that are closest to that point. We evaluate WEAN on two prominent paraphrase-oriented tasks: English text simplification (STS) and Chinese short text abstractive summarization. These tasks present different challenges and require varying degrees of semantic transformation.

Sentiment classification, the task of determining the emotional tone expressed in text, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its broad range of applications, including opinion mining, market research, and customer feedback analysis (Pang and Lee, 2008;Liu, 2012). Traditional sentiment classification approaches typically rely on supervised learning techniques trained on labeled datasets, often specific to a particular domain, such as movie reviews, product reviews, or social media posts. However, acquiring large, labeled datasets for every domain is expensive and time-consuming. This limitation motivates research into cross-domain sentiment classification, where models trained on one or more source domains are applied to a new, unseen target domain. A key challenge in cross-domain sentiment classification is domain adaptation—addressing the discrepancy between the feature distributions of the source and target domains (Ben-David et al., 2010). Various techniques have been proposed to tackle this challenge, including feature-based approaches (Blitzer et al., 2006), instance-based approaches (Dai et al., 2014), and parameter-based approaches (Glorot et al., 2011). More recently, joint sentiment-topic (JST) modeling has emerged as a promising framework for sentiment classification, simultaneously discovering latent topics and sentiment orientations within text (Lin and He, 2009;Blei and Ng, 2009). JST models capitalize on the inherent relationship between topics and sentiment, reasoning that different topics may evoke different sentiments. The original JST model, and many subsequent variations, offer a significant advantage: they only require domain-independent polarity word priors for learning, reducing the need for extensive labeled data. This characteristic makes them particularly attractive for cross-domain adaptation scenarios. However, leveraging the full potential of JST models requires effective exploration and utilization of the learned topics. Prior work often treats these topics as latent variables without explicit consideration of their polarity-bearing nature. In this paper, we build upon the foundational JST model, focusing on enhancing the extraction of polarity-bearing topics – topics that are strongly associated with either positive or negative sentiment. We propose a modification to the JST model that effectively incorporates word polarity priors by modulating the topic-word Dirichlet priors. This allows the model to naturally gravitate towards extracting topics that are aligned with specific sentiment orientations. We then demonstrate that augmenting the original feature space with these polarity-bearing topics significantly improves the performance of in-domain supervised classifiers. Specifically, we achieve state-of-the-art results on a movie review dataset and competitive results on a multi-domain sentiment dataset.

Dependency parsing has become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, providing a rich structural representation of sentence meaning that underpins many downstream applications such as information extraction, machine translation, and question answering (Kübler et al., 2009; McDonald et al., 2013). The standard evaluation metric for dependency parsing, Parseval (Black et al., 1999), focuses on labeled attachment score (LAS) and unlabeled attachment score (UAS), measuring the accuracy of predicting both the head and the dependency relation between words. While Parseval has served the community well, its limitations as a comprehensive assessment of parsing capability are increasingly acknowledged (Nivre et al., 2007; McDonald and Nivre, 2011). Specifically, Parseval predominantly evaluates local dependencies – connections between adjacent or closely related words in the sentence – and often overlooks the ability of a parser to correctly identify  unbounded dependencies . Unbounded dependencies, also known as long-distance dependencies, refer to relationships between words where the intervening span is not limited by syntactic constraints like immediate dominance or adjacency. These dependencies typically arise from constructions such as relative clauses, wh-questions, topicalization, and scrambling. While they may be relatively infrequent in typical corpora, accurately resolving these long-range connections is crucial for a complete understanding of sentence structure and meaning. Failures in capturing unbounded dependencies can lead to misinterpretations and errors in downstream tasks. To address this gap, and to provide a more nuanced evaluation of parsing technology, this paper introduces a new evaluation corpus specifically designed to assess the recovery of unbounded dependencies. The corpus contains approximately 700 sentences annotated with seven different grammatical constructions that frequently exhibit these challenging dependencies. We evaluate a range of state-of-the-art dependency parsers on this corpus, reporting LAS and UAS scores specifically for the unbounded dependency relations. The results, ranging from 25% to 59% accuracy, are significantly lower than those typically reported on standard benchmark datasets, highlighting a substantial deficiency in current parsing systems’ ability to handle long-distance relationships. These findings raise critical questions about the validity of relying solely on Parseval scores as a generalized measure of parsing competence. We argue that a parser’s ability to handle unbounded dependencies, despite their relatively low frequency, is a key indicator of its overall linguistic understanding. We further analyze the error patterns made by one of the more successful parsers on this corpus, providing insights into the specific challenges contributing to the low performance and pointing to potential avenues for future research.

The demand for effective Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) systems is continuously rising, fueled by the increasing number of non-native English speakers and the desire for personalized, accessible language instruction. A critical component of such systems is the ability to automatically detect and correct errors in learner writing, providing timely and targeted feedback. While significant progress has been made in Natural Language Processing (NLP) in recent decades, error correction in learner language remains a challenging task due to the unique characteristics of learner errors – which often deviate systematically from native-like language in ways not easily captured by standard language models. Traditional approaches to grammatical error correction (GEC) often rely on large, natively-produced corpora to train statistical language models (LMs) or classify erroneous spans. Language models, such as n-gram models or neural network-based LMs, excel at fluency assessment and suggestion of plausible alternatives. However, they often struggle with the subtle and systematic errors frequently made by language learners, particularly those related to articles or prepositions – areas known to be particularly difficult for many learners. Alternatively, error-specific classifiers can be trained to identify particular error types (e.g., incorrect article usage, preposition errors) directly. While these classifiers can achieve high precision for the errors they are specifically trained for, they often suffer from limited generalization and require extensive labeled data for each error type. A key limitation in applying these techniques to learner language is the disparity between native and non-native data. Models trained exclusively on native data may not generalize well to the distinctive error patterns exhibited by language learners. Conversely, training models solely on learner data can be hindered by its limited size and potential for noise. In this paper, we explore a novel approach that leverages the strengths of both native and learner data. We propose a  meta-classification  framework that combines evidence from a language model (trained on a large corpus of native English) and error-specific classifiers (also trained on native data) as input features to a meta-classifier. Critically, the meta-classifier is  trained on error-annotated learner data , allowing it to learn how to best combine the outputs of the LM and classifiers to optimize performance on the specific domain of learner writing. This approach effectively utilizes the readily available wealth of native data while adapting to the nuances of learner errors through the meta-classifier's learned weights. We investigate the performance of this meta-classification approach on a large, error-annotated corpus of learner English, focusing specifically on article and preposition error correction.

Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) remain a cornerstone of natural language parsing, offering a principled framework for modeling syntactic structure (Chomsky, 1963;Booth et al., 1969). However, learning effective PCFGs from limited training data is a notoriously difficult problem, often leading to sparse data issues and poor generalization performance (Perreira et al., 2002). Latent Variable Grammars (LVGs) offer a potential solution, introducing hidden structure to account for variations in syntactic realization and overcome data sparsity (Johnson et al., 2006;Petrov et al., 2006). In an LVG, the observed syntactic structure is generated from a latent, lower-dimensional structure via a stochastic mapping. By inferring the latent structure, LVGs can effectively pool data and improve parameter estimates, particularly for infrequent constituents. Recent work by Petrov et al. (2006) presented an efficient Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for automatically inducing LVGs from treebanks, achieving significant improvements in parsing accuracy. However, a critical observation highlighted in their work, and further investigated here, is the sensitivity of the learned grammar to the random initialization of the EM algorithm. Different initialization points can lead to significantly different underlying latent representations, despite all converging to locally optimal solutions. This presents a challenge: which learned grammar represents the “best” underlying structure for a given language? We hypothesize that rather than selecting a single “best” grammar, the diversity of these automatically induced grammars can be leveraged to create a more robust and accurate parsing system. The differing latent representations captured by each grammar may encode complementary information about the syntactic structure of the language. Therefore, combining multiple grammars, each representing a different perspective on the underlying syntax, could lead to improved performance. This paper introduces a simple but effective approach to combining multiple automatically learned LVGs into an unweighted product model. Our key insight is to estimate the probability of a constituent as the product of the posteriors obtained from each individual grammar, without any learning or tuning of combination weights. This approach is predicated on the assumption that each grammar provides an independent signal regarding the likelihood of a given constituent, and that multiplying these signals together will yield a more reliable estimate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this product model on both English and German parsing tasks. Experimental results show that combining just eight automatically learned grammars yields significant improvements in parsing accuracy, exceeding the performance of any individual grammar and achieving state-of-the-art results. These improvements highlight the benefits of exploiting the diversity inherent in the automatic induction process of latent variable grammars, and offer a simple yet powerful technique for enhancing parsing performance.

Language models (LMs) are a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, powering applications ranging from speech recognition and machine translation to text generation and error correction. N-gram language models, in particular, remain a widely used and effective approach due to their simplicity and computational efficiency. However, their practical application is often hindered by a significant drawback: their substantial memory footprint. As the size of the training corpus grows, so too does the size of the N-gram model, quickly consuming considerable storage space and posing challenges for real-time applications. Traditional implementations, based on hash tables or trees, struggle to efficiently manage the exponentially growing vocabulary and N-gram counts. Therefore, the development of compact and efficient language model representations has become a critical research area. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a novel implementation of N-gram language models based on double-array structures. Double-arrays, initially proposed by Sato et al. (2001), offer a space-efficient representation of trie structures, which are naturally suited for representing sequences of symbols like N-grams. Our work builds on this foundation by introducing several key innovations. Firstly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of representing backwards suffix trees – crucial for efficient N-gram lookup – using double-array structures. This representation significantly reduces the memory overhead compared to traditional tree-based approaches. Secondly, we propose two optimization techniques designed to further enhance the efficiency of data representation within the double-array structure. These optimizations focus on intelligently embedding probabilities directly into unused spaces within the array, thereby minimizing the overall model size. Moreover, we present a method for tuning word IDs, strategically re-assigning identifiers to words in the vocabulary to promote compaction and accelerate query execution. Beyond optimizing the core data structure, we also address the scalability issue by introducing a division method for constructing large language models from massive corpora. This approach allows us to handle datasets that would otherwise be intractable due to memory limitations. Finally, and crucially, we provide a comprehensive experimental evaluation showcasing the advantages of our approach. Our results demonstrate that, when combined, our optimization techniques lead to a significant reduction in model size and a considerable improvement in query speed compared to state-of-the-art methods described in recent related works. This work, therefore, presents a practical and effective solution for constructing and deploying large-scale N-gram language models with improved efficiency and performance.

The meanings of words are not static; they evolve over time, a phenomenon known as semantic shift (or semantic change). Understanding how and why word meanings change is crucial for a variety of tasks, including historical linguistics, computational philology, and even understanding contemporary language use. For example, the word ‘nice’ historically meant “foolish” or “ignorant,” a meaning drastically different from its current positive connotation. Traditionally, historical linguists have relied on manual analysis of texts to chart these shifts, a process that is both time-consuming and limited in scale. More recently,  diachronic distributional semantics  has emerged as a powerful computational approach to tracking semantic change. These methods leverage large historical corpora to analyze how the contexts in which a word appears change over time, inferring meaning shifts from changes in usage patterns (Burrows, 2002; Hamilton et al., 2016; Sagi et al., 2009). Previous work in this area has largely focused on representing word meaning as a time series – a sequence of vectors, each corresponding to a specific time period – and then analyzing changes in these vectors over time. These approaches often rely on comparing vector differences between time slices to quantify semantic drift. However, these time-series based methods often treat time as a discrete variable, partitioning data into pre-defined eras.
