The core principle underpinning this language is to separate the  specification  of a transduction from its  implementation . This decoupling allows for a high-level, declarative description of the transformation logic, independent of the underlying execution engine. This paper details the design and capabilities of this transduction language, illustratively demonstrating its applicability to several commonly encountered treebank transformation tasks drawn from the existing literature. We present a tree transduction tool built upon this language, showcasing its practicality and ease of use. However, our primary goal extends beyond simply presenting a working system; we seek to initiate a dialogue with the NLP community, soliciting feedback and aiming to converge towards a de facto standard for representing and executing treebank transductions.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has become a dominant paradigm in machine translation (MT) over the past two decades (Koehn et al., 2003; Och & Ney, 2004). The performance of SMT systems is heavily reliant on the availability of large, high-quality parallel corpora— collections of text paired with their translations in another language. Traditionally, building such corpora involved significant manual effort and expense, often using professional translators. This necessitates innovative approaches to automatically acquire parallel data. While manually translated corpora remain the gold standard, their limited size and high cost motivate exploration of automatic acquisition methods. One common approach leverages comparable corpora—large collections of non-parallel texts in multiple languages that cover similar topics (e.g., news articles from different national sources). Techniques like sentence alignment are then employed to identify potential translation pairs within these corpora (Gale & Church, 1993; Fung & Church, 1994). However, the accuracy of sentence alignment can vary significantly, and often a large proportion of the identified pairs are not true translations. Moreover, comparable corpora aren’t always readily available for all language pairs, and the topical overlap might not be sufficient for effective translation model training. A more direct, yet considerably more challenging, approach involves directly mining parallel sentences from the web. The vastness of the web presents a potentially enormous source of parallel data. However, it also introduces significant noise and requires robust methods to identify and extract truly aligned sentence pairs. Prior work has explored various techniques for web mining of parallel data, including querying search engines with specific patterns (Yamada & Knight, 2001; Resnik & Smith, 2003) and employing heuristics based on anchor text and HTML structure. However, these methods often suffer from low precision and require extensive manual tuning of query terms and filtering rules. This paper presents an empirical study of web mining for parallel corpora, focusing on improving both the retrieval and filtering stages. We depart from traditional approaches by formulating the search query generation as a “Learning to Rank” problem, aiming to optimize queries based on their likelihood of retrieving parallel sentence pairs. Furthermore, we utilize the well-established IBM Model 1 (Brown et al., 1993) alignment model as a sophisticated filter to identify and discard noisy or misaligned document pairs. By combining these techniques, we aim to efficiently extract high-quality parallel data directly from the web. We then conduct a thorough end-to-end evaluation of the mined data, demonstrating a significant improvement in the performance of a statistical machine translation system trained on this augmented data.

Natural Language Generation (NLG) systems are increasingly employed in a variety of applications, ranging from report generation (Reiter & Belz, 2009) to dialogue systems (Luu et al., 2017). A key challenge in NLG is producing text that is not only accurate and informative, but also natural and engaging for human readers. While early NLG systems often focused on grammatical correctness and content planning, more recent research has highlighted the importance of stylistic variation in generating human-like text (Gatt & Krahmer, 2018; Li et al., 2016). One crucial aspect of stylistic variation lies in the choice of referring expressions – how entities are referred to in text. For instance, consider referring to the same person as “John,” “he,” “the man,” or “my colleague.” The selection of the appropriate referring expression significantly impacts the fluency, coherence, and even the perceived politeness of the generated text. Despite the acknowledged importance of referential variation, many existing NLG systems tend to produce overly uniform and repetitive referring expressions. This lack of variation can lead to text that feels unnatural and robotic, ultimately diminishing the user experience. While deterministic rules can be employed to govern referential choice (e.g., Dale, 1992), these approaches often fall short of capturing the subtle nuances of human language use. Humans naturally vary their referring expressions, driven by factors such as context, cognitive load, and individual preferences (Arts et al., 2011; Stevenson et al., 2000). To address this limitation, we introduce a new approach towards more flexible and human-like referencing in text generation. We propose a non-deterministic method for referring expression generation that incorporates models explicitly designed to capture variation in referential form. This work centers on two key contributions: first, we develop and evaluate both a Naive Bayes model and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) – two distinct modeling approaches – to predict the probability of different referring expressions given a specific context. Second, we evaluate the impact of incorporating these variation models into a complete text generation pipeline, assessing the coherence and comprehensibility of the generated text through a human evaluation experiment. Our evaluation utilizes the VaREG corpus (Belz & Inkpen, 2008), specifically designed for assessing variation in referring expression generation. Further, we extend our assessment to a more complex domain, employing the GREC-2.0 corpus (Gasic et al., 2014) and comparing our generated texts against both original human references and a random baseline. The aim of this comparative evaluation is to demonstrate the benefits of utilizing variation models in enhancing the quality and naturalness of automatically generated text.

Event extraction (EE) – the task of identifying event triggers and their associated arguments from unstructured text – is a core component of many information extraction systems. The ability to automatically identify  what  happened,  when  it happened,  where  it happened, and  who  was involved forms the foundation for applications ranging from news summarization and crisis management to business intelligence and scientific discovery. While event extraction has received considerable attention in the natural language processing community, particularly in the context of formal newswire text (e.g., ACE evaluations), applying these techniques to the burgeoning world of social media presents unique and significant challenges. Social media platforms, such as Twitter, Facebook, and Reddit, have become primary sources of real-time information about unfolding events. However, the nature of social media text differs dramatically from the carefully edited, grammatically correct language found in traditional news sources. Key characteristics—brevity, informality, slang, misspellings, and a reliance on implicit context—make event extraction considerably more difficult. Specifically, social media messages often lack the rich contextual information necessary to accurately identify event triggers and resolve coreferences to event arguments. For example, a tweet simply stating “Protests downtown!” provides minimal explicit information about the  type  of protest, the  location  of “downtown,” or the  participants  involved. Existing event extraction systems struggle with these characteristics. Models trained on formal text often generalize poorly to the noisy and informal language of social media. Furthermore, the limited context within individual social media posts hinders accurate event identification. While recent work has explored techniques for adapting event extraction models to social media (e.g., through domain adaptation or the use of character-level embeddings), these approaches often fall short of achieving satisfactory performance. In this paper, we present a novel approach to event extraction for social media that addresses the limitations of existing methods by leveraging  cross-genre knowledge enrichment . Our central hypothesis is that incorporating information from more formal sources—specifically, news articles pertaining to the same or related events—can provide the necessary contextual grounding to improve event extraction accuracy on social media data. We do  not  rely on parallel corpora or any additional annotations; instead, we exploit the inherent semantic relationships between news and social media content. We achieve this by retrieving relevant news articles based on the content of social media messages and leveraging them to augment the representations used for event trigger classification and argument role labeling. Our experimental results, conducted on a challenging dataset of event-related social media messages, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

The increasing globalization of communication has led to the frequent mixing of languages, particularly in written form. This phenomenon is especially noticeable in Chinese online content, where English words are commonly interspersed within Chinese text, particularly in informal contexts such as emails, social media posts, and online literature. This linguistic trend presents a significant challenge for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, especially Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, a fundamental step in many downstream applications like machine translation, information extraction, and sentiment analysis. Traditional POS taggers, trained on monolingual corpora, struggle to accurately process these mixed texts. Specifically, English words embedded within Chinese sentences are often incorrectly tagged as a generic “foreign word” category, losing valuable linguistic information and hindering subsequent analysis. The core issue lies in the scarcity of large, manually annotated corpora of Chinese-English mixed texts. Creating such a corpus is a costly and time-consuming undertaking. Consequently, existing POS taggers lack the necessary training data to learn the nuanced POS distributions of English words within a Chinese context. While some approaches attempt to leverage existing English POS taggers in conjunction with Chinese taggers, these methods often fail to capture the specific syntactic and semantic roles that English words assume when integrated into Chinese sentences. For example, an English noun might function as an adjective modifier in a Chinese sentence, a distinction a standalone English tagger would miss. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method for POS tagging of Chinese-English mixed texts that incorporates  dynamic features . Unlike traditional sequence labeling approaches that rely solely on static features (e.g., word shape, prefix/suffix), our method dynamically adjusts feature weights based on the surrounding linguistic context, specifically considering the interplay between Chinese and English words. These dynamic features capture the contextual cues that indicate the likely POS of an English word, even in the absence of extensive training data on mixed texts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the incorporation of these dynamic features not only improves the accuracy of POS tagging for mixed texts but also surprisingly boosts the performance of POS tagging for  pure  Chinese texts, suggesting a beneficial transfer of linguistic knowledge. This paper details our dynamic feature engineering approach, outlining the specific features implemented and the mechanism for their dynamic weight adjustment. We present experimental results on a manually annotated dataset of Chinese-English mixed texts, comparing our method against several baseline POS tagging systems, including standard sequence labeling models and a hybrid approach utilizing separate Chinese and English taggers.

The rapid growth of microblogging platforms like Twitter has created a wealth of data for understanding public opinion, tracking emerging events, and personalizing user experiences. A crucial task in analyzing this data is topic modeling - discovering the underlying thematic structure within a large collection of text. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) has become a cornerstone of topic modeling, and its application to Twitter data has yielded valuable insights in areas such as user profiling (Agarwal et al., 2012) and event summarization (Mathioudakis & Koudas, 2010). Traditional applications of LDA to Twitter often treat the aggregated tweets of a single user as a single document. This approach, while straightforward, overlooks the dynamic nature of user interests and the evolving trends within the Twitter stream. Recognizing this limitation, Wang et al. (2012) proposed Twitter-LDA, a model specifically tailored for short texts like tweets, operating under the assumption that each tweet predominantly focuses on a single topic. Twitter-LDA demonstrated significant improvements in topic semantic coherence compared to standard LDA when applied to Twitter data, highlighting the importance of modeling tweets as independent units. However, a key challenge remains: Twitter-LDA, in its original formulation, lacks the capability for  online inference . Real-world Twitter data is continuously generated, demanding a topic model that can adapt to new information without requiring complete re-training. Batch-based methods like Twitter-LDA struggle to handle this continuous influx of data efficiently. Moreover, understanding  how  user interests and topic prevalence change over time—the dynamics of these elements—is critical for many downstream applications, such as personalized recommendations and proactive event detection. To address these limitations, we present an extension of Twitter-LDA that incorporates online inference and explicitly models the dynamics of both user interests and topic trends. Our approach builds upon Twitter-LDA by first refining the generative process of tweets to more accurately capture the balance between topic-specific vocabulary and more general language used by individuals. We introduce a mechanism for estimating the ratio between topic-related words and general words for each user, allowing for a more nuanced representation of their tweeting behavior. Furthermore, we leverage the Topic Tracking Model (TTM) (Hu et al., 2009), originally designed for modeling consumer purchase behaviors, to enable online estimation of these dynamic changes. By adapting TTM principles, we can track the evolution of user topic preferences and simultaneously monitor the trends of different topics over time, providing a more comprehensive and responsive understanding of the Twitter landscape.

Abstractive text summarization aims to generate concise and fluent summaries that capture the salient information from source documents. While significant progress has been made in this field with sequence-to-sequence models (Rush et al., 2015; Chopra et al., 2016; See et al., 2017), effectively representing the  content  of the source document remains a crucial challenge. Specifically, news articles frequently report on events – happenings involving actors and their relationships – and a successful summarization system must understand and accurately represent these events. Traditional approaches to summarization often rely on sentence extraction or relatively shallow feature representations. However, capturing the nuance and variability in how events are expressed requires a more sophisticated approach capable of reasoning about underlying semantic structures. We propose modeling events as clusters of Open Information Extraction (Open IE) patterns. Open IE (e.g., Banko et al., 2007; Yahav et al., 2013) automatically extracts relational triples from text without requiring a predefined set of relations. We envision each event – such as a “marriage”, a “protest”, or a “company acquisition” – being represented by a cluster of patterns. Each pattern  within  the cluster constitutes a different linguistic realization of the event (e.g., “X married Y”, “X and Y tied the knot”, “Y became X’s wife”). This allows for flexibility in capturing the diversity of language used to describe the same event, while still grounding the summarization process in concrete textual evidence. A key contribution of this work is a comparative evaluation of three methods for extracting these event patterns: a heuristics-based approach inspired by prior work in multi-document abstraction (Leban et al., 2015), a compression-based method leveraging statistical regularities in the corpus, and a novel memory-based approach. While the heuristics-based method provides a simple baseline, its performance is limited by the reliance on predefined rules. The compression-based method attempts to discover patterns based on frequency but struggles with long-tail event descriptions. The memory-based method, however, offers the most promising potential. It leverages a large corpus of grammatically correct utterances to extrapolate event patterns. The core idea is to retrieve and adapt relevant patterns from this “memory” to represent events observed in the source document. However, this approach presents a significant computational challenge: searching a vast space of potentially hundreds of millions of parse trees to identify matching sub-trees. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel data structure and search method designed to efficiently extrapolate event patterns from known grammatical utterances.

Narratives are fundamental to human communication and understanding. They structure our experiences, convey information, and facilitate reasoning about the world. A key element of narrative comprehension lies in recognizing recurring patterns of events, often referred to as narrative schemas or frames. These schemas represent abstract knowledge about typical sequences of actions and the participants involved. For example, the “arrest” schema typically involves a police officer, a suspect, and a crime, unfolding in a predictable sequence. Automatically discovering these schemas from text is a challenging but crucial task for natural language processing, with applications ranging from story understanding and summarization to question answering and knowledge base construction. Existing approaches to narrative schema learning have largely relied on supervised techniques (Pichotta & Mooney, 2014; Ruppenhofer et al., 2010), requiring manually annotated data which is costly and domain-specific. Other approaches utilize hand-built knowledge resources, like PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005) or FrameNet (Baker et al., 1998), imposing significant limitations on adaptability to new domains and the discovery of novel schemas. Furthermore, many systems focus on either event structure  or  semantic role labeling independently, missing potentially important synergies between the two. This paper presents a novel, completely unsupervised system for learning narrative schemas and simultaneously identifying the semantic roles occupied by different words within those schemas. Unlike prior work, our system requires no labeled data, curated knowledge bases, or predefined event classes. Instead, we leverage the inherent structure of natural language, specifically the coreference relationships between arguments across sequences of verbs, to induce both the event sequences themselves and the semantic roles that define the participants in those events. Our core hypothesis is that words appearing in similar participant roles across multiple instances of the same event schema will tend to co-refer, enabling us to effectively cluster words into meaningful semantic roles. For example, if “police,” “officer,” and “detective” consistently appear as agents in an “arrest” schema, the system should identify them as belonging to a shared “POLICE” role. We accomplish this through a joint learning algorithm that iterates between discovering event structure based on verb sequences and refining semantic role assignments based on coreference chains. By jointly addressing both schema induction and semantic role learning, we demonstrate improvements over previous unsupervised results in both tasks. Notably, our system induces rich, frame-specific semantic roles that capture subtle nuances in participant types, offering a deeper understanding of narrative content than existing approaches. The following sections detail our algorithm, experimental setup, and empirical results, demonstrating the effectiveness of our unsupervised approach to narrative schema and participant role discovery.

The ability for machines to comprehend natural language text remains a fundamental, yet persistently challenging, goal within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Truly understanding a document necessitates not simply identifying keywords, but rather grasping its meaning, inferring relationships, and leveraging contextual knowledge – capabilities that remain elusive for many current systems. A significant bottleneck hindering progress in this area is the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality human-annotated datasets, crucial for training and evaluating machine learning models. Traditionally, tasks requiring deep linguistic understanding have been limited by the expense and time required for expert annotation. Recent work by Hermann et al. (2015) offered a novel approach to address this data limitation, proposing a large-scale reading comprehension task built upon readily available news articles from CNN and the Daily Mail. Their methodology involves automatically pairing these articles with their corresponding summarized bullet points, creating a dataset of over a million question-answer pairs. Demonstrating the promise of this approach, they showed that a neural network model could be effectively trained on this dataset to achieve reasonable performance. This work, however, raises a crucial question: what level of genuine language understanding is  actually  required to perform well on this specific task? Is success indicative of true comprehension, or does the task, as constructed, lend itself to simpler, potentially superficial strategies? In this paper, we undertake a thorough examination of the CNN/Daily Mail reading comprehension task, aiming to dissect these questions and gain a deeper understanding of its characteristics. Our investigation proceeds along two complementary lines of inquiry. First, we conduct a detailed, hand-analysis of a representative subset of the question-answer pairs, carefully scrutinizing the types of reasoning and linguistic skills needed to arrive at correct answers. This qualitative analysis aims to pinpoint the core challenges and reveal potential shortcuts exploited by successful systems. Second, we explore the performance limits of relatively simple, yet thoughtfully engineered, systems. We demonstrate that by focusing on key features and employing effective matching strategies, it’s possible to surpass existing state-of-the-art results – achieving accuracies of 72.4% and 75.8% on the CNN/Daily Mail datasets – by over 5%. These results suggest that the task, in its current form, may have a performance ceiling lower than initially anticipated and doesn't necessarily demand the full spectrum of human-level comprehension. We believe these findings are critical for charting a more informed path towards building truly intelligent reading comprehension systems.

Recommendation systems have become increasingly prevalent in a wide range of applications, from e-commerce and online advertising to social networking and content delivery. Traditionally, these systems have relied heavily on collaborative filtering (CF) techniques (Resnick et al., 1994; Su and Khoshgoftaar, 2009) and matrix completion methods (Koren et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012) which leverage user-item interaction data, such as ratings or purchase history, to identify patterns and make predictions about user preferences. However, these approaches often suffer from the well-known “cold-start” problem – the difficulty of making accurate recommendations for new users or items with limited interaction data. Furthermore, they largely ignore the rich semantic information contained within textual reviews provided by users, which can offer valuable insights into their opinions, preferences, and the attributes of items. More recently, there has been growing interest in incorporating textual data into recommendation systems. Opinion mining and sentiment analysis techniques (Pang and Lee, 2008; Liu, 2012) have been employed to extract sentiment polarity and identify key features mentioned in reviews, which can then be used to enhance recommendation accuracy. However, these approaches typically focus on analyzing individual reviews or aspects and often require hand-crafted feature engineering, which can be time-consuming and domain-specific. Moreover, they generally do not offer a unified framework for representing both users and items in a common vector space, making it challenging to directly apply these features to standard recommendation algorithms. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for learning distributed representations of both users and items directly from text reviews. Our method utilizes a unified framework based on maximizing the likelihood of word appearances in reviews, effectively capturing both user preferences and item characteristics in lower-dimensional vector spaces. By representing users and items as vectors, we can leverage their similarity – as measured by cosine similarity or other distance metrics – to predict scores for unobserved user-item pairs, circumventing the limitations of traditional collaborative filtering approaches, particularly in the cold-start scenario. The key contribution of this work lies in its ability to learn informative and coherent profiles for both users and items simultaneously, effectively bridging the gap between textual data and recommendation tasks. Our approach is scalable and can efficiently handle large datasets, ensuring its practicality for real-world applications. We evaluate our system on several real-world datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art baseline systems. Through these experiments, we show that the recommendation-aware distributed representations learned by our method can effectively capture the underlying semantic relationships between users and items, leading to more accurate and personalized recommendations.

Anaphora resolution, the task of identifying what expressions in text refer to, is a core problem in natural language processing (NLP) with broad implications for tasks like machine translation, information extraction, and discourse understanding. Traditional approaches to anaphora resolution have largely focused on  referential  anaphora, where an anaphor (e.g., a pronoun) directly refers to a previously mentioned entity. However, a significant portion of anaphoric relations fall outside this category.  Bridging anaphora , for example, introduces entities implicitly, requiring the listener or reader to infer a relationship between the anaphor and its antecedent. A particularly challenging subtype of bridging anaphora is  associative anaphora , where the connection between the anaphor and antecedent is based on general world knowledge or typical associations rather than direct coreference. Consider the Japanese example in (1): (1) Kinou katta hon wa omoshiroi. Sono kansetsu ga utsukushikatta. Yesterday bought book TOPIC interesting. That binding TOPIC beautiful. (Yesterday I bought a book. Its binding was beautiful.) Here, “sono kansetsu” (that binding) is an associative anaphor. It doesn’t  refer  to the book itself, but is associated with it as a part-whole relationship—bindings are typically parts of books. Resolving such anaphora requires reasoning about typical properties and relationships between concepts, making it significantly harder than resolving coreferential pronouns. The challenge of resolving associative anaphora is particularly acute in Japanese due to its highly elliptical nature. Japanese frequently omits explicitly stated subjects and objects, leading to  zero anaphora , where anaphoric links are simply not marked linguistically. Zero anaphora is known to exacerbate the difficulty of associative anaphora resolution as it requires simultaneously identifying both the omitted antecedent and the associative link. Existing approaches to anaphora resolution often struggle with these combined challenges, often treating associative and zero anaphora as separate, unrelated phenomena. In this paper, we propose a novel probabilistic model for associative anaphora resolution in Japanese that specifically addresses these issues. Our core insight is to frame associative anaphora as a specific type of zero anaphora. By considering it within the broader framework of zero anaphora resolution, we can leverage techniques developed for identifying implicit arguments and apply them to the associative case. Our model utilizes automatically acquired lexical knowledge, specifically focusing on verb-argument relations, to infer likely antecedents based on semantic compatibility. Crucially, we adopt a joint probabilistic framework enabling simultaneous resolution of both zero and associative anaphora, capitalizing on the inherent relationship between these phenomena. We demonstrate, through quantitative evaluation, that this approach yields significantly improved performance on a challenging Japanese benchmark dataset, outperforming baseline systems and highlighting the benefits of a unified probabilistic treatment of zero and associative anaphora.

Taxonomy induction – the task of automatically building hierarchical classifications of concepts – has long been a central problem in natural language processing (NLP) and knowledge representation. Such taxonomies, also known as hypernym hierarchies (where a hypernym is a more general concept, e.g.,  animal  is a hypernym of  dog ), are fundamental to many applications, including information retrieval, text categorization, and question answering. Traditionally, building these taxonomies relied heavily on manual curation, a process which is both time-consuming and expensive. As a result, there has been growing interest in developing automatic methods for inferring taxonomic relations from textual data. Early approaches to taxonomy induction often focused on distributional semantics, leveraging the idea that words appearing in similar contexts tend to be semantically related (Lin, 1998; Pereira et al., 1993). These methods typically rely on measuring the similarity between word representations derived from large corpora, such as co-occurrence statistics or latent semantic analysis. However, such approaches often struggle to capture the hierarchical nature of taxonomic relations and can produce flat, uninformative taxonomies. More recently, researchers have begun to incorporate richer linguistic features and structured learning techniques to improve the accuracy and coherence of induced taxonomies. These methods often leverage relational information, such as patterns derived from Web searches (Snow et al., 2005) or Wikipedia abstracts (Strube and Sevilla, 2009), to identify hypernymy and siblinghood relations. Several approaches have also explored probabilistic graphical models to represent the complex dependencies between concepts in a taxonomy (Resnik, 1995; Fellbaum, 1998). In this paper, we present a novel structured learning approach to taxonomy induction based on a probabilistic graphical model formulation. Our model incorporates both hypernymy and siblinghood relations, capturing heterogeneous evidence from semantic features based on Web n-grams and Wikipedia abstracts. A key contribution is the efficient inference algorithm employed, utilizing loopy belief propagation, combined with a directed spanning tree structure to handle the core hypernymy factor. Furthermore, we employ adaptive subgradient stochastic optimization to discriminatively learn the model parameters, guiding the system to reproduce known taxonomy structures, specifically sub-structures extracted from WordNet. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing a significant error reduction compared to a chance baseline and substantial improvements over previous work on ancestor F1-score. Importantly, we find that incorporating non-hypernym-factored sibling features yields a notable performance gain, highlighting the importance of relational information beyond direct hypernymy links. This suggests that leveraging the interconnectedness of concepts within a taxonomy is critical for accurate induction. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm in machine translation, surpassing traditional Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT) approaches in many language pairs (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). The success of NMT stems from its ability to learn complex, non-linear relationships between source and target sentences using deep neural networks, particularly encoder-decoder architectures with attention mechanisms. However, standard NMT models operate solely on textual data, largely ignoring potentially valuable contextual information that may be available in other modalities. In many real-world scenarios, translation occurs not in isolation but in conjunction with visual information, such as images accompanying news articles or product descriptions. Exploiting this multi-modal context can significantly improve translation quality, particularly in cases of ambiguity or when the text relies heavily on visual references. Recent work has begun to explore multi-modal NMT, integrating visual features into existing NMT frameworks (Calixto et al., 2017; Pasunuru et al., 2017; Elliott et al., 2017). These approaches typically involve extracting visual features from images using pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and incorporating them into the encoder and/or decoder. While promising, the optimal strategies for integrating these visual features remain largely unexplored. Questions remain regarding whether to treat global image features as additional “words” in the source sentence, utilize them to initialize hidden states, or employ other methods to effectively leverage the visual context. Moreover, the availability of large-scale, parallel multi-modal datasets is limited, motivating research into data augmentation techniques, such as synthetic data generation. In this paper, we investigate the incorporation of global visual features into attention-based NMT models. We explore three distinct strategies for incorporating these features – as part of the source input, for encoder initialization, and for decoder initialization – and compare their relative performance on both English-to-German and English-to-English (for robustness evaluation) translation tasks. We further investigate the effect of augmenting the training data with synthetic multi-modal data, specifically focusing on its impact on the performance of our multi-modal models. Our findings demonstrate that combining visual features with encoder and decoder initializations yields the best results and that synthetic data augmentation consistently improves performance. Notably, our best models achieve state-of-the-art results on the Multi30k dataset, and, to the best of our knowledge, are the first purely neural models to significantly outperform a comparable PBSMT system across all evaluated metrics.

Temporal relation extraction – identifying the temporal relationships between events described in text – is a crucial component of many natural language processing applications, including information extraction, event timeline construction, and clinical decision support (Bethard et al., 2005; Allen, 1998; Schatzle et al., 2012). Identifying these relationships, however, is a challenging task due to the often complex and implicit nature of temporal expressions and events in natural language. Consider, for example, the sentence “The patient received chemotherapy before undergoing surgery.” The temporal relationship between “chemotherapy” and “surgery” –  before  – must be inferred from the linguistic cues and world knowledge. Recent approaches to temporal relation extraction have increasingly leveraged the power of deep learning, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) (Lample et al., 2016; Miwa and Sasaki, 2016). These models benefit significantly from the use of pre-trained word embeddings, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), which capture semantic and syntactic information from large unlabeled corpora. These embeddings are often used either to initialize the embedding layer of the neural network or as fixed word representations throughout training. While effective, this approach treats the word embeddings as static, learned from a general corpus before the task-specific training begins. This can limit the model’s ability to learn word representations that are optimally suited for the specific task of temporal relation classification. There’s a trade-off: pre-trained embeddings provide valuable general linguistic knowledge, but they may not capture the nuances of the temporal relations present in the target domain. In this work, we propose a method to address this limitation by extending the standard task-specific loss function with an unsupervised auxiliary loss that operates directly on the word embeddings. Our approach allows the word embeddings to be  continuously  refined during training, adapting to both the general linguistic patterns encoded in the pre-trained embeddings and the specific temporal relationships present in the target dataset. This joint optimization encourages the learned word representations to capture both task-specific and general features. We evaluate our approach on the challenging task of narrative containment relation extraction from clinical records, using the THYME dataset (UzZaman et al., 2013). Our results demonstrate that the proposed word-level loss extension leads to significant improvements over state-of-the-art performance, achieving a new best result on the THYME dataset while relying on only a general-domain part-of-speech (POS) tagger as external linguistic resource.

Determining the semantic similarity between sentences is a fundamental task in natural language processing with broad applications ranging from information retrieval and question answering to machine translation and text summarization. Unlike tasks focused on document-level semantics, sentence similarity (SS) presents unique challenges due to the inherent sparsity of word occurrences within a sentence. A sentence, by its nature, is a relatively short unit of text, and thus contains a limited vocabulary, demanding robust and nuanced modeling of each individual word to accurately capture the overall semantic meaning. Simply counting word overlaps, as in early approaches, proves insufficient to capture the subtleties of language and often fails to accurately reflect semantic relatedness. Recent advancements in distributed representations, such as word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), have significantly improved performance on SS tasks. These models learn vector representations of words based on their contexts, enabling the capture of semantic relationships. However, even these powerful techniques often struggle with infrequent words or those with multiple meanings, highlighting the continuing importance of refining lexical semantics. While contextualized word embeddings (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019) have shown remarkable progress, they often require substantial pre-training data and computational resources, and may not always fully exploit readily available lexical knowledge. We hypothesize that enhancing the representation of individual word semantics, independent of contextual information, can significantly improve sentence-level semantic understanding. This paper explores the incorporation of two distinct sources of lexical semantic information – corpus-based selectional preference and knowledge-based similar words – into a latent variable model to achieve this goal. Selectional preference, observed through distributional statistics, captures the typical syntactic and semantic environments in which a word appears (Resnik, 1993; Erdmann and Kitchen, 2002). For example, the verb "eat" preferentially selects animate agents and edible objects. Incorporating this preference adds valuable constraints on word meaning, reducing ambiguity. Additionally, leveraging external lexical resources, such as dictionaries and thesauri, allows us to explicitly model semantic relatedness between words – for instance, recognizing that “car” and “automobile” are highly similar. By explicitly modeling these aspects of lexical semantics within a probabilistic framework, we aim to create more informative word representations that contribute to improved sentence similarity estimation. Our approach integrates these lexical features into a latent variable model, allowing the model to learn optimal combinations of these signals. Experimental results on two benchmark SS datasets demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among unsupervised methods, confirming the effectiveness of incorporating both selectional preference and similar words for improving lexical semantics and ultimately, sentential semantics.

The increasing adoption of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has created a wealth of clinical data, offering unprecedented opportunities for improving healthcare quality, patient safety, and biomedical research. However, the vast majority of this data exists as unstructured text within clinical notes – encompassing physician assessments, discharge summaries, and radiology reports. Extracting meaningful information from this unstructured text is crucial to unlock the full potential of EHRs, enabling applications such as clinical decision support, automated coding, and population health management. A key step in this process is the accurate detection of  medical events  – instances of diagnoses, treatments, symptoms, and other clinically relevant occurrences – and their associated attributes, such as dates, dosages, and negations. Traditionally, approaches to medical event detection have relied on rule-based systems and feature engineering techniques applied to Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (McDonald et al., 2010; Murthy et al., 2009). These systems typically involve manually crafting a comprehensive set of features derived from fixed-size context windows around each word in the clinical note. While effective to a degree, this approach is labor-intensive, requires significant domain expertise, and often struggles to generalize to new datasets or clinical settings. Furthermore, the fixed-window approach fails to capture long-range dependencies within the text, which are common in clinical narratives. More recently, deep learning models have shown promising results in various NLP tasks, including sequence labeling. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), in particular, are well-suited for processing sequential data like text, as they can inherently capture contextual information and long-range dependencies. These models learn distributed representations of words and phrases, avoiding the need for extensive feature engineering. However, standard RNNs process sequences in a single direction, potentially missing important contextual clues from both past and future information. In this work, we investigate the application of recurrent neural network frameworks, specifically Bidirectional RNNs (BiRNNs), to the task of medical event detection in EHR notes. BiRNNs combine two RNNs – one processing the sequence from left to right, and the other from right to left – allowing the model to consider both past and future context when making predictions. We hypothesize that this bidirectional approach will enable more accurate and robust event detection compared to traditional CRF models and unidirectional RNNs. We demonstrate, through rigorous experimentation on a real-world EHR dataset, that BiRNNs significantly outperform state-of-the-art CRF models in the detection of medical events, suggesting a promising direction for automated semantic understanding of clinical text.

Entity linking (EL), also known as named entity disambiguation, is the task of identifying mentions of real-world entities in text and linking them to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB) such as Wikipedia or Freebase. It is a crucial component in many natural language processing applications, including question answering, information extraction, and text summarization. A robust EL system must contend with several challenges. First, many entity mentions are ambiguous; for example, “Washington” could refer to the U.S. state, the city, or a person. Disambiguating these mentions requires considering the context in which they appear. Second, KBs are vast and constantly evolving, containing millions of entities with potentially overlapping descriptions and types. Finally, a practical EL system should generalize well across different domains without requiring expensive, domain-specific training data or hand-engineered features. Early approaches to EL relied heavily on hand-crafted features and machine learning algorithms like conditional random fields (CRFs) (Cucerzan, 2007; Chambeaux et al., 2009). These systems often leveraged lexical similarity, contextual features, and prior probability estimates derived from the KB. More recently, neural network models have gained prominence due to their ability to learn complex representations directly from data (Yamada et al., 2016; Naik et al., 2018). These models typically encode entity mentions and candidate entities into dense vector representations and then compute a similarity score to determine the best match. Despite the progress, existing neural EL models often focus on single aspects of entity representation, such as context (Lee et al., 2017) or entity descriptions (Sun et al., 2019). However, effective entity linking requires integrating multiple sources of information, including the entity’s textual description in the KB, the contexts in which it’s mentioned in the text, and its semantic type. Moreover, many current systems struggle with entities not present in the KB, or “nil” entities, which require accurately assessing whether a mention refers to a known entity or a previously unseen concept. In this work, we present a novel neural entity linking system that addresses these limitations by learning a unified, dense representation for each entity using a joint encoding of its type, description, and surrounding context. Our system is modular, allowing for flexible incorporation of different encoding methods. Critically, it operates without requiring any domain-specific training data or hand-engineered features, making it readily applicable to a wide range of text corpora. We demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive—and in some cases, state-of-the-art—performance on standard EL benchmarks.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm in machine translation, achieving remarkable progress in recent years (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017). While traditional NMT models typically operate at the sentence level, ignoring broader document context, it is widely acknowledged that capturing document-level information is crucial for improving translation quality, especially for maintaining coherence and consistency across sentences (Rush et al., 2015; Freitag and Al-Onaizan, 2008). The ambiguity inherent in natural language often requires contextual information beyond the immediate sentence to resolve properly, and document-level context can offer valuable cues for lexical choice, pronoun resolution, and overall stylistic consistency. Early approaches to incorporating document context primarily involved pre-processing techniques like feature engineering or incorporating external memory (Li et al., 2016). More recently, attention mechanisms have been extended to attend over previous source sentences (Tu et al., 2016; Rocktäschel et al., 2016) or even hidden states from previous translations (Hokamp and Ferri, 2017), demonstrating promising results. However, these methods often treat document context as a flat sequence, failing to account for the inherent hierarchical structure present in documents – namely, that sentences relate to each other in complex ways, and that context isn’t simply a cumulative sum of prior information. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical attention model for document-level NMT. Our approach introduces an additional level of abstraction  on top  of the standard NMT architecture, designed to explicitly capture the hierarchical relationships between sentences within a document. This hierarchical attention mechanism dynamically computes context vectors, conditioning on both the content of previous sentences and the NMT model’s own internal hidden states. The intuition is that the NMT model itself already encodes valuable sequential information, and the hierarchical attention layer can leverage this information to more effectively incorporate document-level context. Our model is relatively simple to integrate into existing NMT architectures, building upon established components like recurrent neural networks and attention mechanisms. We hypothesize that both the encoder and decoder can benefit from document-level context, but in complementary ways – the encoder can leverage context to better understand the meaning of the current sentence, while the decoder can use it to ensure fluency and coherence in the generated translation. We evaluate our model on a standard machine translation benchmark dataset, comparing its performance to a strong NMT baseline and other state-of-the-art context-aware methods.

The ability to automatically infer opinions expressed in text is a core task in natural language processing, with applications ranging from market research to political analysis. Traditional approaches to opinion inference have largely focused on identifying sentiment explicitly directed towards entities – for example, determining whether a review expresses positive or negative sentiment towards a particular product (Liu, 2012). However, a significant proportion of opinions are expressed indirectly, through descriptions of events that  affect  entities, and these events carry inherent positive or negative connotations. Consider, for instance, the sentence “The company’s profits soared, delighting investors.” While the sentiment “delighting” is directed towards “investors”, the event “profits soared” itself has a positive effect, and understanding this relationship is crucial for accurate opinion inference. This phenomenon, which we term "+/-effect events”, has recently received attention in NLP (Zhu et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2022), highlighting the need for resources and methods capable of identifying events with inherent positive or negative effects. A key component of tackling this task is the creation of a lexicon identifying words denoting events and labeling them according to their effect (positive or negative). However, simply compiling a word-level lexicon is insufficient. Many words are polysemous – possessing multiple meanings – and the effect associated with an event can vary depending on the specific sense being used. For example, the word “increase” can describe a beneficial increase in salary (positive effect) or a detrimental increase in prices (negative effect). Thus, we require a  sense-level  lexicon, mapping individual word senses to their corresponding effect polarity. Acquiring such a lexicon presents several challenges. Manual annotation is expensive and time-consuming, and existing resources like sentiment lexicons (e.g., SentiWordNet, WordNet-Affect) are often not fine-grained enough to distinguish between the nuanced effects of different event senses. Semi-supervised approaches offer a promising solution, leveraging existing lexical resources and employing automated techniques to expand the lexicon. This paper explores a hybrid approach to building a sense-level lexicon for +/-effect events, combining the strengths of graph-based methods utilizing the semantic relationships encoded in WordNet (Miller, 1995) with supervised classification based on the textual definitions (glosses) associated with each sense. We hypothesize that the structured knowledge within WordNet, coupled with the informative power of sense glosses, will yield a more accurate and comprehensive lexicon than either method alone. Furthermore, we investigate the potential of our model to act as a guide for manual annotation, identifying senses likely to be +/-effect events but not present in our initial seed lexicon.

Sentence compression, the task of shortening a sentence while preserving its key information, has emerged as a valuable technique in natural language processing (NLP) with applications ranging from text summarization (Knight & Marcu, 2002) to dialogue systems (Hwang & Liberatore, 2008). Traditionally, research in sentence compression has largely focused on monolingual scenarios, where the input and output sentences exist within the same language. However, an increasingly globalized world and the growing demand for multilingual NLP applications necessitate extending this capability to a bilingual or multilingual context. In this paper, we investigate the problem of  parallel sentence compression  – generating compressed versions of sentences in one language, conditioned on a corresponding parallel sentence in another language. This differs from simply compressing each sentence independently and offers significant potential advantages. For instance, knowing the equivalent sentence in a different language can provide valuable contextual cues, helping to identify redundant or less crucial information within the original sentence. Furthermore, parallel compression can foster consistency across translations, ensuring that the core meaning remains preserved even after simplification. This is particularly useful in machine translation post-editing, where simplified source sentences can lead to more accurate and fluent translations (Simard et al., 2014). The benefits of parallel sentence compression extend beyond machine translation. It can be used to create simplified parallel corpora for language learning, aid in cross-lingual information retrieval by focusing on the essential content, and improve the performance of various multilingual NLP tasks reliant on aligned data. The central question driving this work is how best to leverage the available bilingual information during the compression process. We explore two distinct approaches: one that employs a direct translation-aware compression model, and another that utilizes cross-lingual embeddings to capture semantic similarity between the parallel sentences. We hypothesize that incorporating bilingual signals will lead to more coherent and accurate compressions compared to monolingual methods. To evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches, we perform extensive experiments on a parallel corpus of news articles. The results demonstrate the relative strengths and weaknesses of each method, providing valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities of parallel sentence compression. Through a comparative analysis, we aim to identify the most promising directions for future research in this emerging field, paving the way for more sophisticated and effective multilingual text simplification techniques. Chinese, as a widely spoken language, presents unique challenges for natural language processing (NLP) tasks due to its inherent ambiguities. Unlike languages like English where spaces clearly delineate word boundaries, Chinese requires explicit word segmentation before further analysis can be performed. This initial segmentation step is crucial, as errors propagate through subsequent stages, impacting the accuracy of part-of-speech (POS) tagging and, ultimately, syntactic parsing. Traditionally, Chinese NLP pipelines have tackled these tasks sequentially – first segmenting the text into words, then assigning POS tags, and finally constructing a dependency parse tree. While effective to a degree, this pipeline approach suffers from the well-documented error propagation problem: errors made in earlier stages directly impact the performance of later stages, creating a cascading effect that diminishes overall accuracy. Recent advancements in neural network architectures have shown promising results in various NLP tasks, including dependency parsing (Chen & Manning, 2014; Kiperwasser & Goldberg, 2016). However, applying these neural models to Chinese language processing requires careful consideration. Existing neural approaches for Chinese syntactic analysis, while demonstrating improvements over traditional methods, often still rely on pipeline architectures, thus continuing to grapple with error propagation. Moreover, a key component of effective dependency parsing – pre-trained word embeddings – cannot be directly leveraged in a joint modeling framework where word boundaries themselves are not yet known. Simply put, embeddings require pre-defined words; a joint model must  determine  those words simultaneously with other tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel neural joint model for Chinese word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing. Our approach simultaneously learns to perform all three tasks, leveraging the inherent interdependencies between them to mitigate error propagation. This is, to the best of our knowledge, the first fully joint neural model for Chinese syntactic analysis. Crucially, we overcome the challenge of utilizing word embeddings in a joint setting by incorporating embeddings of  character strings , rather than relying solely on pre-defined word embeddings. This allows the model to learn representations based on the underlying characters, providing a robust foundation for both segmentation and parsing, even in the absence of clear word boundaries. In this paper, we detail the architecture of our joint model, including the character-level embeddings and the interplay between the three interconnected tasks. We present extensive experimental results demonstrating the superior performance of our approach compared to existing state-of-the-art systems in Chinese word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing.

Ontologies play a critical role in modern knowledge representation and reasoning, providing a formal and structured way to represent concepts, relationships, and axioms within a specific domain. They serve as the semantic backbone for a wide range of applications, including information retrieval, data integration, and knowledge discovery (Fensel et al., 2001; Staab & Studer, 2004). However, in real-world scenarios, different ontologies are often developed independently by different organizations or research groups, even when addressing the same domain. This proliferation of “parallel” ontologies introduces a significant challenge: the need to establish correspondences, or  alignments , between their entities (i.e., classes, properties, and individuals). Ontology matching, the automated process of identifying these semantic relationships, is therefore crucial for unifying and extending existing knowledge, fostering interoperability, and enabling more sophisticated reasoning capabilities. Traditional ontology matching approaches often rely on linguistic similarity measures (e.g., string edit distance, n-gram overlap) and logical reasoning techniques. While these methods can be effective in certain cases, they often struggle with issues such as synonymy, polysemy, and the inherent ambiguity of natural language. More recently, representation learning techniques, particularly those based on distributional semantics, have emerged as promising alternatives for ontology matching. These techniques aim to learn vector representations of ontological entities that capture their semantic meaning in a continuous vector space. The core idea is that entities with similar meanings will be located close to each other in this space, enabling accurate alignment. However, the performance of these representation-based methods is heavily dependent on the quality of the underlying entity representations. Pre-trained word embeddings, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), often serve as a starting point for deriving these representations. However, these embeddings are typically trained on general-purpose corpora and may not capture the nuanced semantic information specific to the ontological domain. In this work, we argue that refining these pre-trained embeddings to better reflect the characteristics of the target ontologies can significantly improve ontology matching performance. We present DeepAlignment, a novel unsupervised entity alignment method that addresses this challenge. DeepAlignment refines pre-trained word vectors by leveraging the structural information within the ontologies themselves, without relying on any explicit alignment supervision. The refinement process aims to create ontological entity descriptions specifically tailored for the matching task. This is achieved through a careful design of a loss function that encourages embeddings of related entities (based on ontological relationships) to be closer in the vector space.

The increasing availability of electronic health records (EHRs) presents a unique opportunity to improve healthcare delivery and research. A crucial component of these records is the clinical note – a free-text narrative documenting the patient encounter, including symptoms, examinations, diagnoses, treatments, and follow-up plans. Alongside these notes, medical codes, such as those from the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) and Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) systems, are routinely assigned. These codes serve as standardized representations of the medical concepts discussed within the notes, facilitating billing, claims processing, epidemiological studies, and clinical decision support. However, the process of assigning these codes is a significant bottleneck in healthcare workflows. It’s a labor-intensive task typically performed by trained medical coders, and is prone to human error, inconsistencies, and delays. Beyond the practical challenges, a critical limitation exists: the association between the clinical text and the assigned codes remains largely unannotated. This opacity obscures the reasoning behind each diagnosis or treatment selection, hindering efforts to understand clinical reasoning, improve documentation quality, and support physician learning. In this work, we address the problem of automatically predicting medical codes from clinical text, with a particular focus on  explainability . While previous research has explored automated code assignment, often achieving reasonable accuracy, these approaches frequently lack transparency. They treat the coding process as a black box, offering little insight into  why  a particular code was assigned. Our goal is to move beyond mere prediction and develop a system that can provide clinically meaningful explanations for its coding decisions. To achieve this, we propose an attentional convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture. Our model leverages the power of CNNs to effectively aggregate information across the entire clinical document, capturing long-range dependencies and contextual nuances. Crucially, we incorporate an attention mechanism that allows the model to dynamically focus on the most relevant segments of text for each specific medical code being predicted. This attention mechanism doesn’t just improve predictive performance – it also provides a clear visualization of  which  parts of the clinical note the model deemed most important when assigning each code. We evaluated our method on a large corpus of clinical notes and demonstrated significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art approaches, achieving a precision@8 of 0.71 and a Micro-F1 of 0.54. However, the primary contribution of our work lies in the interpretability evaluation conducted in collaboration with a practicing physician. This evaluation convincingly demonstrates that the attention weights generated by our model align with clinical expectations, highlighting the key phrases and concepts that would genuinely lead a clinician to assign a particular medical code.

The rapid adoption of smartphones and voice assistants has fueled a significant increase in voice search, particularly for local business directory assistance. Users increasingly rely on voice commands – “Find me a pizza place nearby,” or “Call the closest hardware store” – to quickly access information about businesses in their vicinity. While Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technology has made substantial strides, a persistent challenge remains: accurately recognizing business listing names. Unlike common words, business names often consist of unusual combinations of words, colloquialisms, and proper nouns, leading to significantly lower recognition rates. This issue is exacerbated in the context of local search, where the potential space of recognizable business names is extremely large and varies dramatically by geographic location. Current approaches to address this often rely on large, nationwide acoustic and language models (LMs). However, these models are inherently limited in their ability to capture the localized nuances of business naming conventions. A national LM, for example, assigns equal probability to "Joe's Pizza" in New York City and in Los Angeles, failing to account for the fact that one instance might be far more relevant – and acoustically plausible – in a specific user query. Furthermore, maintaining and updating these large, nationwide models is computationally expensive and resource-intensive. In this paper, we propose a novel approach centered around  geo-centric language models  specifically designed for local business voice search. Our core innovation lies in the dynamic generation of localized language models tailored to the user’s geographic location. This allows us to leverage the inherent spatial correlation between user queries and relevant business listings, significantly improving ASR accuracy. The key benefits of our algorithm are threefold. First, it provides a language model for  any  user, regardless of location, simply by leveraging their estimated position. Second, the geographic scope of each LM is  adaptively adjusted  to reflect local business density. In sparsely populated areas, the model covers a wider region to encompass a meaningful set of potential businesses, while in densely populated urban centers, the scope is narrowed for more precise recognition. Finally, our models are pre-compiled, enabling  fast recognition times  – a critical requirement for a responsive voice search experience. We demonstrate, through experiments utilizing a real-world business directory assistance service, that our geo-centric approach yields a substantial 16.8% absolute improvement in recognition accuracy and a 3-fold speedup in recognition time compared to employing a traditional nationwide language model. This represents a significant advancement towards a seamless and frustration-free voice search experience for local business discovery.

Humans routinely encounter large numbers in everyday life – in news reports, financial statements, and scientific publications. Yet, comprehending the true scale of these quantities can be surprisingly difficult. Abstract numerical values often lack inherent meaning without a relatable frame of reference. Consider the figure “$131 million.” While mathematically precise, it’s challenging for most people to intuitively grasp its magnitude. To address this, we often rely on  perspectives  – short, descriptive statements that offer context and anchor the number to familiar concepts. For example, “$131 million is about the cost to employ everyone in Texas over a lunch period” provides a tangible point of comparison. This paper explores the problem of automatically generating such perspectives, enabling systems to help users better understand and contextualize numerical information. We frame this as a novel task: given a numeric mention, generate a natural language description that provides a meaningful and relatable perspective. This is distinct from tasks like number-to-text conversion (e.g., “131 million” to “one hundred thirty-one million”) which focus on linguistic realization rather than contextual understanding. Our approach aims to bridge the gap between abstract numbers and concrete, human-understandable comparisons. A key challenge lies in identifying relevant and informative comparisons. Simply stating a large number alongside another large number (e.g., “$131 million is less than $200 million”) is unhelpful. Effective perspectives require drawing connections to familiar quantities and employing relatable analogies. To achieve this, we propose a two-stage system. The first stage,  formula construction , leverages a knowledge base of numeric facts to compose potential comparison formulas. For example, to provide perspective on $131 million, the system might construct a formula relating it to the average annual salary of a worker, or the total population of a city. We rank these formulas based on three criteria: how familiar the concepts are to users, how numerically close the components are to the target number, and how semantically compatible the comparison is. The second stage,  description generation , translates the selected formula into fluent natural language using a sequence-to-sequence recurrent neural network. This converts the structured formula (e.g., “$131 million ≈ yearly salary   number of workers”) into a human-readable perspective (e.g., “$131 million is about the cost of employing 1,000 workers for a year”). We introduce a new dataset of numeric mentions extracted from news articles, each labeled with multiple human-rated perspectives.

Word embeddings have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, enabling substantial improvements across a variety of tasks (Mikolov et al., 2013;Pennington et al., 2014). Traditional word embedding models, however, represent each word with a single vector, effectively ignoring the phenomenon of polysemy – the existence of multiple meanings for a single word. This simplification can lead to vector representations that are an average of multiple senses, hindering performance on tasks requiring fine-grained semantic understanding. Consequently, there has been growing interest in learning  multi-sense  word embeddings, where each sense of a word is represented by a distinct vector (Nechaev et al., 2017;Pilehvar et al., 2018;Chen et al., 2018). Existing approaches typically rely on context clustering or sense inventories to disambiguate word senses. However, these methods often require substantial external resources or introduce biases inherent in the clustering or inventory process. In this work, we propose a novel approach to learning multi-sense embeddings that leverages both monolingual and bilingual information. Our model aims to implicitly discover word senses by jointly learning to encode contextual information from both a monolingual corpus and a parallel corpus. The core idea is that parallel data, providing translations of sentences between two languages, offers valuable cross-lingual constraints that can aid in sense disambiguation. Different languages may emphasize different aspects of a word’s meaning, and aligning translations forces the model to learn more robust and sense-specific representations. Specifically, our model consists of an encoder and a decoder. The encoder takes as input both monolingual context (i.e., the words surrounding the target word in a single language) and bilingual context (i.e., the corresponding sentence in the parallel language). It then selects a sense representation for the target word. The decoder uses the chosen sense to predict the surrounding context words. Critically, these components are estimated jointly, enabling the model to learn an encoder that effectively utilizes both monolingual and bilingual information for sense disambiguation and a decoder that accurately reconstructs context given a specific sense. Our experiments demonstrate that word representations induced from bilingual data significantly outperform those learned using monolingual data alone, across a range of evaluation tasks including word similarity, word analogy, and translation ranking. Notably, this improvement is observed even when cross-lingual information is not available at test time, suggesting that the bilingual training signal induces representations that generalize well to monolingual scenarios. We believe this work presents a valuable contribution towards learning more nuanced and effective word representations by harnessing the complementary strengths of monolingual and bilingual data.

Linguistic alignment – the tendency for individuals to converge towards similar linguistic features during interaction – is a well-documented phenomenon in sociolinguistics and psycholinguistics (Levelt & Giles, 1984; Clark, 1996). Recent research has posited that this convergence is not merely a byproduct of communicative efficiency, but is also modulated by social factors, particularly the relative social power of interacting individuals (Ng & Kraus, 2012; Dale & Giles, 2006). Specifically, a recurring finding suggests that individuals of higher social status or perceived power elicit more linguistic alignment from their interlocutors than those of lower status (Mastroianni et al., 2015; Burghardt & Braun, 2018). This has led to the notion that alignment serves as a subtle, often unconscious, signal of deference or accommodation towards those perceived as dominant. However, the conclusions drawn from these studies often overlook a crucial complication: linguistic alignment is also demonstrably influenced by a host of low-level linguistic features, entirely independent of social dynamics. These include factors such as utterance length, lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, and even phonetic similarity (Chung & Pennebaker, 2008; Levelt et al., 1989). It’s plausible that observed correlations between power and alignment are, in fact, spurious – driven by these lower-level linguistic variables that co-occur with social power, rather than a direct causal effect of power itself. For instance, individuals with higher status may consistently produce longer, more complex utterances, which naturally invite greater alignment from their conversational partners simply due to their structural properties, not their social standing. This work seeks to disentangle the effects of social power and low-level linguistic features on observed alignment patterns. We re-examine the relationship between power and alignment in two separate datasets, employing logistic regression models that explicitly control for a range of these confounding linguistic variables. Our primary hypothesis is that the effect of social power on linguistic alignment will diminish or even reverse when these low-level features are accounted for, suggesting that the previously reported power effects are substantially overestimated. We demonstrate precisely this – that utterance length, in particular, is a strong predictor of alignment, and that its influence overshadows any direct effect of social power. These findings necessitate a recalibration of our understanding of linguistic alignment. We propose that future research investigating the role of social factors in language use must adopt a more nuanced approach, carefully accounting for the myriad cognitive and linguistic processes that contribute to conversational dynamics. Dismissing these lower-level factors risks attributing alignment to social inferences when simpler, cognitively-driven mechanisms provide a more parsimonious explanation.

The ability to accurately identify relationships between words in a sentence – specifically, predicate-argument dependencies – is a cornerstone of many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. From information extraction, where we aim to automatically populate knowledge bases, to question answering systems designed to understand and respond to complex queries, a robust understanding of sentence structure is paramount. While local dependencies, those between nearby words, are relatively straightforward to identify, a significant challenge lies in accurately recovering  unbounded dependencies . These dependencies involve relationships between words that may be separated by potentially intervening clauses or phrases, posing a considerable hurdle for traditional parsing methods. Consider, for instance, the well-known example: “The book that the man read was interesting.” Establishing the dependency between “book” and “interesting” requires traversing the embedded clause structure, a task that many parsers struggle with. Existing approaches to dependency parsing often rely on statistical models trained on treebanks annotated with dependency relations (Kübler et al., 2009; McDonald et al., 2013). However, the performance of these models often degrades when faced with unbounded dependencies, due to the difficulty of capturing long-range relationships without explicitly modeling the underlying grammatical structures. Furthermore, many current parsers are heavily reliant on feature engineering, requiring significant expertise and effort to develop effective feature sets. This paper proposes a novel approach to dependency recovery grounded in the formal framework of Generalized Categorial Grammars (GCG). Categorial Grammars (CG) offer a compelling alternative to traditional parsing approaches, based on the principle of compositional semantics. They define a small, uniform set of semantic composition operations based on functor-argument relations – analogous to applying a function to its argument – that provide a principled way to combine words and phrases. Unlike purely statistical approaches, CG allows for explicitly modeling grammatical structures, potentially leading to more robust performance on challenging linguistic phenomena like unbounded dependencies. However, standard CG can suffer from combinatorial explosion, as the number of possible categories increases rapidly with sentence length.
