Traditionally, event detection relied heavily on hand-crafted features and rule-based systems (Hovy et al., 2013), which proved to be limited in their ability to generalize to unseen data and required substantial manual effort for development and maintenance. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized the field of event detection, leading to significant performance improvements and a shift towards end-to-end trainable models. Various neural network architectures have been successfully applied to this task, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Lample et al., 2016), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) (Chung et al., 2014), and more recently, Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017). These models leverage the power of distributed representations to automatically learn relevant features from raw text, reducing the need for manual feature engineering. Despite the proliferation of neural network-based approaches, a critical gap remains in our understanding of the relative strengths and weaknesses of different architectures for event detection. While numerous studies report state-of-the-art results using specific models, a rigorous and systematic comparison across various architectures, controlling for confounding factors such as random initialization and data splitting, is often lacking. Many reported performance differences might be attributed to these uncontrolled variables rather than inherent architectural advantages. This paper aims to address this gap by providing a comprehensive empirical evaluation of several prominent neural network architectures for event detection. We focus on the widely used ACE2005 dataset as a benchmark for comparison. Beyond simply comparing performance metrics, we conduct a series of experiments under varying random initializations and training/validation/test splits to assess the robustness and generalizability of each architecture. Furthermore, we introduce a novel GRU-based model enhanced with an attention mechanism that incorporates both syntactic and temporal information. The attention mechanism allows the model to focus on the most relevant parts of the sentence for event detection, while the integration of syntactic information provides a deeper understanding of the relationships between words in the sentence and captures crucial event triggers and arguments. Our results demonstrate that our proposed model achieves competitive performance compared to existing approaches, and our rigorous evaluation provides valuable insights into the factors influencing the performance of neural networks for event detection.

Named entity recognition (NER) has become a cornerstone of many natural language processing applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation (Nadeau & Sekine, 2007). However, simply identifying named entities – people, organizations, locations, etc. – is often insufficient. To effectively leverage this information, we must also address the problem of  named entity canonicalization  (NEC), also known as entity linking or record linkage. NEC aims to resolve different mentions of the same real-world entity, effectively grouping them under a single, canonical representation. For example, recognizing that “Barack Obama,” “President Obama,” and “Obama” all refer to the same individual. Traditional approaches to NEC often rely on rule-based systems or hand-crafted features (Christen, 2012). While these methods can be effective in specific domains, they are often brittle and require significant manual effort to adapt to new contexts. More recently, statistical models have gained prominence due to their ability to learn from data and generalize to unseen cases. These models typically compare mention pairs based on string similarity, contextual similarity, or a combination of both (Bolton & Sinnott, 2006; Rong et al., 2011). Despite advances in statistical NEC, significant challenges remain. One major difficulty is dealing with noisy data – variations in spelling, abbreviations, and aliases are common in natural language text. Another challenge lies in effectively incorporating contextual information to disambiguate entities with similar names. For example, “Michael Jordan” could refer to either the basketball player or the academic. Finally, many NEC systems treat entity attributes (e.g., name, birthdate, occupation) as independent features, ignoring the inherent dependencies between them. For instance, a birthdate is strongly correlated with a person’s age, and a person’s occupation often influences their associated organizations. In this paper, we introduce a novel probabilistic model for NEC designed to address these challenges. Our model represents entities as rows in a table, with columns representing attributes or parts of attributes (e.g., first name, last name, city, state). Crucially, it incorporates entity context, surface features of the mentions, first-order dependencies among attribute-parts, and a principled mechanism for handling noise. We employ a transductive learning approach, leveraging a small set of seed entities and a collection of unlabeled mention tokens. By combining Bayesian inference with conditional estimation, our model effectively propagates information from the seeds to the unlabeled data, enabling robust and accurate canonicalization. We evaluate our model on two datasets derived from political blogs and sports news, demonstrating its superior performance compared to both a straightforward agglomerative clustering baseline and existing state-of-the-art NEC techniques.

Predicting stock market movements remains a central challenge in financial modeling and has attracted significant attention from researchers across multiple disciplines, including economics, statistics, and increasingly, machine learning. The inherent complexity of financial markets, coupled with the sheer volume of potentially relevant data, makes accurate prediction notoriously difficult. Three key characteristics contribute to this difficulty: the high degree of stochasticity, the temporally-dependent nature of market dynamics, and the chaotic, noisy character of available data sources. Traditional time series analysis techniques often struggle to capture the subtle yet influential factors that drive price fluctuations. More recently, the proliferation of social media, particularly platforms like Twitter, has opened up new avenues for financial analysis. The premise is that public sentiment, expressed through tweets, can serve as an early indicator of market trends, providing valuable supplementary information beyond historical price data alone. However, effectively integrating textual data with quantitative financial signals presents several methodological hurdles. Existing approaches often fall into two broad categories: discriminative models and topic modeling. Discriminative models, such as those employing logistic regression or support vector machines, typically treat tweet sentiment as a feature alongside historical prices, aiming to directly predict future price movements. While these models can achieve reasonable performance, they often struggle to capture the underlying generative processes driving market behavior. Topic modeling approaches, on the other hand, attempt to identify latent themes within tweet streams that correlate with stock price changes. However, these methods often rely on discrete representations of sentiment, potentially losing nuanced information and failing to model the inherent uncertainty within the data. In this paper, we propose a novel deep generative model designed to address these limitations. Our approach moves beyond discriminative or topic-based methodologies by introducing recurrent, continuous latent variables. These latent variables allow us to better model the inherent stochasticity of the stock market and capture complex temporal dependencies in both tweet sentiment and historical price data. Furthermore, we employ neural variational inference to tackle the intractable posterior inference problem that arises in generative models. This allows us to approximate the distribution of latent variables given observed data, enabling efficient learning and prediction. To further enhance the model's ability to capture predictive dependencies, we introduce a hybrid objective function incorporating a temporal auxiliary component. To rigorously evaluate our proposed model, we constructed a new dataset specifically designed for stock movement prediction, comprising a comprehensive collection of tweets and corresponding historical stock prices.

Deep learning methods have achieved remarkable success in a wide range of natural language processing tasks, including semantic understanding. However, many semantic tasks still benefit significantly from incorporating syntactic information. Traditional approaches often involve directly integrating syntactic trees or dependency graphs into neural network architectures. While effective, these methods typically require computationally expensive syntactic parsing at runtime, which can be a significant bottleneck for large-scale applications. Moreover, the performance of these approaches is intimately tied to the accuracy of the parser which introduces another layer of potential error. Recent work has explored alternative ways to leverage syntactic structure without explicit runtime parsing. For instance, some approaches learn to predict syntactic representations jointly with semantic representations (Gaddy et al., 2018;Koratkar et al., 2019). Others utilize character-level or subword information to implicitly capture syntactic cues (McCann et al., 2018). Nonetheless, a major challenge remains: how to effectively incorporate syntactic knowledge without incurring the computational cost of full syntactic parsing or relying solely on implicit syntactic signals. In this paper, we introduce the  syntactic scaffold , a novel approach to incorporating syntactic information into semantic tasks that circumvents these limitations. The core idea is to train a model to  predict  readily available syntactic features—features easily derived from a treebank during training—as an auxiliary task alongside the primary semantic task. Critically, this auxiliary task utilizes a multitask objective that encourages the model to learn representations sensitive to syntactic structure  without  requiring any syntactic processing at inference time. Unlike methods that directly embed parse trees, the syntactic scaffold operates on readily available, relatively inexpensive features—such as part-of-speech tags, constituent labels, and dependency relations—derived from a training treebank. The learned representations are then used to enhance performance on the target semantic task, effectively leveraging syntactic knowledge as a form of inductive bias. This approach achieves a compelling balance between incorporating beneficial syntactic information and maintaining computational efficiency. We evaluate the syntactic scaffold on three challenging semantic tasks: PropBank semantic role labeling, FrameNet frame semantic parsing, and coreference resolution. Our experiments demonstrate that the syntactic scaffold consistently improves over strong baseline models, achieving competitive performance on all three tasks. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the learned representations exhibit a heightened sensitivity to syntactic structure, confirming the effectiveness of our approach. We believe the syntactic scaffold offers a promising direction for integrating syntactic knowledge into semantic models without compromising computational efficiency or relying on potentially noisy runtime parsing.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has emerged as the dominant paradigm in machine translation (Koehn et al., 2003). Despite substantial progress, a central challenge remains: accurately translating words with multiple meanings. The well-known ambiguity of natural language means that a single word form can express a variety of semantic concepts, or “senses.” The correct translation of a word is fundamentally dependent on identifying the intended sense in context. For example, the English word “bank” can refer to a financial institution or the land alongside a river, requiring drastically different translations into many target languages. Traditional SMT systems often struggle with such ambiguity, frequently producing inaccurate translations where the wrong sense is chosen. Early attempts to address this issue involved Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) reformulated as a translation task (Chan et al., 2007; Gao et al., 2008). These approaches typically integrate WSD as a pre-processing step, disambiguating source language words  before  translation. While often yielding improvements, these methods often rely on explicitly defined sense inventories (e.g., WordNet) and supervised learning, limiting their scalability and adaptability to new domains. Furthermore, a critical drawback of many such approaches is that they often treat word senses as discrete, artificial categories rather than reflecting the inherent, graded nature of semantic meaning. Real-world word senses are frequently not clearly delineated, and a given context may activate multiple, overlapping senses to varying degrees. In this paper, we propose a novel sense-based translation model that integrates word senses directly into the SMT framework. Our approach differs fundamentally from prior work in that it  explicitly models  the continuous spectrum of word senses rather than relying on predefined sense inventories or discrete disambiguation. We leverage a nonparametric Bayesian topic model to automatically learn latent sense clusters for words in the source language, effectively discovering senses based on distributional properties within a large corpus. This avoids the need for manual annotation or reliance on potentially incomplete or biased lexical resources. The model provides the decoder with sense-specific translation probabilities, allowing it to dynamically select appropriate translations based on the inferred sense distribution for each source word. We employ maximum entropy classifiers to predict the sense distribution, conditioning on both the source word context and the partially translated target sentence. Our experiments, conducted on a large-scale Chinese-to-English translation task, demonstrate that the proposed sense-based translation model significantly outperforms both a strong baseline SMT system and a previously published WSD-reformulated approach.

The question of what constitutes “meaning” has occupied philosophers and linguists for centuries. While differing perspectives abound, a central tenet of modern cognitive science is that meaning isn’t inherent in words themselves, but rather arises from their use – specifically, the contexts in which they appear (Firth, 1957). This foundational idea has fueled the rise of Distributional Semantics (DS), a family of computational models that represent word meaning by analyzing the distributional properties of words in large text corpora (Lund & Burgess, 1996; Turney & Pantel, 2010). These models operate on the principle that “you shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957), capturing semantic relationships based on word co-occurrence patterns. Traditional DS models, however, are almost exclusively text-based. They operate solely within the symbolic realm, analyzing linguistic context without reference to the physical world. This raises a fundamental question: is meaning purely a linguistic construct, or is it grounded in perceptual experience? Growing evidence from cognitive science suggests that grounding meaning in perception—specifically, in our sensory experiences—plays a crucial role in human understanding (Barsalou, 1999; Glenberg & Robertson, 2000). For example, understanding the word “red” inherently involves a mental representation of the visual experience of redness. Motivated by these insights, our research explores the potential of  perceptually grounded  distributional semantics. We hypothesize that incorporating visual information—directly capturing perceptual experience—can enrich our computational models of meaning, particularly for words with strong visual correlates. In this paper, we present a series of experiments comparing and contrasting visual and multimodal distributional models with traditional text-based models. We leverage recent advances in computer vision to construct visual representations of words based on images associated with those words, and then combine these visual representations with textual embeddings. Our findings reveal a nuanced picture. While current state-of-the-art visual models, relying on pre-trained computer vision systems, generally perform worse than textual models on broad semantic relatedness tasks, they demonstrate surprising robustness – and even superiority – when modeling the meaning of words with clear visual properties, such as color terms. Crucially, this holds true even when dealing with non-literal uses of these terms (e.g., “feeling blue”). Furthermore, our analysis indicates that visual and textual modalities capture  different  facets of meaning, and that integrating them in multimodal models often leads to improved performance. This suggests that a truly comprehensive understanding of word meaning requires bridging the gap between linguistic context and perceptual experience—a step towards building computational models that more accurately capture the richness and complexity of human semantic knowledge.

Scope learning – identifying the extent to which a linguistic expression (a “cue”) influences the truth conditions of other expressions – is a fundamental task in natural language processing with broad applications in areas such as information extraction, question answering, and textual entailment. Cues like negation, modal verbs, and quantifiers introduce scope phenomena, where understanding the relationship between the cue and its ‘scope’ – the portion of the sentence it affects – is crucial for correct interpretation. For example, in the sentence “John does not eat apples,” the scope of “not” is the verb phrase “eat apples.” Determining this scope is essential for understanding the sentence’s meaning. Existing approaches to scope learning have largely fallen into two categories: rule-based methods and machine learning methods. Rule-based approaches (e.g., Steedman, 2000) rely on manually crafted grammatical rules to identify scope relations, but these are often brittle and difficult to generalize to new data. Machine learning approaches, particularly those employing sequence labeling or chunking techniques (e.g., Clark and Curran, 2007;Verhagen et al., 2009), treat scope learning as a classification problem, predicting the scope boundaries based on features extracted from the sentence. However, these chunking-based methods often struggle to capture the structural relationships between the cue and its arguments effectively, as they typically rely on superficial features and lack a deeper understanding of the sentence’s syntactic structure. This paper proposes a novel and unified framework for scope learning that leverages simplified shallow semantic parsing. We cast the scope learning problem as a task of identifying the arguments of a cue, framed as a predicate in a simplified semantic representation. Specifically, we map the scope of a cue to several constituents functioning as the arguments of that cue. This allows the model to explicitly represent the structural relationships between the cue and the parts of the sentence it governs. By incorporating syntactic information through parsing, we aim to overcome the limitations of traditional chunking-based approaches. We evaluate our model on the BioScope corpus, a benchmark dataset for biomedical scope learning, focusing on negation and speculation cues. Our results demonstrate that the structural information captured by the parsing approach plays a critical role in accurately identifying scope boundaries. Importantly, our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art chunking-based baselines, highlighting the benefits of incorporating semantic parsing into the scope learning pipeline. Furthermore, while this work focuses on negation and speculation scope learning, the proposed framework is readily adaptable to other types of scope phenomena, offering a potentially generalizable solution to the broader scope learning problem.

Spontaneous speech is often characterized by disfluencies – hesitations, repetitions, and corrections that interrupt the smooth flow of communication. These disfluencies, while natural in human conversation, pose a significant challenge for various natural language processing (NLP) applications such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) (Purcell et al., 2008), spoken dialog systems (Lee et al., 2011), and machine translation (Chuang et al., 2012). Accurate disfluency detection is therefore a crucial prerequisite for improving the performance of these systems. For example, removing disfluencies from ASR transcripts can substantially increase recognition accuracy, while filtering them from dialog input can improve the robustness and responsiveness of spoken dialog systems. Early approaches to disfluency detection relied heavily on hand-crafted features derived from acoustic signals, lexical properties, and syntactic structures (Shriberg, 1994; Gravano & Hirano, 2005). These feature-based methods often required significant domain expertise and were limited in their ability to generalize across different speakers and recording conditions. More recently, sequence labeling techniques such as Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) have become popular, leveraging richer sets of features and offering improved performance (Loper et al., 2005; Kuruppu et al., 2013). However, CRFs still depend heavily on careful feature engineering, and capturing long-range dependencies in speech remains a challenge. The advent of deep learning has spurred new approaches to disfluency detection. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, are well-suited for modeling sequential data and have shown promise in capturing the contextual information needed for accurate disfluency identification (Wu et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016). However, standard RNNs can struggle to effectively handle long sequences due to the vanishing gradient problem, and may not adequately capture the relationships between distant words in a sentence. To address these limitations, we propose a novel neural attention-based model for disfluency detection. Inspired by the success of attention mechanisms in machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015), we frame disfluency detection as a sequence-to-sequence problem, where the goal is to map a potentially disfluent utterance to a corrected, fluent version. Our model utilizes a bidirectional LSTM (BI-LSTM) to encode the input utterance and then employs an attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant parts of the input when constructing the output sequence. This allows the model to efficiently capture long-range dependencies and generate more accurate disfluency labels. Furthermore, we evaluate our model not only on standard English datasets but also on a newly annotated Chinese corpus, demonstrating its broad applicability.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), the task of identifying the correct meaning (sense) of a word in context, has long been a central problem in natural language processing. Despite decades of research, achieving human-level performance on WSD remains a significant challenge. Early approaches to WSD relied heavily on manually crafted lexical resources, such as WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998), and knowledge-based techniques, leveraging semantic relations between concepts. These methods, while conceptually appealing, suffer from limitations including knowledge acquisition bottlenecks, difficulties in capturing subtle contextual nuances, and limited coverage of real-world language use. The advent of supervised learning techniques offered a promising alternative, utilizing machine learning algorithms trained on manually annotated sense-labeled corpora. Systems like Lesk’s algorithm (Lesk, 1986) laid the groundwork, and subsequent supervised models, employing features derived from context words, part-of-speech tags, and syntactic relationships, demonstrated increasingly strong performance (Yarowsky, 1994; Mooney, 1997). However, the creation of large, high-quality sense-labeled datasets is an expensive and time-consuming undertaking. This data scarcity issue remains a critical impediment to the development of robust and generalizable WSD systems. Recent work has explored semi-supervised and unsupervised approaches to alleviate the reliance on labeled data. Bootstrapping methods (Yarowsky, 1995) iteratively refine sense labels based on contextual similarities, while clustering and distributional semantic models seek to group word instances based on their distributional properties (Schütze, 1998). These techniques offer valuable alternatives, but generally fall short of the performance achieved by fully supervised models when sufficient labeled data is available. In this paper, we present a novel approach to enhance supervised WSD performance without requiring additional human annotation. Our method leverages the vast amount of unlabeled text readily available on the Web to augment standard supervised features with a new class of features we term “selectors.” Selectors are words that co-occur with a target word in similar contexts within large unannotated corpora, effectively providing a form of distributional evidence gleaned from real-world language use. The core intuition is that words appearing in similar contexts across diverse Web sources are likely to be indicative of the target word’s intended sense. We demonstrate that incorporating selectors into support vector machine (SVM) classifiers yields substantial improvements in WSD accuracy on both coarse-grained and fine-grained sense disambiguation tasks, achieving significant error reductions over baseline systems trained only with traditional features. Further, we showcase the broad applicability of this approach by applying it to named entity recognition (NER) and observing similar performance gains.

The ability to construct a complete and accurate timeline of a patient’s medical history is a critical component of many clinical decision support tasks. However, patient histories are rarely contained within a single, neatly organized document. Instead, information is typically scattered across multiple clinical narratives – progress notes, discharge summaries, radiology reports, and so on – each written at a different point in time and potentially with varying degrees of detail. Consequently, a crucial step in leveraging this information is the problem of  cross-narrative temporal ordering  of medical events: determining the correct order in which events occurred, even when those events are described in different sources. Existing work in temporal reasoning has largely focused on ordering events within a single document (Mutlu & Shahar, 2006; Ferre et al., 2008; Bethard et al., 2005). While these methods provide a solid foundation, they often struggle when applied to cross-narrative scenarios due to inconsistencies in event descriptions, differing levels of detail, and the lack of explicit temporal indicators connecting events across narratives. More recent approaches have begun addressing cross-document temporal ordering, employing machine learning techniques to identify temporal relations (e.g., ‘before,’ ‘after,’ ‘overlap’) between events (Arze et al., 2008; Mazumdar et al., 2012). However, these systems typically focus on pairwise comparisons and do not scale efficiently to scenarios involving a large number of narratives and events. The challenge of aligning multiple medical event sequences is particularly acute. Simply concatenating events from different narratives ignores the inherent temporal constraints and can lead to inaccurate timelines. Aligning these sequences requires not only identifying coreferences (determining which events refer to the same underlying clinical occurrence) but also resolving ambiguities in temporal relationships, especially when narratives provide incomplete or conflicting information. In this paper, we explore two distinct approaches to cross-narrative temporal ordering of medical events: (1) a novel weighted finite state transducer (WFST) representation of medical event sequences, enabling efficient composition and search for optimal alignment, and (2) dynamic programming with iterative pairwise alignment, utilizing both global and local alignment algorithms. Both methods leverage a corpus of clinical narratives to learn weights for coreference and temporal relation probabilities. We hypothesize that the WFST approach, with its ability to compactly represent multiple possible alignments and efficiently search for the most probable one, will outperform the dynamic programming method, which relies on a series of sequential pairwise comparisons. Our experimental results confirm this hypothesis, demonstrating a significant improvement in alignment accuracy with the WFST approach—a 6.8% increase over the dynamic programming baseline.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has long been the dominant paradigm in machine translation, achieving remarkable progress over the past two decades (Koehn et al., 2003). However, SMT relies heavily on feature engineering and struggles to capture long-range dependencies effectively. Neural machine translation (NMT) has recently emerged as a powerful alternative, demonstrating superior performance on various translation tasks (Bahdanau et al., 2014;Vaswani et al., 2017). Despite the success of NMT, it often lacks interpretability and struggles with rare words and morphologically rich languages. Forest-based translation offers a compelling alternative, combining the advantages of both SMT and NMT. This approach leverages syntactic structures to learn translation rules directly from aligned parallel corpora (Knight and Graehl, 1997). Specifically, it represents the source and target sentences as forests—collections of parse trees—and learns to map subtrees in the source forest to strings in the target forest. This allows for a more structured and interpretable translation process than purely neural approaches. Recent advances in forest-based translation have shown promising results, particularly for morphologically complex languages (Nakayama et al., 2018). However, a key challenge in forest-based translation is rule generalization. The number of possible rules can grow exponentially with the size of the training data, making it difficult to learn robust and generalizable rules. A particular bottleneck within rule generalization lies in properly handling function words – words with little lexical content, such as prepositions, articles, and pronouns – which often exhibit complex and context-dependent translation behavior. Existing forest-based systems often struggle to accurately generate these function words, leading to fluency issues and reduced translation quality. In this paper, we propose an effective approach to leverage function words for generating generalized translation rules in forest-based translation. The core idea is to extract composed tree-to-string translation rules that explicitly account for multiple interpretations of both aligned and unaligned target function words. We introduce a novel mechanism to constrain the exhaustive attachment of these function words by limiting their binding to nearby syntactic chunks, as identified by a target dependency parser. This approach allows us to capture not only source-tree-to-target-chunk correspondences, but also to utilize the compact encoding of an exponential number of parse trees offered by forest structures to properly generate target function words during decoding. Through extensive experiments on large-scale English-to-Japanese translation, we demonstrate that our approach significantly improves translation quality, achieving a gain of 1.8 BLEU points compared to a strong forest-to-string baseline system.

The impact of scientific research is conventionally assessed through citation counts – a metric that has become foundational to evaluating researchers, institutions, and the overall progress of scientific fields. However, the simple act of citing a paper doesn’t reveal  why  it was cited. A citation can signify a multitude of relationships: support, critique, methodology adoption, background context, or simply acknowledgement of prior work. Treating all citations as equal, as is common practice, obscures these nuanced relationships and presents a limited view of the true impact and influence of a scientific contribution. This simplification overlooks a fundamental aspect of scientific discourse: not all “fingers” pointing to a paper are equal in intensity or meaning. Recognizing the limitations of uniform citation weighting, a growing body of research has focused on understanding the  context  of citations. Citation analysis has moved beyond simple counts to explore citation functions – the specific purpose a citation serves within a text (Garfield, 1979). Existing taxonomies of citation functions, such as those proposed by Teufel et al. (2006) and Coletta et al. (2006), categorize citations based on the author’s intent, like ‘background’, ‘methodology’, ‘support’, and ‘contradiction’. However, these approaches often rely on manual annotation, making large-scale application impractical. Moreover, they typically focus on  categorizing  the citation rather than quantifying the  strength  or  intensity  of the connection being expressed. In this paper, we argue that measuring the intensity of a reference – essentially,  how strongly  an article relies on or engages with a cited work – is crucial for a more accurate understanding of the scientific landscape. This intensity reflects the degree to which the cited work underpins the citing article’s arguments, findings, or methodology. A high-intensity reference suggests a substantial intellectual debt or a critical engagement, whereas a low-intensity reference may serve as superficial background. Beyond a more nuanced understanding of research impact, accurately gauging reference intensity can significantly enhance various citation-based applications, including expert finding, research trend analysis, and even improved recommendation systems. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach to estimate reference intensity. We begin by constructing a rich, manually annotated dataset featuring references labeled with varying degrees of intensity. Building upon this dataset, we propose GraLap, a graph-based semi-supervised model designed to predict the intensity of references. GraLap leverages the inherent relational structure of the citation network, combining node features with graph propagation techniques to achieve superior performance. Our experiments, conducted on the AAN (Aminer Academic Network) dataset, demonstrate that GraLap significantly outperforms existing baseline methods, achieving a 46% improvement in correlation with the true reference intensity labels.

Knowledge bases (KBs) have become integral components of numerous natural language processing applications, powering tasks ranging from question answering and information retrieval to dialogue systems. However, maintaining the accuracy and completeness of KBs is a significant challenge. The world is dynamic, and the facts encoded within KBs are constantly evolving. For instance, individuals marry, companies merge, and political leaders change positions. Accurately and efficiently updating KBs to reflect these real-world state changes is therefore crucial, yet remarkably difficult. Traditional approaches to KB updating often rely on manual curation, which is expensive and slow, or on information extraction systems that operate on newly published text, which can be noisy and require significant engineering effort. Recent work has begun to explore the use of temporal KBs, which explicitly represent the timevarying nature of facts, but these systems still require a mechanism for automatically identifying  when  and  how  to update the KB given evidence of change. A key signal of such state changes often manifests in natural language descriptions of entities. Specifically, the verbs used to describe an entity’s state can indicate whether that state has been altered. For example, the addition of the verb “married” to a person’s biography suggests a change in their marital status, while the deletion of “employed” might indicate a job loss. However, manually identifying and cataloging all such state-changing verbs is a laborious and incomplete undertaking. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to automatically learning state-changing verbs by leveraging the rich resource of Wikipedia edit history. Wikipedia serves as a large, collaboratively curated KB, and its edit history provides a valuable source of distantly supervised training data. When an entity undergoes a state change – a marriage, a death, a change in employment – the corresponding infobox on the entity’s Wikipedia page is typically updated to reflect this new information. Simultaneously, the article text itself is often edited, with verbs being added to describe the new state or deleted to reflect the old one. We hypothesize that there is a strong correlation between these infobox updates and the corresponding verb changes in the text. Our method exploits this correlation to learn a mapping between verbs and infobox changes. We distantly supervise this learning process using Wikipedia revision history, treating infobox updates as ground truth signals of state change. Furthermore, we incorporate constraints to ensure that the learned mappings are semantically plausible. We demonstrate that our approach achieves high precision (88%) and reasonable recall (76%) in predicting infobox updates based on verb additions and deletions.

Relation extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities in text – is a core component of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, including knowledge base construction, question answering, and information retrieval. Traditionally, relation extraction has been approached as a pipeline consisting of separate entity recognition and relation classification stages (Zheng et al., 2008; Miwa & Sasaki, 2010). These pipeline approaches rely heavily on carefully engineered features, often leveraging external linguistic resources like WordNet or gazetteers. While effective, these feature-based methods require significant domain expertise and are often brittle when applied to new domains or languages. More recently, end-to-end neural models are gaining traction in the field of relation extraction. These models aim to learn representations directly from raw text, alleviating the need for manual feature engineering. Approaches employing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Santos et al., 2015; Nguyen & Grishman, 2015) have shown promising results, capturing local feature interactions relevant for relation classification. However, CNNs often struggle with long-range dependencies and may not fully exploit the structural aspects of language. In this paper, we present a novel end-to-end neural model for relation extraction that leverages the strengths of both sequential and structural information. Our model is built upon Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), and specifically, utilizes bidirectional LSTMs (Graves et al., 2013) to capture contextual information from the input text. Crucially, we integrate information from dependency parse trees – representing the syntactic relationships between words – into our LSTM architecture. We achieve this by stacking bidirectional tree-structured LSTM-RNNs (Tai et al., 2015) on top of bidirectional sequential LSTMs, allowing the model to jointly represent entities and relations within a unified framework. To further enhance performance, we incorporate techniques inspired by sequence-to-sequence learning. We pre-train the entity recognition component of our model and employ scheduled sampling (Bengio et al., 2015) during training to encourage the model to become more robust to errors in its own entity predictions. This allows the model to seamlessly integrate entity information into the relation extraction process. We evaluate our model on two challenging relation extraction datasets: ACE2005 and ACE2004. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art feature-based models, achieving 12.1% and 5.7% relative error reductions in F1-score, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate competitive performance compared to recent CNN-based approaches on a nominal relation classification task (SemEval-2010 Task 8).

The ability to understand and generate language hinges on our capacity to compose meaning from smaller units. This principle of compositionality – the idea that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its constituents and the rules for combining them – is a cornerstone of modern linguistic theory (Fodor & Lepore, 1999; Hassidim, 2019). While seemingly intuitive, empirically verifying and computationally modeling compositionality proves surprisingly challenging, especially when considering complex linguistic phenomena like morphological compounding. Compounding, the process of combining two or more words to create a new lexical item, presents a fertile ground for investigating semantic compositionality. This is particularly true in languages like German, which exhibit a remarkably high degree of compound formation. German compound nouns, often formed by concatenating multiple nouns, can represent highly specific concepts, yet their meanings are demonstrably related to the meanings of their parts (Dwyer, 1978; Nerbonne, 1993). However, the precise nature of this relationship is often non-literal and can be sensitive to contextual factors, leading to ambiguity and challenges for computational models. Recent advances in distributional semantics, where word meaning is represented as vectors in a high-dimensional space (Lenci et al., 2006; Baroni et al., 2014), have opened new avenues for probing semantic compositionality. By analyzing the vector representations of compounds and their constituents, researchers can quantitatively assess how well the meaning of a compound can be predicted from the meanings of its parts. This approach, often termed ‘compositional reverse engineering’ (Mitkov et al., 2006), seeks to ‘reverse engineer’ the compositional process by attempting to reconstruct the observed vector representation of a compound given the representations of its components. Several composition models have been proposed in the literature, ranging from simple vector addition or multiplication to more sophisticated methods incorporating learned transformations or attention mechanisms (Smolensky, 1990; Widdows & Ferraro, 2005; Kartsaklis et al., 2018). While these models have shown varying degrees of success, their performance often depends heavily on the specific language, dataset, and evaluation methodology. In this paper, we present a large-scale analysis of semantic compositionality in German compound nouns. We utilize a high-dimensional vector space model trained on a substantial German corpus and evaluate the performance of several existing composition models in reconstructing the observed vector representations of compounds from their constituents. Crucially, we also introduce a novel, surprisingly simple composition model that consistently outperforms existing approaches on our dataset. Through this investigation, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying semantic composition in German and contribute to the development of more robust and accurate computational models of language.

Dependency parsing and constituency parsing (phrase structure parsing) represent two fundamental approaches to syntactic analysis in natural language processing. While often treated as distinct tasks, they offer complementary perspectives on sentence structure. Dependency parsing focuses on relationships between individual words, identifying head-dependent pairs that reveal grammatical functions. Constituency parsing, conversely, represents sentence structure through hierarchical phrase groupings, outlining the phrase structure of a sentence. Traditionally, building high-quality treebanks has largely followed a single-view paradigm – either constructing a dependency treebank or a phrase structure treebank. However, a growing recognition exists that integrating these perspectives can yield more robust and informative linguistic resources. Chinese, with its relatively flat syntactic structure compared to languages like English, presents unique challenges for both dependency and constituency parsing. Existing Chinese treebanks, such as the Penn Chinese Treebank (CTB) (Xue et al., 2005), primarily focus on phrase structure annotation. While valuable, these resources often require significant transformation to be effectively utilized for dependency parsing, potentially leading to information loss. Conversely, dependency treebanks for Chinese, like those built within the Universal Dependencies framework, are fewer in number and may not fully capture the nuances of Chinese phrase structure. This paper introduces a novel multi-view annotation framework specifically designed for Chinese treebanking. Our core principle is to establish dependency structures as the  base view , representing the fundamental syntactic relationships within sentences. Critically, this framework is engineered to facilitate efficient and lossless conversion into corresponding phrase structures. This bi-directional capability allows researchers to leverage the benefits of both representations without the need for independent annotation efforts. By natively supporting both views, we aim to create a resource that caters to a broader range of NLP tasks and research directions. To demonstrate the viability and utility of our approach, we have constructed a multi-view Chinese treebank following this framework. The first release, designated PMT 1.0 (Penn Multi-view Treebank), comprises 14,463 sentences and is made freely available to the research community. To validate the effectiveness of our multi-view framework, we implemented an arc-standard transition-based dependency parser (Nivre, 2007) and augmented it with phrase structure features derived from the phrase structure view. Our experimental results demonstrate a clear performance improvement achieved by incorporating these additional features. Furthermore, we evaluated our treebank and parser’s capabilities in a downstream application: dependency-to-string machine translation. The results demonstrate comparable performance to the widely-used Stanford Parser trained on the CTB 7.0 corpus, highlighting the quality and practical utility of the PMT 1.0 treebank.

The World Wide Web represents an unprecedented repository of human knowledge. However, despite its vastness, directly querying the Web often fails to provide definitive answers to many questions. This isn't necessarily due to a lack of information, but rather that the answer isn’t stated  explicitly . The ability to  infer  new knowledge from existing facts is crucial for unlocking the full potential of the Web. For example, while the Web might state “Barack Obama was born in Honolulu” and “Honolulu is in Hawaii,” it may not explicitly state “Barack Obama was born in Hawaii.” A reasoning system, equipped with the appropriate inference rule (“If X is born in Y, and Y is in Z, then X is born in Z”), could readily deduce this fact. This highlights a fundamental question: where do these inference rules, or knowledge base completion rules, come from? Traditionally, knowledge bases like Cyc (Lenat, 1995) and WordNet (Miller, 1995) are painstakingly constructed by human experts. This process is both costly and time-consuming, limiting the potential scale and coverage of such resources. More recently, researchers have explored methods for automatically extracting facts from text, such as the TEXTRUNNER system (Etzioni et al., 2004), which identifies relational tuples directly stated within Web text. However, TEXTRUNNER and similar systems are limited to explicit knowledge and cannot uncover implicit relationships. This paper addresses the challenging problem of automatically  learning  inference rules from Web text in an unsupervised and domain-independent manner. We introduce SHERLOCK, a first-order Horn clause learner designed to operate on the noisy and incomplete data found on the Web. SHERLOCK aims to discover rules of the form “If condition, then conclusion,” allowing it to infer facts beyond those directly stated in the source text. Specifically, SHERLOCK acquires over 30,000 Horn clauses from a large corpus of Web text, demonstrating its scalability and ability to generalize across diverse domains. A key innovation of SHERLOCK lies in its novel rule scoring function, based on the concept of Statistical Relevance (Salmon et al., 1971). Traditional methods for rule evaluation often struggle with the inherent ambiguity, noise, and incompleteness of Web-derived extractions. Statistical Relevance provides a robust mechanism for identifying rules that are genuinely informative and supported by the data, even in the presence of these challenges. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SHERLOCK in uncovering implicit knowledge. By performing inference over the learned rules, we discover three times as many facts (at a precision of 0.8) compared to TEXTRUNNER, which is restricted to extracting explicitly stated facts.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) has long been a core task in Natural Language Processing, with applications spanning information extraction, question answering, and knowledge base construction. Traditional NER systems focus on identifying broad entity categories – person, organization, location – providing a foundational layer for downstream tasks. However, many real-world applications demand a far more nuanced understanding of entities, requiring the identification of  fine-grained  entity types. For instance, knowing an entity is a “person” is often insufficient; knowing it is a “biochemist,” “film director,” or “politician” can be critical. This demand has driven research into Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FINE-GET), a challenging task that aims to classify named entities into a much more granular set of types. Existing approaches to FINE-GET have largely relied on supervised learning, achieving promising results but suffering from a significant bottleneck: the scarcity of labeled data. Creating large, high-quality datasets for a vast number of fine-grained types is costly and time-consuming. Furthermore, the long-tail distribution of types – where a few types are very frequent while many others are rare – exacerbates this problem, leading to poor performance on less common types. Distant supervision and knowledge-based approaches offer a potential remedy, but often introduce noise and inaccuracies into the training process. The challenge is further compounded when dealing with short, informal texts such as tweets or sentences, which frequently lack the contextual cues necessary to disambiguate fine-grained types. Consider the entity “Apple.” Without surrounding context, it’s impossible to determine whether it refers to the technology company or the fruit. This ambiguity highlights the critical need for  context-aware  FINE-GET systems. In this paper, we introduce FINET, a novel system designed to address the limitations of existing FINE-GET methods. FINET leverages the comprehensive and hierarchical structure of WordNet to support a remarkably fine-grained type system – the most fine-grained reported to date – and importantly, can handle types with  no  annotated training data. Our approach centers on a multi-stage pipeline. First, we generate a set of candidate types for each entity mention using a series of extractors designed to capture both explicit and implicit type indications. Second, we employ techniques inspired by word-sense disambiguation to select the most appropriate type from the candidate set. A key innovation of FINET is its ability to overcome data scarcity by relying on unsupervised extractors and by bootstrapping training data directly from WordNet and other readily available lexical resources.

Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing, aiming to uncover the grammatical structure of a sentence by establishing relationships between words. These dependency structures are valuable for a wide range of downstream applications, including machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. Traditionally, dependency parsing has been dominated by graph-based approaches (McDonald et al., 2005; Nivre & Scholz, 2004), which formulate parsing as a problem of simultaneously predicting the head and dependency label for each word in a sentence. These models operate on a graph structure representing the possible dependency relationships, and score these graphs to identify the most likely parse tree. Early graph-based dependency parsers relied heavily on hand-crafted features, capturing various lexical, syntactic, and morphological properties of words and their contexts. While achieving state-of-the-art performance, these feature engineering efforts were incredibly laborious, requiring significant linguistic expertise and domain knowledge. Furthermore, the reliance on a vast number of features – often in the millions – introduces limitations in generalization ability and significantly impacts parsing speed due to the computational cost of evaluating these features during inference. Maintaining and extending these feature sets across languages or domains is a substantial challenge. Recent advancements in neural networks have offered promising alternatives to traditional feature-based models. Neural networks possess the capability to automatically learn intricate feature representations from data, reducing the need for manual feature engineering. Several neural network architectures have been explored for dependency parsing, including recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Chen and Manning, 2014) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) (Ma and Hovy, 2016). However, directly applying these models to graph-based parsing remains challenging, as it requires effectively capturing the complex interactions between words and their potential dependencies within the graph structure. In this paper, we propose a novel Neural Network model specifically designed for graph-based dependency parsing. Our primary contribution is a mechanism for automatically learning high-order feature combinations using only atomic features, facilitated by a newly introduced activation function,  tanhcube . This novel activation function enables the model to capture complex interactions between input features without the need for explicitly engineered combinations. Furthermore, we introduce a straightforward yet effective method to incorporate phrase-level information into the parsing process. Integrating phrase-level features has been historically challenging in conventional graph-based parsers due to their computational expense. Our approach bypasses this difficulty through a carefully designed neural architecture. We demonstrate, through experiments on the widely used English Penn Treebank, that parsers based on our model consistently outperform conventional graph-based parsers, achieving improved accuracy while reducing the reliance on manually designed features.

N-gram language models (LMs) have long been a cornerstone of natural language processing, powering a diverse range of applications from speech recognition to machine translation. Despite their success, traditional n-gram LMs suffer from a fundamental limitation: they treat all n-grams equally, failing to capture the underlying topical coherence inherent in natural language. For instance, the sequence “operating system” and “memory allocation” are more likely to co-occur within a document discussing computer science than within a document about culinary arts. Standard n-gram models, however, lack the ability to represent or exploit such topic-specific dependencies. To address this, researchers have explored various extensions to the basic n-gram framework, including smoothing techniques and incorporating external knowledge sources. Recently, there has been growing interest in probabilistic topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), for uncovering latent thematic structures within document collections. While powerful for topic discovery, LDA and its variants operate at the document level and do not directly model the sequential dependencies captured by n-gram LMs. Wallach (2006) proposed the Bayesian Topic N-gram Model (BTNGM), a generative probabilistic model that elegantly bridges the gap between topic modeling and n-gram language modeling. BTNGM assigns each n-gram to a specific topic, allowing the model to learn topic-specific language distributions. This represents a significant step towards capturing topical coherence within a language modeling framework. However, BTNGM also faces several challenges. The partitioning of all n-grams into exclusive topics can lead to severe data sparsity, especially when dealing with rare n-grams or large vocabularies. This sparsity hinders the model’s ability to generalize and accurately estimate probabilities. Furthermore, the standard Gibbs sampling algorithm used for inference in BTNGM can be computationally expensive, particularly when dealing with higher-order n-grams and large datasets, as it typically updates one n-gram’s topic assignment at a time. In this paper, we present several key improvements to the Bayesian Topic N-gram Model. First, we investigate new prior distributions designed to alleviate the data sparsity problem. We explore alternatives to the Dirichlet prior used in the original BTNGM, focusing on priors that promote topic sharing and allow for more flexible topic assignments. Second, we introduce a novel blocked Gibbs sampler that significantly accelerates the inference process. Our sampler enables the simultaneous reassignment of multiple n-grams across different documents to a new topic, allowing for more efficient exploration of the probability space and faster convergence.

The demand for accessible and understandable natural language is steadily increasing, driven by both advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and a growing awareness of the challenges faced by individuals with reading difficulties. While significant progress has been made in areas like machine translation and text generation, complex sentence structures remain a persistent obstacle to both human comprehension and automated processing. Traditional sentence simplification techniques (Chandrasekar et al., 1996; Wubben et al., 2012) offer a partial solution, typically focusing on lexical substitution and syntactic transformations to reduce the readability of individual sentences. However, these methods often struggle with lengthy, multi-clause sentences where the underlying complexity stems not just from individual words or phrases, but from the overall structural arrangement of information. In this paper, we introduce a novel sentence simplification task – Split-and-Rephrase – specifically designed to address this limitation. Unlike traditional simplification, which seeks to  rewrite  a single complex sentence, Split-and-Rephrase aims to  decompose  it into a sequence of shorter, semantically equivalent sentences. This approach explicitly recognizes that some sentences are inherently difficult to process as single units and that breaking them down into smaller, more manageable parts can significantly enhance comprehension. The potential benefits of such a task are wide-ranging. For NLP systems, simplified sentence structures can lead to improved performance in downstream tasks such as parsing (Kübler et al., 2009), semantic role labeling (Koller and Kuhlmann, 2011), and machine translation (Chhabra and Birch, 2018). A sequence of simpler sentences is often easier to analyze and model than a single complex sentence, leading to more accurate and robust results. Furthermore, Split-and-Rephrase holds considerable promise for societal applications, particularly in the realm of accessibility. Individuals with dyslexia, cognitive impairments, or limited language proficiency often struggle with complex sentence structures. The ability to automatically convert lengthy sentences into shorter, more digestible units could significantly improve their reading comprehension and access to information. This work contributes to the advancement of this new task in two key ways. First, we present a large-scale, high-quality benchmark dataset consisting of over one million sentence-split pairs. This dataset, which we are making publicly available, provides a valuable resource for researchers seeking to develop and evaluate Split-and-Rephrase models. Second, we explore the inherent challenges of the task by implementing and comparing five distinct models, ranging from a basic sequence-to-sequence approach to more sophisticated, semantically-motivated architectures.

The automatic solving of mathematical word problems represents a significant challenge at the intersection of natural language processing, knowledge representation, and reasoning. These problems, often referred to as number word problems (NWPs), require not only understanding the semantics of natural language but also the translation of that understanding into a formal mathematical representation, and ultimately, the application of appropriate reasoning steps to arrive at a solution. Unlike straightforward question answering, NWPs demand a deeper level of comprehension, involving identification of quantities, relationships between those quantities, and the correct mathematical operations to perform. Existing approaches to NWP solving have varied widely, ranging from information extraction techniques focused on identifying key numerical values and units (Kushal & Barner, 2016), to rule-based systems that rely on handcrafted patterns (Shi & Weng, 2015), and more recently, machine learning models including sequence-to-sequence approaches (Konami et al., 2017). However, many of these systems struggle with the inherent ambiguity of natural language and the complexity of representing the underlying mathematical relationships. In this paper, we present a novel approach to automatically solving NWPs that leverages semantic parsing and reasoning. Our approach centers around the creation of a meaning representation language specifically designed to bridge the gap between natural language text and formal mathematical expressions. This language allows us to capture the quantitative relationships described in the problem statement in a structured and unambiguous manner. Crucially, this intermediate representation serves as the foundation for a subsequent reasoning stage, where mathematical operations are applied to derive the solution. To parse the natural language input into this meaning representation, we implement a Context-Free Grammar (CFG) parser built upon a substantial set of grammar rules – over 9,600 in total – created through a semi-automatic process. This allows for robust and flexible parsing of a wide range of NWP structures. We evaluate our approach on a challenging test set comprising over 1,500 diverse NWPs, demonstrating its effectiveness with a precision of 95.4% and a recall of 60.2%. These results indicate a significant advancement in the field, showcasing the potential for semantic parsing and reasoning to effectively tackle the complexities of automated NWP solving. The remainder of this paper details the specifics of our meaning representation language, the CFG parser implementation, the experimental setup, and a thorough analysis of the results, along with a discussion of future directions. References:   Kushal, M., & Barner, K. (2016). Analyzing and overcoming common errors in solving elementary mathematics word problems.

Machine translation (MT) systems typically operate on text that has already been tokenized – broken down into discrete units, ideally corresponding to morphemes or words. However, for languages where orthography does not explicitly mark morpheme boundaries – such as German, Dutch, Turkish, and many others – the tokenization process itself represents a significant challenge and a source of ambiguity. A single orthographic word can often correspond to multiple valid segmentations, each with potentially different translation implications. Traditionally, MT systems have addressed this by employing a single, “best” segmentation, often derived using rule-based methods or statistical segmenters trained on limited data. Recent work, however, has demonstrated the benefits of exploring multiple possible segmentations simultaneously. Specifically, representing the input as a  segmentation lattice  – a graph encoding a set of alternative segmentations – allows the MT system to consider a wider range of hypotheses and potentially select the segmentation that leads to the most accurate translation (Popović et al., 2015; Kocmi et al., 2016). This is particularly advantageous when the optimal segmentation is context-dependent and difficult to predict a priori. A key challenge in building effective segmentation lattices is generating sufficient  diversity  in the segmentations. Previous approaches have largely relied on combining the outputs of multiple, independent segmenters, each trained with different algorithms or on different data (Popović et al., 2015). While this can increase diversity, it requires maintaining and running multiple segmenters, and the performance is limited by the strengths and weaknesses of the individual components. Moreover, achieving consistent performance across diverse languages necessitates tailoring segmenters to specific linguistic characteristics, hindering the development of a general-purpose solution. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach: building segmentation lattices using a single, probabilistic model – a maximum entropy model – trained to predict compound word splitting. This model leverages a small set of linguistically motivated features that are applicable to a broad range of languages with productive compounding. By tuning the model’s parameters, we can control the trade-off between segmentation probability and diversity, generating lattices with a range of possible segmentations suitable for MT. We focus on German as a primary test case, as it poses significant challenges for tokenization due to its free word order and extensive compounding. However, we demonstrate the generalizability of our approach by applying it to Hungarian and Turkish as well, languages with distinct morphological characteristics. We present results on German-English, Hungarian-English, and Turkish-English translation tasks, showing substantial improvements in translation quality – as measured by BLEU score – over strong baseline systems, including those employing state-of-the-art single-segmentation approaches.

The recent resurgence of neural networks has led to significant advances across numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks. A defining characteristic of many state-of-the-art models is the incorporation of character-level information (Luong & Manning, 2016; Kim et al., 2016; Schuster & Nakajima, 2015). Unlike traditional word-level approaches that rely on predefined vocabularies and discrete symbols, character-level models operate directly on the raw text, offering several advantages. They are robust to out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, can better handle morphological variations, and have the potential to learn subword units that capture meaningful linguistic information. Despite these benefits, a critical question remains largely unanswered: what exactly do character-aware neural networks  learn ? While quantitative evaluations consistently demonstrate improved performance, a deeper qualitative understanding of the internal representations and learned patterns is lacking. Do these models simply memorize statistical co-occurrences, or do they, in effect, discover and encode linguistic rules? The “black box” nature of neural networks makes uncovering such insights challenging. Existing interpretability techniques, such as attention mechanisms, often focus on word-level relationships and offer limited visibility into the character-level dynamics. Previous work has begun to address this gap, aiming to disentangle the internal workings of these models (Murdoch et al., 2018). However, much of this research concentrates on recurrent neural networks (RNNs). We argue for a more comprehensive analysis that also encompasses convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which represent a distinct architectural paradigm and are widely used in NLP. CNNs excel at capturing local patterns, making them particularly well-suited for identifying morphological features. In this paper, we delve into the character-level patterns learned by both CNNs and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTMs) networks when applied to the task of morphological tagging – a task inherently sensitive to subword structure and linguistic rules. We extend the contextual decomposition technique introduced by Murdoch et al. (2018) to accommodate CNN architectures, allowing us to systematically probe the internal representations and identify which character combinations are most influential in prediction. We conduct experiments on three morphologically diverse languages – German, Finnish, and Turkish – each presenting unique challenges and opportunities for uncovering linguistic insights. By comparing the learned patterns with manually-defined morphological segmentations and annotations, we aim to determine whether these models are indeed capable of discovering and encoding understandable linguistic rules, or are merely relying on surface-level statistical correlations. Our findings demonstrate that character-aware neural networks implicitly learn patterns that align remarkably well with linguistic principles, suggesting that they are not simply memorizing data but are, to some extent, reconstructing the underlying rules of morphology.

Understanding public opinion is a crucial task with broad applications, ranging from market research and brand monitoring to political analysis and public health surveillance. The proliferation of online review platforms and social media has created an unprecedented volume of textual data expressing opinions on virtually any topic imaginable. Automatically extracting and analyzing these opinions, therefore, has become a central focus of Natural Language Processing (NLP) research. Sentiment analysis, the computational task of determining the emotional tone expressed in text, is a core component of this endeavor. While early work in sentiment analysis often focused on document-level polarity classification (e.g., positive, negative, neutral) (Turney, 2002;Pang et al., 2002), a growing body of research recognizes the limitations of such coarse-grained analysis (Cambria et al., 2013). A crucial refinement lies in analyzing sentiment at the sentence level. This allows for a more nuanced understanding of  why  a user holds a particular opinion, identifying specific aspects of a product or service that are praised or criticized. Moreover, simply classifying sentiment as positive or negative often fails to capture the  strength  of the expressed opinion. A review stating “the battery life is good” conveys a different sentiment than “the battery life is exceptional,” even though both are positive. Therefore, accurately predicting both opinion polarity (positive/negative) and opinion strength (e.g., weak/strong) at the sentence level is essential for building a comprehensive opinion analysis system. However, achieving this fine-grained analysis is hampered by the scarcity of labeled training data. Obtaining large, accurately annotated datasets for sentence-level semantic orientation, including both polarity and strength information, is a costly and time-consuming process. This presents a significant bottleneck for supervised learning approaches. Existing approaches often rely on distant supervision techniques leveraging pre-defined lexicons (Wilson et al., 2005) or heuristics to automatically label data, but these methods often introduce noise and inaccuracies. To address this challenge, we propose the Multi-Experts Model (MEM), a weakly supervised approach to sentence-level semantic orientation analysis. MEM leverages potentially noisy indicators derived from readily available coarse-grained data – specifically, document-level ratings – combined with the predictions of diverse base predictors. These base predictors can include lexicon-based methods, supervised machine learning models trained on limited fine-grained data (if available), and even other existing sentiment analysis systems. We integrate these diverse signals into a unified probabilistic framework inspired by ensemble learning and graph-based semi-supervised learning, allowing MEM to learn from noisy and incomplete information.

Semantic inference – the ability to deduce new facts from existing knowledge – is a cornerstone of natural language understanding and reasoning. A crucial component of many semantic inference systems is the ability to represent and learn  entailment rules ; statements defining when one piece of knowledge logically follows from another. These rules are often expressed in terms of predicates – properties or relations that hold between entities. For instance, the rule “If X is a parent of Y, then X is a relative of Y” expresses an entailment relationship between the predicates ‘parent_of’ and ‘relative_of’. Consequently, learning to effectively represent and utilize these rules is fundamental to tasks ranging from question answering and text summarization to machine translation and commonsense reasoning. A natural way to model these entailment relationships is through  entailment graphs . In an entailment graph, nodes represent predicates, and directed edges denote entailment rules—an edge from predicate A to predicate B indicates that A entails B. These graphs provide a concise and interpretable representation of the knowledge required for semantic inference. However, learning such graphs is computationally challenging, particularly when dealing with large vocabularies and complex entailment relationships. Existing approaches often struggle with scalability, becoming intractable as the number of predicates grows. Recent work by [Cite a recent state-of-the-art exact algorithm here] presents an exact algorithm for learning entailment graphs. While achieving excellent results in terms of graph quality, this algorithm suffers from significant computational complexity, limiting its application to smaller datasets and predicate sets. The core difficulty lies in the potentially exponential search space required to determine the optimal graph structure. In this paper, we present a novel approach to efficiently approximate learning entailment graphs. Our key insight stems from the observation that real-world entailment graphs often exhibit a characteristic “tree-like” property. This structure suggests that the graph can be efficiently decomposed and learned incrementally. We formalize this observation by introducing the concept of  forest-reducible graphs , a novel graph type possessing properties amenable to efficient approximation. Leveraging this structural property, we develop an iterative algorithm that approximates the optimal entailment graph by progressively adding edges based on a locally optimal criterion. Critically, each iteration of our algorithm requires only linear time complexity, enabling its application to significantly larger datasets than previously possible. We rigorously compare our approximation algorithm to the aforementioned state-of-the-art exact algorithm both theoretically and empirically. Our results demonstrate that our method achieves comparable graph quality while offering substantial improvements in efficiency and scalability.

Named entity recognition (NER) has long been a core task in natural language processing, focusing on identifying and categorizing mentions of real-world entities – people, organizations, locations, and so on – within text. Traditionally, NER systems have operated with a limited set of broad semantic classes, sufficient for many information extraction purposes. For example, distinguishing between Person, Organization, and Location provides valuable information for tasks like knowledge base construction or event tracking. However, as natural language processing systems tackle increasingly complex applications, the need for more fine-grained semantic understanding becomes paramount. Consider a system designed to provide nuanced answers to complex questions. Simply knowing that “Apple” is an Organization is insufficient; determining whether it refers to Apple Inc. (the technology company), Apple Records (the record label), or apple (the fruit) is critical for accurate response generation. This motivates the study of semantic subtype induction, a problem where the goal is to automatically assign noun phrases to a much larger and more detailed set of semantic classes than those typically used in traditional NER. While the broader field of NER has seen substantial progress, driven by advances in machine learning and deep learning techniques (Nadeau and Sekine, 2007; Lample et al., 2016), semantic subtype induction remains comparatively under-explored. The challenge lies not only in the increased complexity of the class space – a dramatic increase in the number of potential labels – but also in the inherent data sparsity associated with fine-grained categories. Obtaining sufficient labeled data for each specific subtype is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. In this paper, we address this challenge by focusing on leveraging structural information inherent in the semantic class hierarchy and relationships between noun phrase mentions within a document. We propose an approach that enhances the standard supervised learning paradigm for semantic subtype induction through two key techniques: hierarchical classification and collective classification. Hierarchical classification acknowledges the inherent organization within the set of semantic classes, often represented as a taxonomy (e.g., a tree structure). By exploiting this structure, we can break down the multi-class classification problem into a series of binary classification decisions, potentially improving performance and reducing data sparsity issues. Collective classification, on the other hand, recognizes that noun phrase mentions are not isolated entities. Instead, they occur within a document context, and the semantic class of one mention can provide valuable clues regarding the classes of other mentions in the same document.
