By jointly inferring the classes of all mentions within a document, we can leverage these contextual dependencies to enhance accuracy.

Wikipedia has rapidly become an invaluable resource for a wide range of research areas, from natural language processing and knowledge graph construction to large-scale historical and cultural studies (Halfaker et al., 2011; Sorokina & Gauch, 2014). Its immense size, broad coverage, and readily available, machine-readable format make it uniquely suited for computational analysis. A particularly compelling area of study lies in leveraging Wikipedia’s vast collection of biographical articles – pages detailing the lives of notable individuals. However, effectively utilizing this resource requires the ability to automatically parse and understand the structure of these pages. A typical Wikipedia biographical article is not simply a continuous narrative; rather, it is organized into distinct sections, each addressing a specific aspect of the person’s life. These sections commonly include “Early life,” “Career,” “Education,” “Personal life,” “Awards,” and “Legacy,” among others. Identifying these biographical sections is a crucial step towards enabling a variety of downstream tasks, such as automated biography summarization, relationship extraction, and event timeline construction. For instance, knowing which sections contain information about a person’s education allows for focused extraction of educational achievements, or identifying the “Career” section facilitates the extraction of professional history. Despite the importance of this task, it has received limited direct attention. Existing work often relies on manually curated datasets or heuristics, which are costly to create and may not generalize well across the diverse range of biographical pages in Wikipedia. This paper addresses the problem of automatically recognizing biographical sections within Wikipedia articles. We frame this as a sequence classification problem, where each section of a biographical page is labeled as either belonging to a biographical category or not. A key contribution of our work is a novel supervised learning approach that bypasses the need for costly manual annotation. We demonstrate a method for automatically acquiring training data from the inherent structure and linking patterns within Wikipedia itself. Furthermore, we demonstrate that surprisingly simple features, derived solely from the section titles, prove remarkably effective in accurately identifying biographical sections. Specifically, we show that six carefully selected features – focusing on lexical cues present in section headings – outperform a strong baseline based on general-purpose text features. Our experiments demonstrate a significant performance gain, establishing the viability of a lightweight approach for this important task. This paper proceeds as follows: Section 2 provides a discussion of related work. Section 3 details our proposed methodology, including the automatic data acquisition process and feature engineering.

Syntax-augmented machine translation (SAMT) has emerged as a promising approach to incorporating syntactic information into statistical machine translation (SMT) systems (Chiang, 2005). Unlike phrase-based SMT, which relies on surface-level co-occurrences, SAMT builds upon a formal grammar that encodes linguistic structure. This enables the system to generalize beyond observed phrase pairs and handle long-distance dependencies more effectively, particularly in language pairs with significant structural divergence. A key component of SAMT is the creation of a bilingual grammar, typically induced from a monolingual grammar and a parallel corpus. This involves identifying correspondences between syntactic constituents in the source and target languages, and representing these correspondences as bilingual labels. However, as the complexity of the grammar increases—driven by the desire to capture finer-grained linguistic distinctions—SAMT systems often encounter practical challenges related to data sparsity and ambiguity (De Neefe et al., 2011). A large label set leads to an exponential increase in the number of possible grammar rules, many of which may receive little or no support from the training data. This sparsity hinders parameter estimation and limits the system’s ability to generalize to unseen sentences. Simultaneously, the sheer number of potential rule applications introduces ambiguity during decoding, making it difficult to identify the most likely translation. Several approaches have been proposed to address these issues. Smoothing techniques can help mitigate sparsity, while sophisticated decoding algorithms are employed to manage ambiguity. However, these strategies often come at a computational cost, and may not fully resolve the underlying problem of an overly complex grammar. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that directly tackles the size of the label set through  category coarsening . Inspired by work on tree-to-tree grammars (Hülstaert, 1999), we introduce an algorithm that systematically merges similar syntactic categories, resulting in a “collapsed” grammar that retains the expressive power of the original but with fewer nonterminal labels. Our method differs from related work on grammar induction and simplification (Knight and Graehl, 1998; Sumita et al., 2002). While previous studies often focus on reducing the overall size of the grammar by removing rarely occurring rules, our approach specifically targets the label set, aiming to strike a balance between grammatical precision and computational efficiency. We induce bilingual labels, leverage the category coarsening algorithm to reduce label set size, and project back to monolingual labeling consistent with standard SAMT formalism. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on Chinese-English translation.

The ability to parse non-contiguous, or discontinuous, constituents is a long-standing challenge in natural language processing. Traditional context-free grammars (CFGs), the workhorse of many parsing systems, are fundamentally limited in their ability to represent such structures directly. While CFGs can, in principle, generate discontinuous constituents through the use of empty elements or co-reference, doing so often leads to increased ambiguity and, crucially, drastically increases parsing complexity. Natural languages, however, frequently exhibit discontinuity, manifested in phenomena like coordination, gapping, tough-movement, and free relative clauses. Beyond simply handling these constructions, the efficient and accurate parsing of discontinuous structures is essential for many downstream NLP tasks, including machine translation, information extraction, and semantic analysis. Several approaches have been proposed to address this challenge. One common strategy is to relax the constituency assumption altogether, employing dependency-based formalisms. Dependency grammars allow for non-projective dependencies, directly representing relationships between words regardless of their linear order. However, these approaches often sacrifice the hierarchical structure inherent in constituency-based representations, which can be valuable for capturing long-range dependencies and semantic organization. Another line of research explores extensions to CFGs, such as Tree-Adjoining Grammar (TAG) (Joshi et al., 1975) and Linear Indexed Grammar (LIG) (Gazdar et al., 1988). These grammars introduce mechanisms for combining and re-ordering constituent trees, allowing for the generation of non-contiguous structures, but they often introduce significant computational complexity. Synchronous grammars, initially developed for machine translation (Alshawi, 1992), offer an intriguing framework for representing relationships between parallel structures. They operate by simultaneously generating structures in multiple languages, and can naturally handle certain types of discontinuity when aligning non-contiguous elements. However, synchronous grammars lack a clear mechanism for systematically controlling the degree of discontinuity. In this paper, we introduce  hybrid grammars , a novel formalism built as an extension of synchronous grammars intended to address these limitations. Hybrid grammars achieve discontinuity through the “coupling” of lexical elements, effectively linking parts of the generated structures that are not necessarily adjacent. Critically, hybrid grammars separate the  generation  of linear and hierarchical structures, allowing for a flexible and principled way of modeling discontinuity. One component of a hybrid grammar generates linear strings, while another focuses on representing hierarchical relationships. Combined, they are capable of producing the structures required to represent discontinuous constituents in natural language. Our contribution lies not only in formalizing a new grammar but also in demonstrating its theoretical advantages.

Morphology, the study of word formation, is a core component of natural language processing, impacting tasks ranging from machine translation to information retrieval. A fundamental problem within morphology is the  Paradigm Cell Filling  (PCF) problem, which asks: given a partially completed inflection table for a word – representing its forms across different grammatical categories like tense, number, and gender – can we accurately predict the missing forms? This task, at its heart, requires understanding the systematic relationships within a language’s morphological system and applying those rules to complete the table. Traditional approaches to PCF have relied heavily on rule-based systems, handcrafted feature engineering, and statistical methods like Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Maximum Entropy models (HMMs; Jurafsky & Martin, 2009). While these methods can achieve reasonable performance, they are often labor-intensive to develop, requiring significant linguistic expertise for each language. Furthermore, they often struggle to generalize to unseen morphological patterns or infrequent data points. More recently, neural network-based approaches have begun to emerge, leveraging the power of distributed representations and end-to-end learning. However, many existing neural approaches still require substantial amounts of training data to achieve competitive performance. This is a significant limitation, particularly for morphologically rich languages where annotated data is scarce. Access to large, high-quality parallel corpora necessary for training traditional machine translation-based solutions can also be a hurdle. This paper presents a novel encoder-decoder neural architecture designed specifically for the PCF problem, with an emphasis on data efficiency. Our approach departs from previous neural methods by leveraging the inherent structure of inflection tables, representing them as sequences amenable to sequence-to-sequence learning. We evaluate our models on a diverse set of 18 datasets spanning 8 different languages, demonstrating performance comparable to, or exceeding, existing state-of-the-art systems while requiring significantly less training data. To further facilitate research in this area, we also introduce a new, publicly available dataset for the PCF task, and we release the code implementing our system. The contributions of this work lie in a powerful, data-efficient neural model for the PCF task, a new dataset to further research, and a commitment to reproducibility through readily available code. This work aims to lower the barrier to entry for morphological research and to enable the development of more robust and adaptable NLP systems for a wider range of languages. Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. (2009).  Speech and language processing .

Incremental parsing aims to build a parse tree as input is received token by token, mirroring human sentence processing. This contrasts with batch parsing, which requires the complete sentence before analysis can begin. The benefits of incremental parsing are particularly pronounced in real-time applications such as human-computer interaction, speech recognition, and machine translation, where delays are unacceptable. Transition-based parsing is a popular paradigm for incremental parsing, modelling parsing as a sequence of actions applied to a buffer of input tokens and a stack representing the partially built parse tree. However, a significant challenge for incremental transition-based parsing lies in its inherent limitations when dealing with incomplete input – the parser must make decisions without the benefit of knowing future tokens. This “lack of lookahead” necessitates robust feature engineering to effectively capture the relevant contextual information from the limited available input. Traditional approaches to feature engineering in incremental parsing often involve manually crafting a large set of features, encompassing lexical, morphological, and syntactic information within a fixed-size window around the current token. However, designing such features is a laborious and language-specific process, and it’s often difficult to anticipate which features will be most informative for a given parsing decision. Moreover, not all features are equally relevant in every parsing state; the optimal feature set is likely to be context-dependent. The problem is exacerbated in multilingual settings, where a single feature set may not generalize effectively across languages with different grammatical structures. In this work, we address the challenge of dynamic feature utilization in incremental parsing by introducing an attention mechanism. Our approach frames feature selection as a learning problem, allowing the parser to automatically determine which features are most relevant for each parsing action, based on the current parsing state and the available context. This attention mechanism effectively acts as context-dependent dynamic feature selection, weighting features according to their importance. Specifically, our model learns to focus on specific tokens within the local context, providing insights into which parts of the input are most influential in determining the next parsing action. We present a simple yet effective model that integrates attention into a standard transition-based parsing framework. Through multilingual experiments across a diverse set of languages, we demonstrate the substantial performance gains achieved by our attention-based feature selection method compared to baseline systems relying on static feature sets. Further, to aid interpretability and understanding of the model’s behavior, particularly in instances of local ambiguity, we introduce an augmented test dataset and analyze the attention weights learned by the model, revealing valuable insights into its decision-making process.

Lexical entailment—the relationship between words where the meaning of one word is contained within the meaning of another (e.g.,  dog  entails  animal )—is a fundamental task in natural language processing with broad implications for applications such as text summarization, question answering, and information retrieval. While human judgment of lexical entailment is often straightforward, automating this process has proven challenging. Existing approaches range from knowledge-based methods leveraging lexical resources like WordNet, to corpus-based methods relying on distributional semantics. Recent work has shown the promise of distributional vectors – dense, low-dimensional representations of words learned from large corpora – for capturing semantic relationships, including entailment. However, a crucial question remains:  what  exactly are distributional vector models learning when they successfully identify entailment pairs? Earlier work by Pilehvar et al. (2018) suggested that a popular model, based on retrofitting distributional vectors with Hearst patterns, primarily learns to measure the prototypicality of a word within its presumed hypernym. This conclusion raised concerns that success on lexical entailment datasets might be driven by identifying typical instances of categories rather than true semantic containment. In this paper, we challenge this interpretation. Through a detailed qualitative analysis of the retrofitting model, we demonstrate that it not only captures prototypicality but, crucially,  strongly learns to identify hypernyms via Hearst patterns . Hearst patterns – linguistic patterns such as “X such as Y” or “X or Y” – are well-established indicators of hypernymy (Hearst, 1998). Our analysis reveals that the model effectively exploits these patterns present in training data to discern hypernym-hyponym relationships, even beyond simply measuring typicality. Motivated by this finding, we present a novel model that explicitly leverages the model’s sensitivity to Hearst patterns as a method of feature extraction. Our approach borrows inspiration from Principal Component Analysis (PCA), iteratively identifying and extracting features representative of hypernymic relationships learned through the patterns. These extracted features are then combined with strengths of other distributional models, resulting in a system that matches or outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on multiple standard lexical entailment datasets. Our contributions, therefore, are threefold: (1) a rigorous qualitative analysis demonstrating that the retrofitting model actively learns to leverage Hearst patterns for hypernym identification, (2) a novel feature extraction method based on iteratively exploiting this behavior, and (3) a competitive model for lexical entailment that combines the strengths of multiple approaches. This work suggests a path toward a better understanding of  how  distributional vector models operate and offers a practical method of improving their performance on tasks reliant on semantic relationships like lexical entailment.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) – the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text – is a fundamental component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and knowledge base construction (Nadeau & Sekine, 2007). Traditionally, NER systems heavily relied on hand-crafted features derived from linguistic knowledge and domain expertise (Ratinov & Roth, 2009; Chiang & Lin, 2007). However, the advent of deep learning techniques has led to substantial progress in NER, enabling the development of powerful systems that automatically learn feature representations from raw text (Huang et al., 2015; Ma & Hovy, 2016; Lample et al., 2016). Despite these advances, deep learning models typically require large amounts of manually annotated training data to achieve optimal performance. Annotating data is expensive and time-consuming, particularly for specialized domains where expert knowledge is often needed. This limitation has spurred research into alternative approaches that can leverage readily available, albeit less expensive, resources. Distant supervision, a paradigm that automatically generates training labels by aligning text with existing knowledge bases (KB) or dictionaries, has emerged as a promising solution (Mintz et al., 2009; Hakkani-Tür et al., 2010). In the context of NER, this often involves mapping entity mentions in text to corresponding entries in a dictionary. However, applying distant supervision is not without its challenges. The automatic labeling process is inherently noisy, as a single entity mention can correspond to multiple possible entity types, or even be incorrectly linked to an entity in the dictionary. Furthermore, dictionaries are often incomplete and may not cover all entity variations present in the text. Existing approaches to mitigate the effect of noisy labels have typically focused on incorporating more sophisticated learning algorithms (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017) or employing techniques such as multi-instance learning (Yao et al., 2017). While these methods can improve performance, they often require careful tuning and can still struggle in scenarios with high levels of noise. In this paper, we address the problem of learning effective NER models from noisy data generated through distant supervision. We propose two novel neural models specifically designed to handle the challenges of distant supervision using domain-specific dictionaries. First, within the standard sequence labeling framework, we introduce a revised Fuzzy CRF layer that effectively manages tokens with multiple potential labels. Recognizing the inherent limitations of this traditional approach, we then present a more radical departure: AutoNER, a novel neural model built upon a “Tie or Break” scheme that actively learns to either confidently assign a label based on dictionary evidence or defer to other contextual cues.

Human sentence processing is, at its core, an incremental activity. As we read or hear a sentence unfold, we don’t wait for the entire string to be presented before beginning to construct its meaning. Instead, evidence from both behavioral experiments (e.g., Rayner, 1998) and neuroimaging studies (e.g., Hagoort et al., 2003) suggests that we actively build syntactic structures and associated interpretations in a left-to-right, word-by-word fashion. This contrasts sharply with the vast majority of modern statistical parsers, which operate on the entire input sentence simultaneously, employing bottom-up, dynamic programming approaches to derive a parse at the conclusion of processing. While these bottom-up parsers have achieved impressive accuracy (e.g., Petrov & Klein, 2007), they lack the incremental, predictive nature of human parsing. The discrepancy between human and machine parsing has motivated research into top-down parsing methods. These approaches attempt to mimic the human ability to maintain multiple, partially-completed parse trees as each new word is encountered, effectively hypothesizing syntactic structure before the full context is available. However, top-down parsers have historically lagged behind their bottom-up counterparts in terms of overall accuracy. The primary limitation has been the computational complexity associated with maintaining and exploring multiple parse hypotheses without the benefit of dynamic programming’s efficiency. Previous attempts (e.g., Roark, 2001) have demonstrated the feasibility of top-down parsing, but have struggled to achieve competitive performance. In this paper, we present a novel syntactic parser designed to bridge this gap. Our parser operates left-to-right and top-down, maintaining a set of fully-connected parse trees representing alternative syntactic analyses as processing proceeds. Crucially, we embrace a rich feature set, leveraging the power of modern machine learning techniques, in exchange for abandoning the efficiency of dynamic programming. This trade-off allows us to more effectively model the complexities of natural language syntax and realize the potential of a genuinely incremental parsing strategy. Our experimental results demonstrate a significant advance for top-down parsing. We achieve a parsing accuracy of 89.4%, representing a 20% error reduction over the previous state-of-the-art result of 86.8% for single top-down parsers (Roark, 2001). This improvement underscores the benefits of combining a top-down parsing framework with a robust feature representation. We argue that this work represents a step toward building more cognitively plausible and potentially more robust natural language processing systems. The implications extend beyond parsing accuracy, offering a valuable platform for investigating the interaction between syntax and semantics in real-time language comprehension.

Vector space models have long been a cornerstone of natural language processing, providing a powerful means of representing text as numerical vectors amenable to machine learning algorithms. Recent years have witnessed a surge in the popularity of distributional representations - dense, low-dimensional vectors trained to capture semantic relationships between words and phrases. These representations, such as word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of NLP tasks. Extending this success to the document level has been a primary focus, leading to the development of document embedding techniques like Doc2Vec (Le & Mikolov, 2014) and Paragraph Vectors (Mikolov et al., 2013). These models learn a fixed-length vector representation for each document, capturing its overall semantic meaning. However, existing document vector approaches often fall short when dealing with complex, multi-topic documents. Standard paragraph vector models tend to represent a document with a single, averaged vector, potentially losing nuanced topic information and failing to capture the diverse semantic contexts present within the text. Furthermore, these dense vector representations can be computationally expensive, both in terms of training time and memory requirements, hindering scalability for large datasets. Recent attempts to address these limitations, such as the Non-negative Tensor Singular Decomposition (NTSG) model (Liu et al., 2015a), have shown promising results but still face challenges in balancing performance with computational efficiency and the accurate representation of multifaceted documents. In this paper, we introduce Sparse Composite Document Vectors (SCDV), a novel feature vector formation technique designed to overcome the limitations of current document embedding methods. SCDV leverages the strengths of distributional word embeddings while incorporating a soft clustering mechanism to model multiple semantic contexts within a document. Critically, rather than averaging word embeddings or employing complex tensor decompositions, SCDV clusters word embeddings into semantic groups and then chains these groups together to form document-level topic vectors. This composite structure allows for a more nuanced representation of documents with diverse thematic content. Through extensive experimentation on both multi-class and multi-label classification tasks, we demonstrate that SCDV consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art NTSG model. Moreover, we showcase SCDV’s strong generalization capabilities across heterogeneous tasks including Topic Coherence evaluation, context-sensitive learning scenarios and Information Retrieval tasks. Notably, SCDV achieves significant reductions in both training and prediction times compared to existing methods, offering a compelling balance between performance and computational efficiency.

Bilingual Named Entity (NE) alignment – the task of identifying corresponding NEs in two different languages – is a critical component in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and multilingual knowledge base construction. Accurate NE alignment facilitates better understanding of multilingual documents, improves translation quality by ensuring consistent handling of proper nouns, and enables seamless integration of information extracted from diverse linguistic sources. Despite significant progress in NE recognition and machine translation, the task of  aligning  NEs across languages remains challenging. Existing methods often treat NE recognition and alignment as separate steps, leading to error propagation and suboptimal performance. For instance, a noisy NE recognizer can generate many false positives, which are then passed on to the alignment stage, increasing the search space and lowering alignment accuracy. Furthermore, the inherent ambiguity in NE translation poses a significant hurdle. Named entities can be translated in multiple ways – sometimes semantically equivalent terms are used (e.g., “New York” – “纽约”), while other times phonetic transliteration occurs (e.g., “Google” – “谷歌”), and in some instances, a combination of both or even descriptive paraphrases are employed. Traditional alignment approaches often struggle to account for this diversity and rely heavily on string matching or statistical co-occurrence, which can be unreliable when dealing with varying translation strategies. Recent work has explored more sophisticated alignment strategies, including utilizing parallel corpora and leveraging contextual information. However, these methods rarely capitalize on the strong relationship between NE type and translation behavior. Specifically, the way an NE is translated—whether it's literal translation, transliteration, or a descriptive equivalent—is heavily dependent on its entity type (PER, ORG, LOC, etc.). For example, organizations are frequently transliterated, while locations are more often translated semantically. Moreover, a fundamental assumption of accurate alignment is that NEs in a correctly aligned pair should share the same semantic type; one would not expect to align a person’s name with a location. In this paper, we leverage these observations to propose a novel integrated model for jointly recognizing and aligning bilingual NEs between Chinese and English. Our approach moves beyond treating these tasks as separate pipeline stages and instead frames them as a unified inference problem. We introduce a new feature, the “mapping type ratio,” which quantifies the proportion of internal tokens within an NE that undergo semantic translation – providing valuable evidence about the likely translation strategy. Additionally, we explicitly enforce an entity type consistency constraint during alignment, ensuring that aligned NEs possess the same type.

Chinese Word Segmentation (CWS) remains a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing, serving as a crucial preprocessing step for many downstream applications such as machine translation, information retrieval, and sentiment analysis. Unlike languages that explicitly delineate word boundaries with spaces, Chinese relies on identifying word segments within a continuous stream of characters. Traditional approaches to CWS involved dictionary-based methods, rule-based systems, and statistical models like Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (Xue and Shen, 2003;Zhang and Lee, 2003). More recently, neural network architectures have demonstrated significant advancements in CWS performance. These include Bi-directional LSTMs (BiLSTMs) combined with a CRF layer (Huang et al., 2015), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Liu et al., 2016), and attention-based models (Sun et al., 2017). Despite the progress, effectively capturing the contextual information surrounding a character remains a key challenge. While BiLSTMs inherently model sequential dependencies, they often struggle to fully represent the semantic relationships between characters and their surrounding word contexts. Further, acquiring large, accurately labeled datasets for CWS is both expensive and time-consuming. This limitation motivates research into methods for leveraging unlabeled data and semi-supervised learning techniques. One promising avenue for improving CWS performance is to employ character embeddings. Character embeddings represent each character as a dense vector, enabling models to generalize to unseen words and capture morphological similarities. Existing approaches often train character embeddings directly on the labeled CWS data, or utilize pre-trained embeddings from large text corpora. However, these methods may not fully exploit the potential of contextual information. Inspired by the success of dependency-context word embeddings in neural parsing (Shen et al., 2018), which leverage automatically labeled dependencies to refine word representations, we explore a similar approach for CWS. Specifically, we investigate training character embeddings on a  word-based context —using automatically segmented data generated during training as a source of contextual signal. This allows character embeddings to learn representations that are informed by the likely word boundaries and semantic relationships present in the text. Our method effectively creates a form of self-training, similar to tri-training (Abney et al., 2004), but focuses specifically on refining character-level representations. We demonstrate that this simple yet effective method significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art neural word segmentation models. Our experiments, conducted on standard Chinese datasets, show that character embeddings trained with word-context information consistently outperform baseline models and achieve competitive results compared to tri-training methods for leveraging autosegmented data.

The rapid growth of information available online has created a critical need for techniques capable of automatically extracting structured knowledge from unstructured text. Traditional Information Extraction (IE) systems, while successful in specific domains, rely heavily on manually defined patterns, ontologies, and supervised learning approaches – a process both costly and brittle when faced with the ever-expanding breadth of topics and linguistic variations on the web. Open Information Extraction (Open IE) emerged as a compelling alternative, aiming to automatically discover relations and entities directly from text  without  prior knowledge or domain-specific resources (Banko et al., 2008; Etzioni et al., 2008). This paradigm shift allows for greater scalability and adaptability, making Open IE particularly well-suited for analyzing the vast and heterogeneous content of the web. Since its inception, Open IE has attracted significant research attention, leading to a diverse range of proposed methods. These approaches vary considerably in their underlying linguistic analyses, relation extraction techniques, and overall system architectures. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the evolution of Open IE, detailing the key methods developed to date. We aim to provide a structured understanding of the field, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches, and critically examining the challenges that remain. Our discussion begins with an outline of the core challenges inherent in Open IE, including relation ambiguity, the lack of predefined schemas, and the need for robust handling of linguistic variation. We then trace the development of Open IE techniques chronologically, categorizing them into distinct phases reflecting major shifts in methodology. Early approaches primarily focused on pattern-based extraction, leveraging syntactic parses and heuristics to identify relational triples. Subsequent work explored unsupervised learning techniques, employing clustering and distributional semantics to discover relations without labeled data. More recently, research has incorporated neural network models, leveraging their ability to learn complex patterns and represent semantic information. Furthermore, we critically assess the dominant evaluation methodologies used in Open IE research. While traditional IE evaluation metrics like precision, recall, and F1-score remain relevant, their application to Open IE is often problematic due to the lack of a gold standard and the inherent ambiguity of extracted relations. We discuss the limitations of commonly used benchmarks and propose considerations for developing more robust and informative evaluation procedures. Finally, we conclude by highlighting promising directions for future research in Open IE. These include incorporating knowledge graph integration, developing techniques for handling coreference resolution and event linking, and addressing the challenges of scale and efficiency required to process massive datasets.

The ability to identify paraphrases – different ways of expressing the same information need – is a core task in natural language processing (NLP) with broad applications. These range from improving information retrieval (IR) systems by expanding queries to enhancing the performance of question answering (QA) and machine translation (MT) systems. Traditional approaches to paraphrase identification have often relied on manually constructed datasets, lexical resources like WordNet, or sophisticated semantic analysis techniques. However, these methods can be expensive to develop and maintain, and may not generalize well to novel contexts or domains. More recently, researchers have begun to leverage the vast quantities of data available in search engine logs as a source of paraphrase information. Search logs implicitly contain numerous paraphrases, as users frequently refine their initial queries with alternative formulations in an attempt to find more relevant results. A user's iterative query reformulations within a search session often represent attempts to express the same underlying information need using different wording. However, not all query pairs within a search session constitute true paraphrases. Many pairs may express related, but distinct, information needs, or simply represent navigational queries. This presents a significant challenge: how to accurately distinguish between genuine paraphrases and simply related queries within search log data. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel approach that incorporates user behavior information gleaned from search log sessions. We hypothesize that the ways in which users interact with search results – specifically, their clicking patterns and dwell times – can provide valuable clues as to whether two queries represent the same underlying information need. For instance, if a user submits two queries and clicks on the same set of results for both, this strongly suggests that the queries are paraphrases. Conversely, if a user clicks on different sets of results, it is more likely that the queries represent distinct information needs. We formulate the problem of paraphrase pattern learning as a classification task. Alongside conventional features such as lexical similarity and query length, we introduce three novel types of features that capture user behavior: click overlap, session position, and dwell time. These features, derived from analysis of query sessions, allow our model to better discriminate between true paraphrases and related queries. We evaluate our method using a large-scale query log from a commercial search engine. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and crucially, highlight the significant contribution of the user behavior features to improved paraphrase identification.

The cornerstone of modern Natural Language Processing (NLP) lies in the ability to represent words as dense, low-dimensional vectors – word embeddings. These embeddings, learned from large text corpora, capture semantic relationships between words based on the fundamental distributional hypothesis: words appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings (Harris, 1954; Firth, 1957). Models like Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) have become ubiquitous, serving as crucial building blocks for a vast array of NLP tasks. However, a critical limitation of these standard approaches emerges when dealing with affect – the emotional state conveyed through language. The traditional distributional hypothesis, focused purely on contextual co-occurrence, overlooks the inherent emotional valence of words. Consider the words “happy” and “sad”. While they might appear in superficially similar contexts – for example, describing reactions to events – their emotional connotations are diametrically opposed. Consequently, standard word embeddings may inadvertently place “happy” and “sad” closer together in vector space than “happy” and “joy,” a clear semantic and affective mismatch. This conflation of emotionally distinct words poses a significant challenge in tasks explicitly involving emotion, such as emotion classification, sentiment analysis, and emotion similarity judgments. The failure to adequately represent emotional nuance limits the performance of downstream affective computing applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach for learning  emotion-enriched  word representations. Our method aims to explicitly incorporate emotional information into the embedding space, pushing emotionally similar words closer together and driving emotionally dissimilar words further apart. This is achieved through a two-stage process leveraging distant supervision and recurrent neural networks. First, we automatically curate a large-scale training dataset by exploiting the emotional associations present in existing text resources. This avoids the costly and time-consuming process of manual annotation. Second, we employ two recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures designed to learn embeddings that accurately reflect both contextual similarity  and  emotional congruity. Our experimental evaluation, conducted on two benchmark tasks – emotion classification and emotion similarity – demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed representations. We consistently outperform several competitive baselines, including general-purpose word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) and existing affective word representations. These results validate our hypothesis that explicitly integrating emotional knowledge into the embedding learning process leads to significant improvements in tasks requiring nuanced understanding of affect in language. This work highlights the importance of moving beyond purely contextual representations and embracing a more holistic approach to word representation learning that accounts for the multifaceted nature of human language.

Morphological segmentation – the task of breaking words down into their constituent morphemes – is a fundamental problem in natural language processing. Accurate morphological segmentation is crucial for a variety of downstream tasks, including machine translation, information retrieval, and speech recognition, particularly for morphologically rich languages. Traditionally, morphological segmentation has relied heavily on manually annotated data, which is costly and time-consuming to create, and often unavailable for low-resource languages. Consequently, there’s been growing interest in unsupervised and semi-supervised methods capable of learning morphological structure from raw text. Morfessor (Creutz and Lagus, 2007) is a family of well-established methods designed for unsupervised morphological segmentation. It operates on the principle of Maximum Entropy Markov Models (MEMMs) and has proven effective across a range of languages. Existing Morfessor variants, such as Baseline and Categories-MAP, have achieved strong performance, becoming established baselines in the field. However, these methods can be computationally intensive, and the underlying MEMM framework presents certain limitations in terms of model expressiveness and ease of extension. In this paper, we introduce FlatCat, a novel variant of Morfessor that adopts a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) framework. FlatCat builds upon the foundational components of previous Morfessor models, inheriting the familiar morphotactic and morpheme-selection stages. However, by recasting the segmentation process within an HMM structure, we aim to gain benefits in terms of computational efficiency, model interpretability, and the potential for incorporating richer linguistic information. The HMM formulation allows for a more principled probabilistic treatment of segmentation ambiguity, leading to more robust and accurate results. Our experiments demonstrate that FlatCat, in its unsupervised configuration, achieves performance comparable to, though slightly below, the established Categories-MAP variant. However, the true strength of FlatCat emerges in the semi-supervised setting. Leveraging a small amount of annotated data, FlatCat achieves state-of-the-art results on the Morpho Challenge 2010 tasks for three diverse languages – English, Finnish, and Turkish – surpassing prior unsupervised and many semi-supervised approaches. This highlights FlatCat’s ability to effectively integrate prior knowledge with statistical learning, making it a valuable tool for morphological analysis in both high- and low-resource scenarios. This work contributes a new, computationally efficient, and high-performing morphological segmentation method to the Morfessor family, offering a promising path towards more practical and scalable unsupervised and semi-supervised morphological analysis. We release the code for FlatCat to facilitate further research and development in this area. It is important to note that this introduction sets the stage for the paper and provides the reader with context and justification for the presented work.

Relation extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text – is a cornerstone of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including knowledge base completion (KB completion), question answering, and information retrieval (Etzioni et al., 2008;Popescu et al., 2003;Banko et al., 2007). Traditionally, RE systems have relied on either manually crafted rules (Hsu and Chu-Ren Wang, 2008) or supervised machine learning methods trained on annotated data (Zheng et al., 2017;Miwa and Bansal, 2016). However, manual rule creation is time-consuming and lacks scalability, while supervised learning demands substantial labeled data, a costly and bottlenecking requirement. More recently, a paradigm shift towards distant supervision and pattern-based methods has gained prominence (Mintz et al., 2009;Spoerri et al., 2008). Distant supervision automatically generates training instances by aligning text with existing knowledge bases (KBs), enabling learning without manual annotation. Pattern-based methods, on the other hand, directly extract relations by identifying textual patterns that reliably indicate specific relationships. These patterns often take the form of lexical or syntactic structures surrounding entity pairs. A key challenge within this approach is identifying robust and accurate patterns that generalize well across different contexts. Despite advancements in pattern-based RE, existing resources often suffer from limitations. Many pattern collections are relatively small, domain-specific, or lack semantic organization. Furthermore, evaluating the quality and relationships between patterns remains a significant hurdle. Existing work mostly focuses on identifying patterns for a limited set of relations, and a comprehensive, semantically structured taxonomy of relational patterns is lacking. To address these limitations, we introduce PATTY (Pattern Taxonomy with Typed Yields): a large-scale resource for textual patterns denoting binary relations between entities. PATTY goes beyond simple pattern enumeration; it provides a semantically typed and organized taxonomy of these patterns, leveraging the rich type information from large knowledge bases and efficient algorithms for pattern discovery. Built on the principles of frequent itemset mining applied to web-scale corpora, PATTY effectively captures commonly observed patterns while ensuring a high degree of accuracy. The core contribution of this work is the creation of a comprehensive and organized resource of relational patterns. PATTY contains 350,569 pattern synsets, arranged into a taxonomy with 8,162 subsumption relationships. We present a rigorous evaluation demonstrating that PATTY achieves a pattern accuracy of 84.7% and a subsumption precision of 75%, confirming its reliability and organization. Furthermore, we are making PATTY publicly available to promote further research in relation extraction and related NLP tasks.

Determining the semantic relatedness between words is a core task in natural language processing (NLP), underpinning a diverse range of applications including information retrieval (Voorhees and Harman, 2000), text summarization (Mani, 2001), machine translation (Galley et al., 2006), and question answering (Voorhees, 1999). Traditional approaches to word similarity relied on manually crafted lexical resources such as WordNet (Miller, 1995), offering a structured hierarchy of semantic relations. However, the coverage of these resources is often limited, particularly for specialized domains or emerging vocabulary. Consequently, there has been a surge in interest in distributional semantic models (DSM) which automatically learn word representations from large text corpora (Lund and Feigenbaum, 1991; Deerwester et al., 1990). Early DSMs, like Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), represented words as vectors in a reduced-dimensional space derived from term-document matrices. More recently, neural network-based word embeddings, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), have become the dominant approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance on various word analogy and similarity tasks. These models capture complex semantic relationships by training on massive datasets, but at a significant computational cost. Constructing and storing these embeddings requires substantial memory and processing power, making them challenging to deploy in resource-constrained environments or for applications demanding real-time performance. Furthermore, many real-world NLP applications deal with streaming data, where the text arrives continuously over time. Re-training word embeddings from scratch whenever new data becomes available is impractical, and incremental update strategies can be complex and may compromise the quality of the learned representations (Pilehvar et al., 2017). Thus, there is a continuing need for methods that can efficiently estimate word similarities from streams without incurring the computational burden of traditional approaches. In this paper, we present a novel and lightweight method for streaming word similarity mining, based on explicitly counting second-order co-occurrences between words. Our approach leverages the observation that words exhibiting strong correlations in terms of their second-order co-occurrences also tend to be highly similar when considering first-order co-occurrences – a more traditional measure of association. We maintain compact buffers of co-occurred words per target word, enabling us to estimate similarities in a single pass over the data without the need for computationally expensive similarity calculations. We empirically demonstrate the scalability, rapid convergence, and robustness of our method, revealing that it achieves word similarities comparable to those produced by state-of-the-art word embeddings, but with significantly reduced computational overhead.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, becoming the dominant paradigm for automated translation. However, traditional phrase-based SMT systems often struggle with long-distance dependencies and non-local reordering phenomena, issues that are naturally addressed by formal grammars. Tree-to-string translation, which casts translation as a tree parsing problem, offers a compelling alternative. Early work in this area largely focused on synchronous context-free grammars (SCFGs), leveraging the structured representation of syntax to improve translation quality. However, SCFGs are limited in their expressive power, particularly in handling complex grammatical constructions involving non-projectivity and crossing dependencies common in many languages. Tree Adjoining Grammar (TAG) provides a more powerful formalism, capable of representing a wider range of natural language phenomena. Specifically, Synchronous TAG (sTAG) has proven effective in modeling syntactic correspondences between languages, allowing for flexible reordering and the generation of non-projective structures. Despite these advantages, applying sTAG directly to large-scale translation tasks remains a significant challenge due to the computational complexity of deriving and parsing with TAGs. Traditional TAG-based translation systems require explicit reconstruction of derivations, leading to substantial computational overhead. This paper introduces a novel approach to tree-to-string translation that leverages the expressive power of synchronous TAGs  without  the costly explicit derivation reconstruction. Our framework learns direct “tree-to-string” rules from aligned treebank-style corpora, circumventing the need for full TAG derivation. This is achieved through a specifically designed rule extraction algorithm that identifies correspondences between source tree fragments and target strings. By casting decoding as a tree parsing problem, rather than a traditional parsing process, we maintain a relatively efficient decoding speed, even when incorporating the more complex operations permitted by TAG, such as adjunction. Our experiments, conducted on the NIST Chinese-English translation task, demonstrate that incorporating adjunction into the tree-to-string translation system leads to a statistically significant improvement in translation quality, achieving a +0.7 BLEU score increase over a strong baseline system that relies solely on tree substitution. Crucially, this improvement is achieved with a modest increase in decoding time – less than 2x slower than the baseline – demonstrating the practical viability of our approach. We believe this work represents a significant step towards harnessing the full potential of TAGs for machine translation, offering a compelling balance between translation quality and computational efficiency. The demand for intelligent systems capable of understanding and reasoning over clinical text is rapidly growing. Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) represent a rich, yet largely untapped, source of information for a wide range of applications, including clinical decision support, patient risk stratification, and population health management. However, effectively harnessing the information contained within EMRs requires overcoming substantial challenges, primarily stemming from the complex and often unstructured nature of clinical notes, as well as the need for specialized knowledge to interpret medical terminology and context. Question Answering (QA) offers a particularly promising avenue for accessing and utilizing this information, enabling clinicians and researchers to pose natural language queries and receive concise, evidence-based answers directly from patient records. Despite the potential benefits, the development of robust QA systems for the medical domain has been hindered by a severe lack of large-scale, high-quality training data. Existing medical QA datasets are often limited in size, scope, or the complexity of the questions they address (Shi et al., 2015; Dhingra et al., 2016). Creating such datasets from scratch is a costly and time-consuming endeavor, requiring significant effort from medical experts to manually annotate questions, answers, and supporting evidence. In this paper, we present emrQA, a novel large-scale QA dataset for electronic medical records, generated through a resourceful methodology: re-purposing existing annotations from established NLP tasks. Rather than embarking on a costly new annotation project, we leverage the wealth of expert annotations already available within the i2b2 shared task datasets (Uzuner et al., 2007; Denny et al., 2013; Stark et al., 2016). These datasets contain annotations for tasks such as concept extraction, relation extraction, and de-identification – information that can be effectively transformed into question-answer pairs. Our approach yields a dataset comprising over 1 million questions paired with logical forms representing the underlying query intent, and more than 400,000 question-answer evidence pairs, linking questions to specific spans of text within clinical notes that support the answers. This substantial size positions emrQA as one of the largest publicly available QA datasets for the medical domain. We provide a detailed characterization of the dataset, analyzing question types, answer complexity, and the distribution of underlying clinical concepts. Furthermore, we explore the learning potential of emrQA by training baseline models for both question-to-logical form and question-to-answer mapping, demonstrating the feasibility and value of our approach. We believe that emrQA will serve as a valuable resource for the research community, accelerating the development of more accurate and reliable QA systems for electronic medical records.

Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) – the task of identifying the predicate-argument structure of a sentence – has long been a central problem in natural language processing (NLP). Understanding ‘who did what to whom, when, where, and why’ is crucial for deeper semantic interpretation and downstream applications such as question answering, information extraction, and machine translation (Dorr et al., 2007;Màrquez et al., 2008;Kipper et al., 2009). Traditionally, SRL systems heavily relied on rich linguistic features, particularly those derived from syntactic parsing (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2002;Màrquez et al., 2008). The intuition behind this reliance is that syntactic structure provides valuable cues for identifying semantic roles: arguments often occupy specific syntactic positions relative to the predicate. For example, the subject of a verb is frequently the nominal constituent immediately to the left of the verb in a dependency parse. Indeed, initial successes in SRL were often predicated on high-quality syntactic parsers and meticulously engineered features capturing syntactic relationships (Palmer et al., 2005). These features included dependency path lengths, voice (active/passive), and subtree patterns. However, the rise of deep learning has fundamentally altered the landscape of SRL. Recent neural network-based models (Zhou et al., 2016;He et al., 2017;Tan et al., 2018) have demonstrated impressive performance, often surpassing previous state-of-the-art systems  without  explicitly incorporating a syntactic backbone. These models learn representations directly from raw text, leveraging the power of distributed representations and complex non-linear transformations. This apparent success of “syntax-free” SRL has ignited a debate: is syntactic information truly essential for robust SRL performance, or is it merely a historical artifact that can be bypassed by powerful neural networks? While earlier work consistently pointed to the importance of syntax (Surdeanu et al., 2008;Màrquez et al., 2008), the recent trend raises a critical question: has deep learning rendered explicit syntactic analysis obsolete for SRL? This paper aims to quantify the significance of syntactic information in modern, deep learning-based dependency SRL systems. We hypothesize that, despite the successes of syntax-free approaches, incorporating syntactic information remains beneficial – and even crucial – for achieving state-of-the-art performance. To investigate this, we propose an enhanced argument labeling model that effectively exploits syntactic information, coupled with an extended k-order argument pruning algorithm designed to improve efficiency. Through extensive experimentation on both English and Chinese datasets (CoNLL-2008, 2009), we demonstrate that our model achieves significant performance gains over existing systems, reaffirming the quantitative importance of syntax for neural SRL.

Sentiment analysis, the task of computationally determining the emotional tone expressed in text, has become a core component of many natural language processing applications. From monitoring brand reputation and understanding customer feedback to gauging public opinion and detecting potentially harmful content, the ability to accurately assess sentiment is increasingly vital. Traditional approaches to sentiment analysis often rely on handcrafted lexicons—lists of words associated with positive or negative sentiment—and rule-based systems designed to account for phenomena like negation and intensification (Turney, 2002; Pang et al., 2002). While effective to a degree, these methods suffer from limitations in scalability, domain adaptability, and their inability to capture nuanced emotional expressions. More recently, machine learning techniques, particularly those employing vector space representations of words and phrases, have shown significant promise in sentiment analysis (Socher et al., 2013; Glorot et al., 2011). Distributed word embeddings, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), capture semantic relationships between words, allowing models to generalize beyond the specific words seen during training. However, these methods typically focus on representing individual words and may struggle to effectively capture the compositional semantics of phrases and sentences, where the meaning of a whole is more than the sum of its parts. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for sentence-level sentiment prediction based on recursive autoencoders (RAEs). RAEs learn distributed representations for multi-word phrases by recursively combining the representations of their constituent words and phrases, building a hierarchical structure that reflects the syntactic composition of the sentence. This approach allows our model to capture the complex interplay of words and phrases that contribute to overall sentiment. Crucially, our method does  not  rely on pre-defined sentiment lexicons or manually crafted rules, learning sentiment directly from the data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on standard sentiment analysis datasets, such as movie review datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance without the use of external resources. Furthermore, we explore the model's ability to predict not just a single sentiment label, but a  distribution  over sentiment labels, on a novel dataset comprised of personal narratives from the Experience Project (www.experienceproject.com). This dataset presents a unique challenge, as each story is annotated with multiple labels representing a diverse range of emotional reactions. By modeling sentiment as a multinomial distribution, we can capture the richness and complexity of human emotion with greater fidelity than traditional single-label classification approaches.

The demand for high-quality machine translation (MT) and cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) systems has grown exponentially in recent years, fueled by the increasing globalization of information and commerce. At the heart of these systems lie bilingual lexicons – dictionaries mapping words and phrases between two languages. Traditionally, the construction of such lexicons has been a laborious, time-consuming, and expensive undertaking, requiring the expertise of skilled bilingual lexicographers. While massively parallel corpora and statistical machine translation methods have lessened the dependence on manually curated lexicons to some extent, they haven't rendered them obsolete. Indeed, specialized domains often require tailored lexicons that capture the nuances of terminology not adequately represented in general-purpose resources. Several automatic methods have been proposed to circumvent the limitations of manual lexicon construction. These methods typically leverage comparable corpora – collections of texts in different languages covering the same subject matter – and employ techniques like statistical alignment or cross-lingual document classification to identify plausible translation pairs. However, many of these approaches are constrained by data sparsity, particularly for low-resource languages, and rely on the availability of sizable comparable corpora, a resource not readily available for all language pairs or specialized domains. Furthermore, the performance of these automatically generated lexicons often falls significantly short of that of manually crafted resources, hindering the overall quality of MT and CLIR systems. In this paper, we present a novel approach to automatically building specialized bilingual lexicons, capitalizing on the unique properties of Wikipedia, a massively multilingual and collaboratively edited encyclopedia. Wikipedia’s inherent structure offers a rich source of background knowledge that can be exploited in several ways. First, Wikipedia’s category system allows for identifying specialized domains within each language. Second, interlingual links between Wikipedia articles provide a natural mechanism for linking related concepts across languages. Finally, the textual content of Wikipedia articles offers a foundation for constructing generic translation dictionaries within specific domains. Our approach revolves around leveraging these properties to extract domain-specific terminology and their translations. We systematically extract domains from Wikipedia in multiple languages, align these domains based on interlingual links, and then build translation dictionaries using the textual content of related articles. We evaluate our method on four diverse specialized domains – medicine, computer science, law, and automotive engineering – using two language pairs: French-English and Romanian-English. Through rigorous experimentation and comparison with three state-of-the-art automatic lexicon building approaches, we demonstrate that our Wikipedia-based method consistently outperforms existing techniques, offering a promising path towards efficient and high-quality specialized bilingual lexicon construction for a wide range of language pairs.

The rise of the internet and social media has dramatically altered the landscape of political discourse. Online platforms, particularly political blogs, have become central hubs for the dissemination of information, the formation of public opinion, and increasingly, political mobilization (Chadwick, 2006; Papacharissi, 2002). These platforms are unique in several ways. Unlike traditional media, online blogs facilitate direct interaction between content creators (bloggers) and their audience through comment sections. This interactive element introduces a dynamic feedback loop, where the content of a post is often shaped, challenged, or reinforced by the ensuing discussion. Understanding this dynamic – specifically, predicting how a given post will be  received  by the online community – is a crucial challenge with implications for political campaigning, public communication, and the study of collective behavior. Traditional approaches to analyzing online political discourse often focus on content analysis of posts themselves (Lazersfeld et al., 1960; Krippendorff, 1980), or on network analysis of user interactions (Wasserman and Faust, 1994). However, these methods often treat posts and comments as independent entities, failing to capture the crucial relationship between the initial stimulus and its subsequent reception. More recently, computational social science has turned to topic modeling as a powerful tool for uncovering latent thematic structures within textual data (Blei et al., 2003; Steyvers and Griffiths, 2007). Topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), allow researchers to identify recurring themes or “topics” present in a corpus of text, and to assign these topics to individual documents. In this paper, we build upon existing topic modeling techniques to address the problem of predicting response to political blog posts. We argue that a more comprehensive model is needed – one that jointly captures the characteristics of both the initiating posts  and  the subsequent comments. We extend LDA in several key ways to achieve this goal, explicitly modeling author characteristics as well as the content of the comments themselves. This allows us to not only uncover the thematic structures driving discussions, but also to predict which users are most likely to participate in those discussions given a particular post. Specifically, we introduce a novel comment prediction task wherein our models are evaluated on their ability to forecast which blog users will leave comments on a given post. We evaluate on a newly constructed dataset of political blog posts and comments and demonstrate that our extended models outperform baseline approaches. Beyond quantitative evaluation, we also present a qualitative analysis of the topics discovered by our model, revealing insights into the key themes and dynamics shaping online political conversation.

Determining the gender of an author based on their written text has emerged as a compelling task within the field of computational linguistics, fueled by applications ranging from targeted advertising and personalized content recommendation to authorship attribution and digital forensics. However, a significant challenge in this domain lies in the scarcity of labeled training data. Constructing large, accurately labeled datasets for gender classification is both time-consuming and, potentially, subject to privacy concerns, while the availability of unlabeled text data is often abundant. This disparity motivates the exploration of semi-supervised learning techniques – paradigms that effectively leverage both labeled and unlabeled data to improve model performance. Existing approaches to gender classification have largely focused on utilizing textual features derived from an author’s writing style, encompassing lexical choices, syntactic patterns, and stylistic characteristics (e.g., Argawal et al., 2009; Schler et al., 2006). While these methods demonstrate promising results, their performance can be limited by the size and quality of the labeled training data. Recent work has begun to explore the integration of social information, particularly leveraging social network connections, to enhance gender prediction accuracy (e.g., Ali et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017). These approaches typically analyze direct social ties, such as follower/followee relationships, to infer gender similarities among users. However, a crucial observation is that users often connect with each other not necessarily based on shared gender, but rather on shared interests and preferences. This realization motivates a more nuanced approach to incorporating social information, focusing on  indirect  relationships built around common interests. For instance, two users who frequently participate in discussions about a specific hobby or topic are likely to share certain characteristics, potentially including gender-related patterns in their writing. In this paper, we propose a novel semi-supervised approach to gender classification that leverages both textual features and a specific type of indirect social link, termed "same-interest" links. These links are established by identifying users who exhibit overlapping engagement patterns in online communities or shared content consumption. We model the interplay between textual information and these "same-interest" links using a factor graph, termed the Textual and Social Factor Graph (TSFG). This graphical model effectively captures dependencies between user-specific textual features and their connections within the social network, facilitating robust gender prediction even with limited labeled data. Through empirical evaluation on real-world datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, highlighting the benefits of integrating textual and social modeling in a semi-supervised learning framework.

Sentiment analysis, the task of computationally determining the opinion or emotion expressed in a piece of text, has become a cornerstone of numerous applications, ranging from brand monitoring and market research to personalized recommendation systems and political analysis. Traditional approaches to sentiment classification often rely on bag-of-words models or term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) representations, neglecting the sequential nature of language and the rich contextual information contained within sentences. More recently, deep learning models, particularly Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have achieved state-of-the-art performance by automatically learning hierarchical representations of text (Socher et al., 2013; Kim, 2014). However, these models typically treat each review in isolation, failing to leverage valuable information about the users who wrote the reviews and the products being reviewed. Incorporating user and product information can significantly enhance sentiment analysis, especially in scenarios where reviews are sparse or ambiguous. For example, knowing that a user consistently provides highly critical reviews may suggest that a seemingly negative sentiment is simply reflective of that user’s overall reviewing style. Similarly, understanding the characteristics of a product – its category, price point, or manufacturer – can provide context for interpreting user opinions. Previous work has attempted to integrate user and product features into sentiment models through various techniques, including feature concatenation (Liu et al., 2012), factorization machines (Rendle & Freudenthaler, 2011), and attention mechanisms (Hong et al., 2018). However, a critical challenge remains largely unaddressed: the  cold-start problem . In real-world review platforms, a substantial portion of users and products have limited interaction history, resulting in insufficient data to learn reliable representations. For cold-start users or products, simply relying on their own limited data can lead to inaccurate sentiment predictions. Existing models often struggle with this scenario, as they assume the availability of sufficient data for both users and products. To address this limitation, we introduce the Hybrid Contextualized Sentiment Classifier (HCSC). HCSC incorporates a novel Cold-Start Aware Attention (CSAA) mechanism that explicitly considers the cold-start problem when combining word-level representations with user and product embeddings. Our approach utilizes shared vectors constructed from similar users or products, providing a regularizing effect when individual user/product vectors are unreliable due to limited data. A frequency-guided selective gate controls the contribution of these shared vectors, allowing the model to dynamically adapt to the availability of information. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets that HCSC consistently outperforms existing models, particularly in low-data and cold-start scenarios.

Discriminative training methods have become a cornerstone of modern statistical natural language processing, achieving substantial performance gains over traditional generative approaches (Rosenfeld et al., 1996; Och & Ney, 2002). Among these, Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) (Och, 2003) stands out as a particularly effective technique for optimizing system performance with respect to a task-specific evaluation metric, such as BLEU for machine translation or Word Error Rate (WER) for speech recognition. The core idea behind MERT is to adjust model weights iteratively, favoring hypotheses that yield lower error rates on a development set. However, the optimization landscape presented by typical evaluation metrics is notoriously complex. BLEU and WER, while well-correlated with human judgments, are non-convex, non-differentiable, and often exhibit numerous local optima. The standard MERT algorithm, often employing gradient-based or hill-climbing search strategies, is therefore susceptible to getting trapped in suboptimal solutions. This is particularly concerning as even small improvements in model weights can translate to significant gains in final system performance. In this paper, we address the limitations of conventional MERT algorithms by introducing LP-MERT, an  exact  search algorithm that guarantees finding the globally optimal linear model weights for a given set of N-best lists. Our approach leverages the power of linear programming (LP) to formulate the MERT problem as a set of constraints and an objective function, which can then be solved efficiently and accurately using standard LP solvers. The core innovation lies in a series of reductions – transformations that recast the original, complex problem into a standard linear program. Given N-best lists generated from S input sentences, LP-MERT can determine the linear model parameters that minimize the total error rate across the development set. While theoretically optimal, the computational complexity of LP-MERT presents a considerable challenge. We demonstrate that the algorithm’s runtime is polynomial in N (the size of the N-best lists) and in the model size, but exhibits exponential growth with respect to S (the size of the development set). Recognizing this scalability bottleneck, we explore extensions that enable LP-MERT to handle realistically sized tuning sets. These extensions include strategies for restricting the search space to promising regions of the parameter space and a beam-search approximation that trades off optimality for computational efficiency. Through rigorous experimentation, we demonstrate that LP-MERT consistently outperforms the widely used Och algorithm (Och, 2003) in terms of both optimization accuracy and downstream system performance.

The rapid growth of microblogging platforms like Twitter has created a wealth of user-generated content, offering a unique window into public opinion, emerging trends, and real-time events. However, the sheer volume and velocity of tweets pose significant challenges for effective information summarization and analysis. Unlike traditional document-centric text, Twitter data is characterized by its brevity, noisy nature, and dynamic topicality. Consequently, methods developed for summarizing longer, more formal texts often struggle to effectively capture the essence of Twitter conversations. One promising approach to tackling this challenge is  keyphrase extraction  – the task of automatically identifying the most important phrases that represent the main topics discussed within a given text. Keyphrases provide a concise and informative summary, enabling users to quickly grasp the core themes of a document or a collection of documents. In the context of Twitter, automatically identifying relevant keyphrases can facilitate event detection, trend monitoring, and public sentiment analysis. Existing keyphrase extraction techniques often rely on statistical measures, graph-based ranking algorithms (e.g., TextRank (Mihalcea & Tarau, 2004)), or supervised learning approaches. While these methods have shown success on various text corpora, they often fall short when applied to the unique characteristics of Twitter data. For example, traditional statistical methods may struggle to distinguish between frequently used but uninformative phrases (e.g., “just,” “lol”) and genuinely representative keywords. Graph-based algorithms often fail to capture the contextual nuances of Twitter conversations, treating all words equally regardless of their surrounding context. Supervised learning approaches, while potentially more accurate, require large labeled datasets, which are expensive and time-consuming to create for the constantly evolving language used on Twitter. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to topical keyphrase extraction from Twitter, designed specifically to address these challenges. Our method combines a context-sensitive topical PageRank algorithm with a probabilistic scoring function.
