Simultaneously, the spatial relation extraction model leverages the information-rich dependency parse structures of Korean sentences to accurately identify the arguments participating in spatial relations. By utilizing dependency parse labels, we aim to pinpoint the correct entities involved in a given spatial relationship, overcoming ambiguities stemming from word order variations common in Korean. We present experimental results on a Korean text corpus, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed models for spatial information extraction, and highlighting their adaptability to a language substantially different from those previously explored in this domain. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for a wide variety of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, demonstrating strong performance in areas like text classification, sentence modeling, and relation extraction (Kim, 2014; O’Reilly and McCann, 2018). The success of CNNs in these applications hinges on their ability to effectively capture local patterns within textual sequences. However, traditional CNN architectures, originally designed for image processing, often require adaptation when applied to text. A key component of this adaptation lies in the convolution operation itself. Standard temporal CNNs for text typically operate by concatenating word embeddings and applying a fixed-size filter to consecutive n-grams. While effective, this approach has limitations in modeling complex interactions between words and capturing long-range dependencies. The seemingly simple concatenation operation can be viewed as a first-order interaction model—it primarily captures adjacencies without explicitly representing higher-order relationships. Furthermore, enforcing a strictly consecutive window can miss crucial patterns where intervening words contribute significantly to the overall meaning. For instance, in the phrase “not very happy,” the relationship between “not” and “happy” is central to understanding the sentiment, yet a standard CNN filter might treat “very” as an isolating factor. Existing approaches to address these limitations often involve increasing filter sizes, employing multiple convolutional layers, or incorporating more complex recurrent mechanisms. However, these solutions invariably increase computational complexity and can lead to challenges in training. This paper introduces a novel approach to reshaping the convolution operation within CNNs specifically for text processing. Our core idea is to move beyond simple concatenation and directly model word interactions using tensor algebra. We employ low-rank n-gram tensors to capture the inherent relationships between words at the convolution stage, offering a more efficient and expressive representation of local patterns. Moreover, we extend the traditional n-gram convolution to consider non-consecutive words, allowing the model to recognize meaningful connections even when separated by intervening terms. This extension addresses the limitation of rigidly consecutive filters and enables capturing more nuanced dependencies. Crucially, we demonstrate that the resulting convolution operation can be efficiently evaluated via dynamic programming, mitigating the computational overhead associated with tensor operations and allowing for practical application on large-scale datasets. Through experiments on benchmark sentiment classification and news categorization tasks, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and training speed, surpassing existing CNN-based models and competitive with more complex architectures.

The demand for large, labeled datasets has fueled the growth of crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (AMT) (Kazai et al., 2011;Surana et al., 2010). These platforms provide a cost-effective and scalable means to collect annotations for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including sentiment analysis, text classification, and information extraction (Snow et al., 2008;Callison-Burch & Meurers, 2013). However, relying on non-expert annotators introduces a critical challenge: the potential for low-quality or intentionally inaccurate labels. Annotators may exhibit varying levels of diligence, understanding, or even actively attempt to game the system for financial gain, submitting random or strategically chosen responses to maximize earnings without regard for accuracy (Kamarck et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2013). Traditional approaches to mitigating this issue involve manual inspection of annotator outputs, which is time-consuming and impractical for large-scale datasets. More sophisticated methods explore techniques like gold standard questions interspersed within the annotation task (Whissell et al., 2010) or redundancy, where multiple annotators label the same item and a majority vote is taken (Raykar et al., 2010). While effective, these strategies introduce additional costs and complexities. Gold standards require pre-labeled data, and redundancy significantly increases the overall annotation budget. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised approach, MACE (Multi-Annotator Competence Estimation), to simultaneously identify trustworthy annotators and predict the correct underlying labels for a given set of annotations. MACE utilizes an item-response model (IRT) (Hambleton & Swaminathan, 1985), a statistical framework commonly used in educational testing to estimate both item difficulty and test-taker ability. We adapt this framework to model annotator competence as a latent variable, enabling us to infer the reliability of each annotator based on their responses across a range of items. Crucially, our model operates without requiring any ground truth labels for training, making it particularly well-suited for scenarios where accurate supervision is unavailable or expensive to obtain. We demonstrate that MACE achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases exceeding, more complex state-of-the-art systems designed for annotator agreement and quality assessment. Furthermore, our experiments under adversarial conditions – deliberately introducing unreliable annotators – showcase the robustness of MACE in identifying and mitigating the impact of low-quality annotations. We present improvements achieved through incorporating a prior on model parameters via Variational Bayes inference, as well as techniques for focusing on high-confidence instances and leveraging annotated control examples. Our system offers a practical and scalable solution for addressing the challenges of noisy labels in crowdsourced datasets, and is publicly available for research and development.

Developing intelligent dialog systems that can engage in coherent and meaningful conversations remains a significant challenge in natural language processing. Traditional approaches to dialog generation often rely on sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models (Vinyals & Le, 2015; Sutskever et al., 2014), which learn to map input utterances to output responses. While these models can generate fluent responses, they often struggle with maintaining long-term coherence and generating contextually relevant replies, particularly in multi-turn conversations. The core limitation of these approaches stem from their inability to effectively reason over the conversational history. More recent efforts have explored incorporating attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Luong et al., 2015) to allow the model to focus on relevant parts of the input sequence, but these approaches still largely treat each turn as independent, lacking a true mechanism for multi-turn reasoning. Inspired by advancements in document comprehension, particularly the success of multi-turn reasoning networks (Kadlec et al., 2016; Seo et al., 2017), we propose a novel approach to dialog generation that treats a conversation session as a “document” and the current user query as a “question.” This allows us to leverage the power of attention-based memory reading to iteratively refine the understanding of the conversational context and generate more informed responses. The intuition is that a user’s current query isn’t isolated, and understanding it fully requires grounding it in the prior dialogue history. Our framework represents the conversational history as a collection of memories, which the model can repeatedly access and reason over to dynamically extend the query with contextual cues and generate optimal responses in a step-by-step manner. A key aspect of our work is recognizing that conversations are inherently multi-party interactions. Unlike standard document comprehension tasks, dialog sessions involve multiple speakers, each with their own evolving topic preferences and opinions. To address this, we move beyond a monolithic memory representation and instead partition the memory into speaker-specific groups - a query memory, a response memory, and a unified memory – reflecting the chronological flow of the conversation. This allows the model to better capture the distinct contributions of each participant and maintain a more nuanced understanding of the ongoing exchange. We evaluate our approach on a challenging Japanese dialog dataset consisting of 10-sentence (5-round) conversations. Our results demonstrate that incorporating multi-turn reasoning consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-turn and non-reasoning baseline models, producing more diverse and, crucially, more acceptable responses.

Distributional semantics (DS) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in computational linguistics over the past two decades, offering a compelling approach to representing word meaning based on usage patterns in large text corpora (Lenci et al., 2007; Turney & Pantel, 2010). The core tenet of DS is that “you shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957), meaning that the semantic properties of a word are reflected in the contexts in which it appears. This principle has led to the development of numerous algorithms – including Latent Semantic Analysis (Deerwester et al., 1990), Hyperspace Analogue to Language (Kanerva et al., 1998), and word embeddings like Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) – that successfully map words to vector representations in a high-dimensional space, capturing semantic similarities and relationships. However, despite the success of DS in representing individual word meanings, a significant challenge remains: extending these representations to encompass the meaning of larger linguistic units, such as phrases and sentences. While readily capturing single-word semantics, directly applying distributional methods to compositional semantics—that is, understanding how the meanings of individual words combine to form the meaning of a larger expression—is not straightforward (Clark & Pulman, 2007). The simple summation or averaging of word vectors often fails to capture nuanced semantic interactions and can lead to impoverished representations of compositional meaning. A considerable amount of research has focused on developing composition functions to address this gap (Mitchell & Lapata, 2010; Baroni et al., 2014). These functions aim to model the interplay between word vectors, taking into account syntactic relationships and semantic constraints. A prominent approach is the generalization of lexical functions proposed by Baroni and Zamparelli (2010), which models compositional semantics as a linear transformation of word embeddings. While promising, this method and others often rely on relatively small datasets and lack comprehensive comparative evaluations, making it difficult to discern the most effective composition strategies. This paper presents a twofold contribution to the field. First, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of several prominent composition methods within the distributional framework. We focus on two fundamental compositional constructions – adjective-noun (AN) and noun-noun (NN) combinations – and employ a newly developed dataset specifically designed for evaluating compositional semantics. This dataset enables a rigorous comparison of different approaches across a broad range of lexical items. Second, we propose a novel composition method that builds upon and generalizes the framework introduced by Baroni and Zamparelli (2010).

Knowledge bases (KBs) such as Freebase and Wikidata store structured information as triples of the form (head entity, relation, tail entity). A central task in utilizing KBs is knowledge base completion (KBC), predicting missing relations between entities. Recent approaches have demonstrated that modeling relation paths – sequences of relations connecting two entities – significantly improves KBC performance (Lin et al., 2015;Xie et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2019). For instance, if we want to predict the relation between ‘Barack Obama’ and ‘Michelle Obama’, a path like ‘president_of -> spouse’ can provide strong evidence for the ‘wife’ relation. However, a key challenge when utilizing relation paths is their combinatorial explosion. The number of possible paths between two entities grows exponentially with the path length. Consequently, existing methods typically resort to sampling a subset of potential paths (Lin et al., 2015;Xie et al., 2018), which may miss crucial relational information. This issue becomes particularly problematic when attempting to jointly model KBs with unstructured text. Often, textual mentions provide direct evidence for KB facts, and leveraging relation paths can help ground these facts in the KB. For example, the sentence "Barack Obama’s wife, Michelle Obama, is a lawyer" explicitly mentions a relation that can be validated through a KB path. To fully exploit this synergy, it’s vital to consider  all  relevant relation paths linking entities mentioned in the text. Prior work has made significant progress in incorporating paths, but falls short of exhaustively modeling them. Many methods (Lin et al., 2015;Wang et al., 2018) rely on truncated random walks, inherently limiting path exploration. Others (Zhang et al., 2019) employ path ranking algorithms, which are still approximations. Furthermore, naive concatenation of relation embeddings often fails to capture the compositional nature of paths – the meaning of a path is not simply the sum of its constituent relations, but rather the interaction between them and the entities they connect. Existing approaches also often overlook the importance of intermediate nodes along a path, treating them merely as connectors rather than potentially informative entities themselves. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address these limitations. We present the first exact dynamic programming algorithm that allows for the efficient incorporation of  all  relation paths of a bounded length when jointly modeling KBs and text. Our algorithm leverages a compositional representation of relation paths, explicitly modeling both the relation types  and  the intermediate nodes encountered along each path. We provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating the efficiency gains achieved by our algorithm compared to naive path enumeration.

Discourse relations, the semantic connections between segments of text, are fundamental to understanding natural language. While some discourse relations are explicitly signaled by discourse connectives (e.g., “because,” “however”), a significant portion remain  implicit , requiring inference based on contextual cues and world knowledge. Recognizing these implicit discourse relations is a crucial step towards deeper text understanding, enabling applications such as improved machine reading comprehension, text summarization, and question answering. Despite considerable progress in recent years, accurately identifying implicit discourse relations remains a challenging task. Early approaches to discourse relation classification relied heavily on hand-engineered features, capturing lexical, syntactic, and semantic information about the discourse arguments (e.g., the segments of text connected by the relation). While achieving reasonable performance, these systems were often brittle and required significant domain expertise to adapt to new text types. More recently, neural network models have emerged as a dominant paradigm, offering the ability to learn complex features automatically from data. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been successfully applied to this task, often leveraging attention mechanisms to focus on the most relevant parts of the input arguments (e.g., Li et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2017). However, existing neural models often treat discourse relation recognition as a single-pass process – the input is encoded, features are extracted, and a classification decision is made. We argue that this approach overlooks a crucial aspect of human discourse processing:  repeated reading . When encountering ambiguous or complex text, humans do not typically grasp the relationships between segments in a single pass. Instead, we repeatedly reread the text, gradually refining our understanding and focusing on key signals that help resolve the discourse structure. This iterative process allows us to dynamically identify the most salient features for determining the underlying relation. Inspired by this observation, we present a novel neural network architecture, Neural Networks with Multi-Level Attention (NNMA), designed to mimic the repeated reading strategy. Our model incorporates an external memory component and a multi-level attention mechanism, enabling it to iteratively process the discourse arguments and dynamically refine its focus on informative words and phrases. Unlike previous attention-based models that apply attention once, NNMA progressively adjusts its attention weights across multiple levels, effectively “zooming in” on the most relevant features with each iteration. We evaluate NNMA on the widely used Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) dataset and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in implicit discourse relation classification.

The explosive growth of social media platforms has created a wealth of textual data, offering unprecedented opportunities for natural language processing (NLP) research. However, this data presents unique challenges due to its informal and often non-standard nature. Characterized by misspellings, abbreviations, slang, and grammatical errors, social media text poses a significant hurdle for traditional NLP tools, which are typically designed to process well-formed, standard language (Eisenstein, 2013; Han et al., 2013). To bridge this gap,  text normalization  – the process of transforming non-standard words into their canonical, standard equivalents – has emerged as a crucial pre-processing step. Effective text normalization can significantly improve the performance of downstream NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and information retrieval. Existing approaches to text normalization can be broadly categorized into dictionary-based methods and learning-based methods. Dictionary-based methods (Liu et al., 2012; Awad et al., 2013) rely on manually or automatically constructed mappings between non-standard and standard words. While straightforward, these approaches often suffer from limited coverage and struggle to generalize to unseen variations. Learning-based methods, on the other hand, employ machine learning techniques to learn normalization rules from labeled data (Bahasa and Wilks, 2014; Kulkarni et al., 2015). These methods offer better generalization capabilities but require substantial labeled training data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to acquire, particularly for rapidly evolving social media language. In this work, we introduce a novel, unsupervised text normalization approach that leverages the contextual and grammatical information present in social media text. Our approach moves beyond relying solely on lexical similarity and incorporates a graph-based representation of the textual data. We construct a word association graph from a large, unlabeled corpus of social media text, capturing the co-occurrence patterns and grammatical relationships between words. This graph encodes contextual information, such as the words that typically appear before or after a given non-standard word, as well as part-of-speech tag sequences. This contextual information is then combined with lexical features – including longest common subsequence ratio, edit distance, and double metaphone similarity – to perform normalization. Crucially, unlike many recent normalization approaches that focus on generating comprehensive normalization dictionaries (e.g., Li et al., 2015), our method performs normalization  in context . This allows us to disambiguate non-standard words based on their surrounding words and grammatical structure, leading to more accurate normalization results. Our experimental results on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art F-score performance.

Bilingual dictionary induction (BDI), the task of automatically learning a mapping between the vocabularies of two languages, remains a central challenge in machine translation and cross-lingual natural language processing (NLP) (Haghighi et al., 2008;Klementiev et al., 2007;Levy and Goldberg, 2009). Traditional approaches to BDI relied on statistical methods applied to parallel corpora, which require large amounts of annotated data—a resource frequently unavailable for many language pairs. Recent advances in distributional semantics and cross-lingual word embeddings have opened up new avenues for BDI, particularly leveraging zero-shot learning principles (Lazaridou et al., 2014;Vulić and Možeško, 2013). These approaches aim to learn a mapping function between the vector spaces of different languages, enabling translation even without explicit parallel data. While promising, current zero-shot BDI methods often fall short of achieving the accuracy required for practical applications. A common strategy involves projecting words from both languages into a shared vector space, relying on pivot languages or statistical machine translation (SMT) systems to establish initial alignments (Vulić et al., 2015;Artetxe et al., 2018). However, the quality of these initial alignments, especially when dealing with low-resource languages, directly impacts the performance of the induced dictionary. Errors propagated through the mapping function can significantly degrade accuracy. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach inspired by the field of knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015). In knowledge distillation, a smaller “student” model learns to mimic the behavior of a larger, more complex “teacher” model. In our context, the “teachers” are high-quality translation paths established via rich-resource language pairs (e.g., English-Spanish, English-French), while the “students” are translation paths involving low-resource languages (e.g., English-Swahili, French-Vietnamese). Our central contribution is a distillation training objective that enables the low-resource students to leverage the knowledge embedded in the rich-resource teachers. This approach offers several advantages. First, it allows for the seamless integration of additional teacher paths, strengthening the learning signal for any given low-resource pair. Second, it efficiently transfers knowledge from reliable sources to less reliable ones. Furthermore, recognizing that the quality of monolingual word embeddings heavily influences BDI performance, we also explore methods to enhance vector representations with explicit linguistic information, such as morphological features and part-of-speech tags. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our distillation training objective, achieving substantial performance gains across a variety of language pairs. We observe accuracy improvements of up to 17% compared to baseline models, highlighting the efficacy of leveraging knowledge distillation for improving bilingual dictionary induction in low-resource settings.

Neural dialogue generation has witnessed substantial progress in recent years, largely due to the adoption of sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models (Sutskever et al., 2014; Vinyals & Le, 2015). These models, often augmented with attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and increasingly sophisticated architectures like Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), can generate seemingly coherent and contextually relevant responses. However, a persistent challenge in open-domain dialogue generation remains: producing responses that are truly  human-like  – engaging, diverse, and capable of maintaining a natural flow of conversation. Traditional maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) training, while effective in minimizing perplexity, often leads to generic and repetitive responses, often referred to as the “safe reply” problem (Li et al., 2016). This is because MLE focuses on predicting the most probable next word given the context, rather than optimizing for overall conversational quality. Several approaches have been proposed to address this issue. These include incorporating diverse decoding strategies (e.g., beam search with diversity penalty), utilizing reinforcement learning (RL) with reward functions designed to promote desired qualities like coherence and informativeness (Li et al., 2016; Serban et al., 2017), and employing variational autoencoders (VAEs) to capture latent conversational structures (Zhao et al., 2017). However, defining a robust and comprehensive reward function for RL, or a suitable latent space for VAEs, remains a considerable hurdle. Moreover, many existing metrics for evaluating dialogue quality – such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004) – correlate poorly with human judgment, often rewarding simple lexical overlap rather than meaningful semantic similarity and conversational fluency. Inspired by the foundational concept of the Turing Test, we propose a novel approach to neural dialogue generation based on adversarial learning. The core idea is to train a dialogue generation model to produce responses that are indistinguishable from those generated by humans. This shifts the objective from explicitly defining what constitutes a “good” response to implicitly learning it through competition with a discriminator. We formulate this as a reinforcement learning problem, where the generator (the dialogue model) attempts to “fool” the discriminator (a classifier trained to distinguish between human and machine-generated responses), and the discriminator provides a reward signal to guide the generator’s learning. This adversarial process pushes the generator to produce more realistic and engaging dialogues, mirroring the goal of passing as a human conversationalist. Furthermore, we introduce a framework for  adversarial evaluation —using the success rate of fooling an adversary as a metric for dialogue quality.

Query spelling correction is a crucial component of modern information retrieval systems. Users frequently mistype search queries, leading to zero or suboptimal search results. The task involves identifying and suggesting corrections for misspelled words within a user’s query, aiming to bridge the gap between the user’s intent and the content available on the web. Early approaches to query spelling correction relied heavily on generative models, particularly noisy channel models (Bilmes & Kirchhoff, 2000; Jones & Norvig, 1993). These models estimate the probability of a misspelling given the correct word (the “channel”) and the probability of the correct word itself. While effective, noisy channel models often struggle to capture the complex dependencies between words and the broader context of a query. Recent research has shifted towards a two-stage paradigm (Cai et al., 2010; Jones & Curran, 2009). The first stage employs a noisy channel model to generate a set of candidate corrections for each misspelled word. This is followed by a discriminatively trained ranker, typically a machine learning model, to re-rank these candidates based on various features, ultimately selecting the most likely correct spelling. This approach leverages the strengths of both generative and discriminative modeling. However, this seemingly advantageous combination presents a significant challenge: the performance of the discriminative ranker is fundamentally limited by the quality – specifically, the recall – of the candidate set generated by the initial noisy channel model. If the noisy channel model fails to propose the correct spelling as a candidate, the subsequent ranking stage has no opportunity to select it, leading to a suboptimal correction. This paper introduces a novel discriminative model for query spelling correction designed to mitigate the limitations of the traditional two-stage approach. Our model, a Latent Structural Support Vector Machine (SVM), directly models the mapping from misspelled queries to correct queries, without relying on an explicit candidate generation step. The “latent” aspect of the model allows it to implicitly reason about the underlying structural relationships within queries, capturing dependencies between words and capturing features that might be lost when considering each word in isolation. We argue that by learning a direct discriminative function, we can overcome the recall bottleneck inherent in the two-stage approach and achieve significantly improved correction accuracy. Furthermore, our model allows for the incorporation of rich, overlapping features, capturing nuanced aspects of query context and spelling patterns that traditional feature engineering might miss. In the following sections, we detail the architecture of our Latent Structural SVM, describe the features used to represent queries and their corrections, and present experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness on a standard benchmark dataset.

Tree-to-tree transduction forms a powerful paradigm for modeling complex linguistic transformations, finding applications in areas such as machine translation, question answering, and semantic parsing. These models, often realized as finite-state tree transducers (FSTs), learn to map syntactic structures from a source to a target language, capturing sophisticated relationships beyond simple string-based substitutions. However, successfully building such transducers relies heavily on two key components: accurate word alignments and an effective rule extraction algorithm. Traditional rule extraction methods typically leverage word alignments as a starting point, identifying corresponding phrases and constructing transduction rules based on these correspondences (Knight and Graehl, 1997; Vogel et al., 2003). These alignments effectively serve as anchors, guiding the induction of grammatical rules. However, this alignment-driven approach suffers from a critical limitation, particularly in scenarios characterized by limited training data. When the size of the corpus of paired trees/strings is small relative to the vocabulary size or the complexity of the targeted grammar, the resulting word alignments become unreliable and often contain significant noise (Och and Ney, 2003). This unreliability then cascades through the rule extraction process, leading to the induction of spurious or overly generalized rules, ultimately hindering the transducer's performance. Consider, for example, attempting to build a tree transducer for mapping question structures to their corresponding SQL queries from a small set of question-query pairs. The inherent ambiguity in natural language and the limited data can easily result in inaccurate alignments, leading to a transducer that fails to generalize beyond the training examples. To address these limitations, we propose a novel rule extraction algorithm that minimizes reliance on pre-computed word alignments. Instead, our approach directly optimizes a cost function over tree fragments, formulating rule extraction as a cost minimization problem. This allows the algorithm to identify potentially valuable transduction rules based directly on the structure and content of the training data, independent of potentially noisy alignments. Furthermore, and perhaps more importantly, our formulation naturally lends itself to a dynamic rule creation process. As the algorithm explores the space of possible rules, it introduces ‘back-off states’ – mechanisms through which the transducer can generate right-hand-sides for previously unseen left-hand-sides, effectively creating new rules ‘on-the-fly’. This dynamic capability is crucial for handling the inherent open-endedness of natural language and ensuring adequate rule coverage, especially when confronted with novel inputs. We evaluate the generalization power of our induced tree transducers in the context of a question answering (QA) task over a large knowledge base.

The ability to understand and reason about everyday events is a hallmark of human intelligence, yet remains a significant challenge for computational models of language. This challenge lies at the heart of achieving truly  deep  language understanding - moving beyond syntactic parsing and semantic role labeling to capture the rich web of commonsense knowledge that humans implicitly employ when interpreting narratives. A crucial component of this commonsense knowledge involves understanding the causal and correlational relationships between events: knowing, for example, that dropping a glass often  causes  it to break, or that going to a restaurant is frequently  followed by  receiving a bill. Despite considerable interest within the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, progress in modeling and learning these commonsense relationships has been notably hampered by a lack of robust and targeted evaluation frameworks. Existing benchmarks often focus on isolated fact verification or limited forms of reasoning, failing to capture the nuanced, sequential understanding required to comprehend a full narrative. Consequently, it's difficult to definitively assess whether progress in story understanding is driven by genuine commonsense reasoning or simply by exploiting superficial statistical patterns in the data. This paper addresses this critical gap by introducing a new evaluation paradigm – the “Story Cloze Test” – specifically designed to probe deeper understanding of commonsense stories. The task requires a system to select the most plausible concluding sentence from a set of options, given a four-sentence story as context. This forces models to not only comprehend the preceding events but also to anticipate likely consequences and infer unstated motivations, thus demanding a more holistic and commonsense-driven understanding. To support this evaluation, we present ROCStories, a new corpus of 50,000 five-sentence commonsense stories. This corpus distinguishes itself from existing story datasets in two key aspects. First, it is deliberately constructed to capture a broad spectrum of causal and temporal relations prevalent in everyday human experiences. The stories depict common, plausible situations, mirroring the types of events people encounter and reason about regularly. Second, ROCStories is a high-quality collection of coherent, well-written narratives, intended not only for evaluation but also for applications like story generation – offering a versatile resource for broader research in narrative understanding. Our experimental results, comparing a range of baseline methods and state-of-the-art models, reveal that even sophisticated approaches relying on shallow linguistic analysis struggle to achieve high performance on the Story Cloze Test. This highlights the continuing difficulty of capturing the subtle commonsense reasoning required to truly understand narrative context.

Dialogue is a fundamentally cooperative activity (Grice, 1975). Participants generally assume that their interlocutors are attempting to communicate meaningfully and adhere to a set of implicit conversational principles, often characterized as maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner. However, real-world dialogues frequently exhibit instances of non-cooperation, where one or more participants deviate from these norms. Understanding and modeling non-cooperation is crucial for developing robust and intelligent dialogue systems, as well as for analyzing natural language interactions in diverse contexts. Existing approaches to identifying non-cooperation fall into several broad categories. One line of research focuses on  task-related  non-cooperation, where a participant actively hinders the successful completion of a shared goal (e.g., Trappl et al., 2008). This often manifests in behaviors such as providing misleading information or refusing to answer questions directly. Another approach involves defining specific rules or patterns that characterize non-cooperative acts (e.g., a refusal to answer is explicitly labeled as a non-cooperative behavior), requiring expert annotation and often being domain-specific (e.g., Carberry, 1990; Clark & Brennan, 1991). These rule-based methods often struggle to generalize beyond the scenarios for which they were designed and can be brittle in the face of subtle variations in linguistic expression. A key limitation of previous work is that it frequently defines non-cooperation  directly , rather than measuring it  relative  to an established baseline of cooperative behavior. This paper departs from these approaches by proposing a novel method for quantifying non-cooperation based on the degree to which participants adhere to conventions governing proper dialogue conduct. Rather than predefining non-cooperative acts, we start with a formalization of  cooperative  dialogue behavior – a dialogue game (Searle & Vanderveken, 1976) – and measure the extent to which actual dialogues conform to its rules. This approach allows us to establish a quantitative measure of non-cooperation grounded in a general theory of conversation. Our underlying assumption is that linguistic non-cooperation can be assessed by tracking deviations from expected conversational obligations. For instance, failing to respond to a direct question, or providing an overly vague or evasive answer, represents a breach of conversational norms. We implement this approach by modeling dialogue as a turn-taking interaction governed by a set of rules specifying allowable moves and constraints. By analyzing the extent to which participants’ actions comply with these rules, we can derive a measure of their cooperativeness. This measure is inherently comparative, allowing us to identify which participant in a dialogue is exhibiting more or less cooperative behavior.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) has emerged as a valuable tool in educational assessment, offering a scalable and cost-effective alternative to traditional manual grading (Page, 1966). With the increasing prevalence of online learning platforms and large-scale assessments, the demand for robust and accurate AES systems has grown significantly. Current state-of-the-art AES systems, often leveraging techniques from Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML), can achieve remarkable correlations with human raters (Burstein et al., 2013; Shermis & Burstein, 2013). However, a critical limitation of these systems lies in their dependence on substantial amounts of labeled training data—specifically, essays manually graded by human experts. The challenge is particularly acute when deploying AES systems across diverse educational contexts. The content and style of essays vary considerably depending on the specific prompt or task presented to students. Consequently, an AES model trained on essays from one prompt often exhibits a significant performance degradation when applied to essays generated in response to a different prompt (Landauer et al., 1998). This phenomenon, known as  domain shift , highlights the need for techniques that can generalize AES models to unseen prompts without requiring extensive new labeled data. The traditional approach to addressing this problem involves collecting and annotating a large corpus of essays for each new prompt, which is both time-consuming and financially prohibitive. Domain adaptation offers a more pragmatic solution by transferring knowledge learned from a source domain (an existing prompt with ample labeled data) to a target domain (a new prompt with limited or no labeled data). Various domain adaptation techniques have been explored in AES, including feature-based approaches (e.g., transforming essay representations to reduce domain divergence) and instance-based approaches (e.g., re-weighting training instances to emphasize those most relevant to the target domain). In this paper, we present a novel domain adaptation technique for AES based on Bayesian linear ridge regression. Our approach leverages the concept of  correlated linear regression  (Atay-Kaygin & Bishop, 2011) to effectively transfer knowledge from the source to the target domain. We hypothesize that the underlying scoring functions for different prompts, while varying in their specific parameters, share a common statistical structure. By modeling the correlations between the scoring functions, our method can adapt the source model to the target domain with minimal labeled data requirements. We evaluate our proposed technique on the publicly available Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset, a widely used benchmark for AES research.

Named Entity Recognition (NER), the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text, is a fundamental component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. In recent years, statistical machine learning models, particularly those employing sequence labeling techniques like Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) and increasingly, deep neural networks, have achieved state-of-the-art performance in NER (Lample et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2015). A key strength of these models lies in their ability to generalize to unseen entities – recognizing entities not explicitly observed during training – by leveraging rich lexical and contextual features. However, despite these advancements, NER systems remain vulnerable to errors, particularly when faced with ambiguous entity mentions or when features incorrectly favor a suboptimal entity type assignment. For instance, the mention “Apple” could refer to the technology company or the fruit. Without sufficient disambiguating context, a model might incorrectly classify it based on spurious feature correlations. This issue is exacerbated in multilingual settings, where the availability of large, high-quality labeled training data is often limited, and the nuances of entity typing can vary significantly across languages. While cross-lingual transfer learning and multilingual embeddings offer some mitigation, they often don’t fully address the fundamental problem of accurate entity type disambiguation. To tackle this challenge, we explore the potential of leveraging Wikipedia, a vast and readily available open knowledge base, to enhance multilingual NER systems. Wikipedia provides a wealth of structured information about entities, including their types (e.g., “Person”, “Organization”, “Location”). Our core contribution is the creation of high-accuracy, high-coverage multilingual Wikipedia entity type mappings. These mappings link entity mentions across multiple languages to their corresponding Wikipedia entries and, crucially, to their associated entity types. Importantly, our method for building these mappings relies on weakly supervised techniques, minimizing the need for costly and time-consuming human annotation. Furthermore, our approach is designed to be easily extended to new languages without requiring language-specific knowledge or expertise. Building upon these mappings, we develop several strategies for integrating Wikipedia-derived information into an existing NER pipeline. We hypothesize that enriching the feature set with knowledge of an entity’s Wikipedia type can significantly improve NER accuracy, particularly for unseen entities and in low-resource scenarios. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed approaches through comprehensive experiments on NER systems trained for six different languages. The results demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in F1 score, particularly in discerning entity types for novel entities and when training data is scarce—yielding improvements of up to 18.3 F1 points.

Automatic keyphrase generation (KPG) is the task of automatically extracting or generating a set of representative phrases that summarize the main topics of a given document. It has become an increasingly important problem in natural language processing with numerous applications, including document indexing, information retrieval, and text summarization. Traditional approaches to KPG typically fall into two main categories: extraction-based and generation-based. Extraction-based methods identify and rank existing phrases within the document based on statistical features or graph-based algorithms (e.g., TextRank; Mihalcea & Tarau, 2004). While computationally efficient, these methods are limited by the vocabulary present in the source document and may fail to capture abstractive concepts. In contrast, generation-based methods, also known as abstractive keyphrase generation, aim to generate novel keyphrases that may not explicitly appear in the document, offering more flexibility and potentially better coverage of the document's content (Meng et al., 2017). Recent advances in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models with attention mechanisms have demonstrated promising results in abstractive KPG (Rush et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017). These models typically treat KPG as a multi-label classification problem, where the model predicts a sequence of keyphrases given an input document. However, many existing seq2seq models suffer from limitations that hinder the quality of generated keyphrases. A prominent issue is the tendency to generate redundant or overlapping keyphrases. Another common problem is insufficient coverage, leading to the omission of important concepts from the document. These issues often stem from a neglect of the relationships and correlations  between  the generated keyphrases themselves. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing a novel seq2seq architecture for keyphrase generation named CorrRNN, specifically designed to capture correlations among multiple keyphrases. Our model incorporates two key components: a coverage vector and a dependency on preceding generated phrases. The coverage vector encourages the model to attend to different parts of the source document for each generated keyphrase, improving overall coverage. Simultaneously, by conditioning the generation of each subsequent phrase on the previously generated phrases, we aim to minimize redundancy and enhance the coherence of the final keyphrase set. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that CorrRNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both keyphrase accuracy and diversity. We believe this work represents a step forward in generating more informative and useful keyphrase sets by explicitly modeling the relationships among them. References: Mihalcea, R., & Tarau, P. (2004).

Graphical models provide a powerful framework for representing and reasoning about complex probabilistic systems. However, exact inference in these models is often intractable, necessitating the use of approximate inference techniques. Variational inference and belief propagation (BP) are two prominent approaches, each with its strengths and weaknesses. Belief propagation, in particular, enjoys widespread use due to its conceptual simplicity and efficiency, but its performance degrades significantly on graphs with loops (loopy graphs). Expectation propagation (EP) offers an improvement over standard BP by maintaining tractable message approximations through a series of local projections (Minka, 2001). In essence, EP iteratively refines approximate factors in the model by matching moments with the true posterior distribution, effectively propagating information between variables. While EP often outperforms BP, its computational cost can still be substantial, particularly when dealing with complex factorizations or high-dimensional variables. Moreover, the resulting messages can sometimes be overly complex, hindering both computational efficiency and interpretability. This paper introduces Penalized Expectation Propagation (PEP), a novel algorithm designed to address these limitations. PEP builds upon the foundation of EP by incorporating a structured-sparsity penalty into the message approximation process. This penalty encourages simpler messages, reducing computational burden and promoting generalization. By carefully balancing the accuracy of the moment matching with the complexity of the resulting messages, PEP aims to achieve a favorable trade-off between speed and accuracy. A key contribution of this work lies in the specific instantiation of PEP for graphical models over strings. String-valued random variables are ubiquitous in natural language processing, computational linguistics, and bioinformatics. Representing and reasoning about these variables often requires sophisticated probabilistic models capable of capturing sequential dependencies. We adaptively approximate finite-state distributions, a common choice for string modeling, by leveraging variable-order n-gram models within the PEP framework. This allows us to efficiently represent long-range dependencies while maintaining tractability. We evaluate the performance of PEP on a series of phonological inference problems. These tasks, which involve reasoning about the underlying sound structure of words, provide a challenging testbed for probabilistic inference algorithms. Our experimental results demonstrate substantial speedups over previous state-of-the-art algorithms, including related approaches based on expectation propagation and variational inference, with no significant loss in accuracy. These findings highlight the effectiveness of PEP in balancing computational efficiency and accuracy for graphical models over strings. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a brief overview of expectation propagation.

Relation Extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities in text – is a core component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including knowledge base completion, question answering, and information retrieval (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005; Mintz et al., 2009; Richardson et al., 2013). Traditionally, building high-performing RE systems required large amounts of manually annotated training data, a process that is both expensive and time-consuming. Distant Supervision (DS) emerged as a promising alternative (Mintz et al., 2009), leveraging existing knowledge bases (KBs) to automatically generate training instances. The core idea is to align entities mentioned in text with entities in the KB and assume that sentences mentioning related entities express the corresponding relation. However, DS is inherently noisy. The assumption that any sentence aligning with a KB relation expresses that relation is often incorrect. These errors arise from various sources, including relation ambiguity (a single sentence can express multiple relations), incorrect KB entries, and implicit relations not explicitly stated in the text. This noise can significantly degrade the performance of RE models trained with DS data, diminishing the benefits of reduced labeling effort. Recent research has focused on addressing the noise issue in DS-RE. Several approaches have been proposed, including multi-instance learning (Riedel et al., 2013), selective instance learning (Hoffmann et al., 2016), and attention mechanisms (Lin et al., 2016). These methods aim to identify and mitigate the impact of noisy instances, but often rely on heuristics or auxiliary information to estimate instance labels. In this work, we argue that the noise in DS-RE can be effectively characterized by a  dynamic transition matrix . This matrix represents the probability of transitioning between different relation types in the training data. By learning this matrix, we can capture the patterns of noisy instances and leverage this understanding to improve relation extraction performance. Unlike previous methods that treat noise as a static property, our approach recognizes that the noise level and patterns vary depending on the relation type and the context of the sentence. We propose a novel curriculum learning-based method to effectively train the dynamic transition matrix  without any direct supervision about the noise . The curriculum learning strategy gradually increases the difficulty of the training instances, allowing the model to learn the transition matrix in a stable and efficient manner. We evaluate our approach extensively on a variety of RE datasets and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of our dynamic transition matrix and curriculum learning strategy in enhancing DS-RE performance.

Text readability is a cornerstone of effective communication, impacting comprehension, engagement, and overall user experience. While significant research has been dedicated to assessing and improving readability in languages like English (Flesch, 1954; Dale & Chall, 1948), the study of readability in other languages, particularly those with complex linguistic structures like Bangla, remains relatively underexplored. Bangla, spoken by over 265 million people worldwide, presents unique challenges to computational readability assessment due to its morphological richness, complex sentence structures, and a writing system that differs significantly from Latin-based scripts. Existing readability measures developed for English often fall short when applied to Bangla, highlighting the need for language-specific approaches. Previous efforts to address Bangla readability have largely focused on adapting existing English readability formulas (Islam & Islam, 2013; Rahman et al., 2014). These adaptations often rely on simple word and sentence length calculations, overlooking critical linguistic features specific to Bangla that influence comprehension. Moreover, these studies frequently treat readability as an inherent property of the text itself, neglecting the crucial role of the  reader  in the readability equation. An individual's educational background, prior knowledge, and linguistic proficiency significantly shape their ability to understand a given text. What is considered “readable” for a highly educated native speaker may pose significant challenges for someone with limited formal education or a different linguistic background. This paper addresses these limitations by examining the influence of both target reader background and intrinsic text features on perceived readability in Bangla. We hypothesize that the interplay between these factors is crucial in accurately assessing reading difficulty. To investigate this hypothesis, we present a novel, carefully constructed Bangla readability dataset, meticulously annotated by readers from two distinct background groups. This dataset, comprised of 135 Bangla documents, allows us to directly compare readability perceptions across different reader profiles. We systematically identify and analyze 20 text features categorized as “classic” (e.g., sentence length, word frequency) and “non-classic” (e.g., morphological complexity, use of conjunct verbs) – the latter being particularly relevant to the intricacies of the Bangla language. Through correlation analysis, we reveal varying influences of these features on perceived text hardness across the two reader groups. Finally, we employ machine learning techniques – specifically Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Support Vector Regression (SVR) – to model reading difficulty, tailoring separate models for each reader background and evaluating the contributions of different feature combinations. Our findings demonstrate a significant correlation between reader background and readability perception, establishing that text difficulty is not solely a property of the text but is profoundly influenced by the characteristics of the intended audience.

The ability to understand and reason about entities mentioned in text is fundamental to many natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including information retrieval, question answering, and text summarization. Two core challenges in achieving this understanding are cross-document co-reference resolution (CCR) and named-entity linking (NEL). CCR, also known as entity linking or coreference, aims to identify all mentions referring to the same real-world entity across a collection of documents (Kilgour and Moffat, 2003; Nadeau and Sekine, 2007). NEL, on the other hand, focuses on disambiguating textual mentions to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB) such as Wikipedia or Freebase (Shen et al., 2015; Raiman and Ringer, 2009). While both tasks seek to resolve mentions to their underlying entities, they operate at different granularities and utilize distinct types of information. Traditionally, CCR and NEL have been treated as largely independent problems, with separate algorithms and pipelines developed for each. Standard CCR systems rely on features such as string similarity, syntactic constraints, and contextual information to cluster mentions within and across documents (Ng and McCallum, 2001; Flanigan et al., 2014). NEL systems, conversely, leverage knowledge base information – entity popularity, textual descriptions, and relationships with other entities – to disambiguate mentions (Milne et al., 2008; Hoffart et al., 2011). However, recent work increasingly recognizes the benefits of integrating CCR and NEL. These tasks are inherently synergistic: knowing that two mentions refer to the same entity can aid in disambiguation (and vice versa), and leveraging the structured knowledge contained in a KB can improve co-reference clustering. Prior attempts to combine CCR and NEL have generally fallen into two categories: pipeline approaches where one task is performed before the other, and joint models that attempt to optimize both tasks simultaneously. Pipeline approaches suffer from error propagation – mistakes made in one task negatively impact the performance of the other. Existing joint models (Lu et al., 2018; Wiegand et al., 2019) often rely on supervised learning and require large amounts of manually annotated data, which is expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Furthermore, these approaches often focus on a single aspect of the joint problem, such as utilizing KB information for co-reference, but do not fully exploit the bidirectional dependencies between CCR and NEL. In this paper, we present C3EL, an unsupervised framework for jointly performing CCR and NEL. C3EL is designed to alleviate the limitations of existing approaches by iteratively refining both CCR clusters and NEL predictions through a reciprocal information exchange.

Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm in deep learning, demonstrating substantial improvements across diverse natural language processing (NLP) tasks (Caruana, 1997; Collobert et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2016). The core idea behind MTL is that learning multiple related tasks simultaneously allows the model to leverage shared representations, leading to better generalization and performance compared to learning each task in isolation. A particularly effective approach within MTL involves neural networks, where shared layers are employed to extract common features, followed by task-specific layers for individual predictions (Yang & Yang, 2017; Pham et al., 2018). However, a significant challenge in neural network-based MTL lies in effectively managing the flow of information between tasks. While simply linking layers encourages knowledge sharing, it doesn't address the issue of  what  information should be shared. Naively sharing features can lead to negative transfer, where the presence of irrelevant or misleading features from one task degrades the performance of others (Ruder et al., 2017). This interference stems from the fact that different tasks often operate in distinct feature spaces, and forcing the model to share all features can contaminate these spaces with noise. Consequently, the model may struggle to discern the most relevant features for each task, hindering its ability to make accurate predictions. Existing work has attempted to alleviate this interference through various techniques. Some methods focus on learning task relationships to dynamically weight the importance of shared features (Zhao et al., 2016). Others employ regularization techniques to encourage task-specific representations (Chen et al., 2018). However, these approaches often require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not fully address the fundamental problem of feature selection – deciding  which  features to share and  when  to share them. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to multi-task learning inspired by the principles of memory and forgetting. We propose a Leaky Multi-Task Network (LMTN) which incorporates “Leaky Units” into the shared layers of a convolutional neural network (CNN). These Leaky Units act as dynamic gates, selectively allowing or blocking the flow of feature activations between tasks. This mechanism allows the network to learn what information is beneficial to share and what should be kept private, effectively filtering out irrelevant or detrimental features. The “leak” parameter within each unit is learned during training, enabling the network to adaptively adjust its feature sharing behavior. We validate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on five diverse text classification datasets.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has seen significant advances in recent years, with syntax-based methods consistently delivering state-of-the-art performance (Yamada and Knight, 2001; Chiang, 2005). A cornerstone of many syntax-based SMT systems is the synchronous context-free grammar (SCFG), which provides a formal framework for representing the relationships between source and target language syntax. However, efficient decoding using SCFGs presents a computational challenge. Traditional wisdom, stemming from the work in formal language theory, dictates that SCFGs must be converted into Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) to ensure tractable, specifically cubic-time, decoding (Lee, 1998). The standard technique for converting an arbitrary SCFG to CNF is synchronous binarization (Zhang et al., 2006). This process systematically introduces new non-terminal symbols to decompose unary and binary rules into chains of binary rules. While theoretically guaranteeing cubic-time complexity, synchronous binarization suffers from a significant practical drawback: it dramatically increases the size of the grammar, leading to inflated constant factors and slower decoding speeds. The proliferation of new symbols introduces substantial overhead in both memory usage and computational time during parsing. Recognizing this limitation, DeNero et al. (2009) proposed Lexical Normal Form (LNF) as an alternative grammar format. LNF represents a superset of CNF and, importantly, supports cubic-time decoding under certain, previously implicit, assumptions. Their work demonstrated that by leveraging LNF, one could avoid the drastic grammar expansion associated with synchronous binarization, leading to improved decoding efficiency. However, the conditions under which LNF guarantees efficient decoding weren't fully articulated, leaving room for further exploration and optimization. This paper builds directly upon the work of DeNero et al. (2009) by making these crucial decoding assumptions explicit. In doing so, we demonstrate that LNF can be extended even further to encompass a broader class of grammars—which we term “scope-3” grammars—while retaining the guarantee of cubic-time decoding complexity. We rigorously define the properties of scope-3 grammars and provide a practical method for identifying and pruning non-scope-3 rules from automatically extracted grammars, such as those learned using the GHKM algorithm (Gale and Kirk, 2004; Knight, 2004). Our experimental results demonstrate that pruning to scope-3 grammars consistently outperforms synchronous binarization in terms of translation quality, while simultaneously achieving faster decoding speeds. This indicates that the reduced grammar size and streamlined decoding process afforded by our approach more than compensate for any potential loss of expressivity. These findings challenge the conventional practice of synchronous binarization and provide a compelling alternative for efficient and effective syntax-based machine translation.

Math word problems (MWPs) pose a significant challenge for natural language processing (NLP) systems, requiring both a deep understanding of language and the ability to reason mathematically (Bobrow, 1996; Riley, 2008). Traditionally, solving MWPs has been approached as a multi-stage process involving understanding the problem text, identifying relevant quantities, determining the correct mathematical equations, and finally, computing the solution (Atlason et al., 2014; Konstantinova et al., 2013). Early approaches relied heavily on hand-crafted features and symbolic manipulation, often requiring substantial domain expertise and extensive feature engineering to achieve reasonable performance. These methods typically involve parsing the problem text, identifying keywords, and mapping them to mathematical operations. More recently, statistical machine learning techniques have gained traction, leveraging automatically extracted features from the text to predict the equation template or directly predict the answer (Liang et al., 2011; Kushman et al., 2014). While these approaches reduce the reliance on hand-crafted features, they still tend to focus on carefully engineered feature representations, such as quantity extraction, relation identification, and semantic role labeling. Further, they often struggle with the inherent ambiguity and complexity of natural language, particularly in dealing with variations in phrasing and sentence structure. Despite these advances, the performance of existing methods remains far from human-level, owing to the difficulty of accurately capturing the semantic relationships between words and mathematical operations. The shortcomings of existing approaches motivate the exploration of alternative frameworks capable of learning more robust and expressive representations directly from raw text. In this paper, we present a novel deep neural solver for math word problems that directly translates the problem text into a corresponding equation template using a recurrent neural network (RNN) model. Our approach eschews the extensive feature engineering common in previous statistical methods, instead learning task-specific representations from the data. The core idea is to encode the problem text into a distributed vector representation using an RNN, and then decode this representation into a sequence of symbols representing the equation template. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid model that combines the strengths of the RNN model with a similarity-based retrieval model. By retrieving similar problems from a large dataset and leveraging their solutions, the hybrid model can effectively handle novel and challenging instances. We demonstrate through extensive experiments on a large-scale MWP dataset that both the RNN model and the hybrid model significantly outperform state-of-the-art statistical learning methods, achieving substantial improvements in accuracy and robustness.

Estimating the prevalence of different classes within a collection of unlabeled data is a fundamental problem in machine learning with applications spanning diverse domains. From assessing public opinion on social media to estimating disease incidence rates from clinical records, accurate prevalence estimation provides critical insights. This task, often referred to as class prevalence estimation, differs from traditional supervised classification where labeled data is readily available. Instead, it requires inferring the proportion of instances belonging to each class solely from the unlabeled collection itself. Early approaches to prevalence estimation largely relied on techniques like expectation-maximization (EM) algorithms applied to latent class models (e.g., Bishop, 2006). However, the performance of these methods is heavily dependent on strong assumptions about the underlying data distribution, which are often violated in real-world scenarios. More recently, a prevalent paradigm has been to aggregate predictions from multiple discriminative classifiers, and then calibrate or adjust these predictions to obtain point estimates of prevalence (e.g., Bart et al., 2012; Chen & Guestrin, 2016). While these methods have shown promising empirical results, a crucial limitation remains: they typically fail to adequately quantify the  uncertainty  associated with the estimated prevalence. In many scientific and practical applications, providing a point estimate alone is insufficient. Knowing the range of plausible prevalence values—expressed, for example, through confidence intervals—is essential for sound decision-making and statistically valid inference. Simply calibrating classifier outputs rarely yields well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, as it doesn’t account for the inherent limitations and potential inaccuracies of the underlying classifiers. Imperfect classifier accuracy should naturally translate into uncertainty about the overall prevalence estimate. In this work, we address this critical gap by developing an uncertainty-aware framework for prevalence estimation. Our approach is grounded in a generative probabilistic modeling perspective, where we explicitly model the likelihood of observing the unlabeled data given different prevalence distributions. Crucially, we demonstrate that even an off-the-shelf discriminative classifier can be re-interpreted within a generative framework by “backing out” an implicit individual-level likelihood function. This allows us to perform fast and straightforward Bayesian inference at the group level, yielding not only prevalence estimates but also credible intervals that reflect the inherent uncertainty in our predictions. We empirically evaluate our approach on several datasets and demonstrate that it provides superior confidence interval coverage compared to a strong baseline method based on classifier aggregation. Furthermore, we show that our approach is remarkably robust to shifts in the class prior distributions between training and testing, a common challenge in real-world applications.

The interplay between power dynamics and linguistic behavior has long been a subject of study across disciplines, from sociology and psychology to communication and linguistics. A robust body of research demonstrates that power imbalances manifest in distinct patterns of language use, influencing everything from lexical choices and syntactic structures to conversational strategies and politeness markers. Critically, these patterns are not uniform; they are significantly shaped by social factors, and among the most salient of these is gender. Traditional sociolinguistic studies have posited that gender influences how individuals exercise and perceive power, leading to divergent communicative styles. For instance, research suggests that women are more likely to employ indirectness, hedges, and qualifiers in their speech – strategies categorized as “face-saving” – potentially reflecting societal expectations and constraints on assertive behavior. Conversely, men are often observed to utilize more direct and assertive language, aligning with culturally constructed norms of dominance and authority. While these observations have been extensively documented in spoken communication, the dynamics within written mediums, particularly large-scale digital interactions, remain comparatively underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by investigating the relationship between gender, power, and language use within the uniquely rich dataset of the Enron email corpus. This corpus, comprising over half a million emails from a large corporate environment, provides an unprecedented opportunity to analyze real-world communication patterns at scale and to examine how gender intersects with power structures within a professional context. We begin by presenting a significant contribution to the research community: a comprehensively annotated extension of the Enron corpus, reliably identifying the gender of senders for approximately 87% of all messages. This annotated corpus is publicly available, fostering further research into this critical area. Leveraging this resource, we test two specific hypotheses drawn from established sociolinguistic literature. First, we investigate whether women in managerial roles are predisposed to employ face-saving communicative strategies more frequently than their male counterparts. Second, we explore whether women utilize language more explicitly than men to establish and maintain social relationships within the workplace. Beyond examining the direct relationship between sender gender and linguistic features, we introduce a novel concept - the “gender environment” – to the computational study of written interactions. We define gender environment as the composition of an email thread (i.e., the gender distribution of all participants), and demonstrate that manifestations of power can vary considerably depending on this environmental context. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating gender information into the task of automatically predicting power dynamics between individuals engaging in email communication, showcasing the practical applications of our findings.

Human sentence processing is a remarkably efficient cognitive skill, yet it’s not without its challenges. While reading, people don’t simply absorb words in a linear fashion; they actively construct hierarchical representations of sentence structure (Frazier, 1987; Gibson, 2000). Understanding the cognitive mechanisms underlying this process is a central goal of psycholinguistic research, and a key component of this understanding lies in quantifying the incremental difficulty of parsing a sentence. This difficulty isn’t uniform; some sentence structures are easier to process than others, leading to variations in reading times and other behavioral measures. One approach to modeling these difficulties is through the development of  complexity metrics  – quantitative measures that attempt to predict processing load based on structural properties of the sentence. Early psycholinguistic models relied on relatively simple metrics like sentence length or the number of constituents (Miller & Kutas, 1963; Just & Carpenter, 1992). More recently, researchers have exploited the power of probabilistic parsing models to derive more nuanced metrics. Specifically,  surprisal  – the negative log probability assigned to a word given its preceding context – has emerged as a strong predictor of reading times (Levy, 2008). The intuition behind surprisal is that lower probabilities indicate more unexpected words, and therefore, greater processing effort. Chart-based parsers, which maintain a complete representation of all possible parse trees, are frequently used to calculate these probabilities. However, chart-based parsers are computationally expensive and don’t necessarily align with the incremental, memory-limited nature of human parsing. Hierarchical Hidden Markov Models (HHMMs) offer an appealing alternative. HHMMs utilize a bounded model of working memory, pursuing multiple, parallel hypotheses in an incremental fashion – mirroring aspects of human cognition (Roark et al., 2001; Hale, 2001). Recent advances in HHMM parsing have demonstrated competitive accuracy with chart-based techniques (Sutton & Andrew, 2003), suggesting they possess a powerful parsing capability. Despite this success, a crucial question remains: can HHMM parsers also generate valid complexity metrics to predict human processing difficulty? This paper explores this question, focusing on a right-corner HHMM parser. We aim to validate the ability of this parser to not only accurately parse sentences, but also to quantify the incremental difficulty a reader might experience. We define standard metrics like surprisal within the HHMM framework and, importantly, introduce a novel metric,  embedding difference . This new metric is rooted in the hypothesis that the internal states of the HHMM represent a form of syntactic working memory, and that differences in these states reflect the cognitive effort required to integrate new information into the current representation.

In an increasingly data-driven world, the collection, use, and sharing of personal information by websites and online services have become ubiquitous. Website privacy policies represent the primary mechanism by which companies inform users about their data practices, theoretically granting individuals agency over their personal information (Acquisti et al., 2016). However, a growing body of research demonstrates that these policies are often lengthy, complex, and, critically, rife with vagueness (Solove, 2013; McDonald & Cranor, 2008). This opaqueness hinders users’ ability to make informed decisions about their privacy and presents a significant challenge for regulators aiming to enforce compliance (Litman, 2013). The average internet user spends mere seconds reviewing a privacy policy, if they read it at all (Bawden & Robinson, 2009), and comprehension is frequently limited by legal jargon and intentionally ambiguous phrasing. The prevalence of vague language in privacy policies is not accidental. Companies may employ it to maintain flexibility in their data handling practices, avoid legal liabilities, or simply to conceal potentially unfavorable details (Cate, 2007). Terms like “may,” “reasonable,” “appropriate,” and “potentially” appear repeatedly, creating loopholes and ambiguities that leave users unsure of their rights and the extent to which their data is being exploited. This vagueness undermines the very purpose of a privacy policy – to provide clear and transparent information. Addressing this problem requires automated methods for identifying and flagging vague content within privacy policies. Manually reviewing these documents is a time-consuming and expensive undertaking, especially considering the vast number of policies published online. Existing work has begun to explore this space, focusing on aspects like policy readability (Reich et al., 2017) and the presence of potentially problematic clauses (Følstad & Brandtzæg, 2017). However, a dedicated and comprehensive approach to  automatic vagueness detection  remains a critical gap. In this paper, we take a significant step towards filling this gap.
